She: "Mr. Slow, are those two men that have just passed brothers ?" He.: " I—aw—know that one of them is; but rea—aw—not quite sure of the other." "Science enumerates 538 species of organic forms in the air we breathe." Just think of it! Every time you draw in a breath a whole zoological garden slips darn your wind- Vire- A physician says that the temperature of the water for a bath in winter should not be more than one hundred degrees, and the time of taking it should be not more than from three to five minutes. Idle people take the most pains.—Quarrelling dogs Corte limping home.—Ready money is the secret of economy.— Forbear and forgive as long as you live.—He who always complains will never be pitied.—A bridle for the tongue is a fine piece of harness.—Drive the nail that will go; let the obstinate alone. Six eases of inscriptions have arrived at the British Museum from Van. Amongst the objects which have been sent over ars two shields with concentric rows of animals, several architectural and other ornaments in bronze, some ivories of Assyrian style, an inlaid leaden tube, some in- ' scriptions, and paper impressions of others. Most of these objects belong to about B.C. 700. He afterwards mentioned the circumstance to abosom companion, and, in answer to the latter, who wished to know why he had joined the corps, he replied, "Wey, becaas an think they'll nivvor be caall'd oot, an' aa might get a lass, man, when as get the claes Maid of money: A young heiress.—You can tell dog wood by its bark.—How to save time: Let your watch run down.—Teachers of penmanship set things to write. Wry; rie well-known itutho'; tried this joke on once, and peremp- torily ordered of a wafter a sphinx dla Marengo. "I am sorry to say we have no more, monsieur," replied the g argon. The waiter lowered his voice, and murmured, in a confidential whisper, "We have some more, monsieur; but the truth is, I should not care to serve ihem to you, ad they are not quite fresh." Tnis TRNSODIENT OF INDIGESTION, OR -DYSPEPSIA.—The greatritecret js to take the moat easily,assimilable food, and at the same time to avoid overloading your stomach. Your food should be varied, but " selected for its digestibility. Three moderate mealfrh day ard; usually sufficient unless you are a very hard-worker, butt sometimes four are neces- sary. Meat should be eaten at least twice a day. Beef and Mutton, and game with the exception of hares and rabbits, are excellent; but pork and veal are very indigestible, and should be avoided. If you like chicken, or sweetbread, or triiie, take them by all mean's. You Must 'avoid. all _meats that have been hardened by_culieary art or by condiments, and all cured meat such as ham, tongue, sausages, and so forth. Ego, lit- they agree with you, are to be recom- mended., Fielr'isr not so good, but may be eaten in modera- tion. Oysters often agree :well, but differences in this respect are observed -.in different individuals, and some psople cannot take theist. Vegetables should be by no means excluded from your diet, but a certain amount of caution is requisite in their use. If they cause much flatulence, their , place !nay be aupplied.by-rice or macaroni, or by some kind of fruit, such as grapeit or strawberries, Or, better Still, stewed prunes. Your potafbeekhould always be well boiled, unless ' you like them fried or mashed, and they should not be new. 'Other kinds of Vegetables should always be fresh and care- fully cooked. Turnips, parsnips, carrots, and Jerusalem artichokes, may, perhaps, not agree with you; but you may take spinach, vegetable marrow, beet-root, and young peas and French beans, with perfect safety. All raw vegedbles, such as salads, cucumbers, and pickles, must be eschewed. Bread should not be eaten new. If you _cannot get on with the ordinary household bread, Sri' the aorated bread ;" it is very nice for a change„ although friss', people like it for a permanency.' If this does not do for you, you sill have to fall back on biecults or toast. Fresh butter you tray eat in , . moderation.—The Family Physician. ' THB Maw wit° Troxit.trength is like a tool, good for much or little as the handler is good fer much or little. The pen that with a hard day's work earns the clerk a few shil- lings might, in an artist's hand, produce fifty pounds with a , few scratches. People pay far less for what they see than ' they paYfor what is not semi. When they buy a book, they ' get more than paper and print ; when they pay thousands for a painting, they bay 'lr•few squire .feet of canvas, paint which may have cost a shilling or two stucco and gilding, and brains—with-which Opie and all'his fraternity mixed their colours. Those who have no brains become machines in the hands of those who have brains. The simple labourer plods on his way on- foot; but the , man of brains comes riding past, and_gives him a seat behind him. The farmer who gathers hia twenty or thirty men of a morning and sends them about various kidds of work, has been thinking for every one of them, and so lag saved each a certain amount of time and trouble. Brassey, in the course of a forenoon, thought and ivrote'enough to keep large armies of workmen steadily engaged for many days. Or look at Lon- don. The proverb has it, "All reads, lead to Rome ;" but trade snaps its fingers at that old-world saying; all roads Lead now-a-days to London. When Londoners speak of the , City, they mean a cluster of streets and buildings that mayl I easily be traversed from side to side in a few minutes. The City is iike the heart, or better say the brain, of the world. In that subdued, intense hum, you hear the world thinking. Nothing but thinking goes on here. No bales of cotton, no cheats of tea, no sacks of grain, no loads of timber, are to be found in the City—few workmen of any kind, only those who can think. These City men do most of the thinking for the great companies of the world —the railway com- panies in the far West, or in Russia, or in India; the sub- marine telegraph companies; the trading companies in North America, or in Africa, or on the Nile, or in China and Japan; the gas companies and the water companies in Bet- lin, or elsewhere ; the ocean steamship companies ; the mining companies; and hundreds of such schemes. Now, the world pays these men to think, and pays them better than , any others, because they really, do the most work and save 1 the most time—best exemplify the maximum of result with the minimum of labour.—Cassell's Family Magazine. _ _ .

THE EMANCIPATION OF MAN.—She looked just like that kind of woman when she came into the sanctum, and all the seniors became instinctively very busy and so absorbed in their work that they did not see her, which left the youngest man on the staff an easy prey, for he looked at the visitor with a little natural politeness, and was even soft enough to offer her a chair. "You are the editor ?" she said, in a deep.baas voice. He tried to say "Yes," so that she could hear, whilst his colleagues in the sanctum couldn't, but it was a failure, for the woman gave him dead away in a minute. "You are !" she shouted, "then listen to me. Look at me; what am I?" The foolish youngest man looked at her timidly, and veatured to say in a feeble voice that she looked about forty-ser "Am I not a woman ?" she said. The youngest man weakly tried to correct his former error, and said she looked more like a girl— But again she broke in on him with a scornful hiss, " Gir-r-1," she said, "I am a woman! A woman with all the heaven- born aspirations, the fathomless feelings, the aggressive courage, and the indomitable will of a woman. What can you see on my face ?" The position of the youngest man on the staff was pitiable, but none of the old heeds appeared to observe it, at least they didn't offer to help him out. So he looked at her face for a second, and said timidly, If " Nursling," she shrieked, " had you the soulful eyes of a free man you could see shining on my brow the rising light of a brighter day." "Could I?" asked the youngest man timidly. "Yes, you could I," the woman said in tones of unmeasurable scorn. "Now heat me, hare you a—but I cannot bring myself to use the hateful expres- sion in the style of masculine possession—are you anybody's husband?" The youngest man blushed bitterly, and said that he Wasn't as yet, but he had some hopes "knit you expect the woman whose husband you will be to support you?" The youngest man blushed more keenly than before, and tremblingly admitted that he had some expec- tations--that—that—that the only daughter of his pro- posed father-in-law, if he might put it that way— yah I" snarled the woman, now let use tell you, the day Of woman's emancipation is at hand. From hi time we are fete, ferree. Yon must look for oth slaves to bend and cringe before your majesties, and wait upon you like slaves. Yen will feel the change in your affairs since we have burst our chains, and how will you live without the aid of women? Who makes your shirts now ?" she added fiercely. The youngest man miserably said that a tailor in Jefferson-street made his. " Fl'm," said the woman, some- what disconcerted. "Well, who washes 'em then?" she asked triumphantly. "A Chinaman just west of Fifth-. street," the youngest man said with a hopeful look in his eyes. The ViOtnall glared at him and groaned under her breath ; but she came at him again with—" Proud worm, I who cooks your victuals ?" The youngest man said truly that he didn't know the name of the cook at his restaurant, but he was a man about forty years old, and round as a barrel, with whiskers like the stuffing of a sofa. 11-r, --oman looked as though she was going to strike him. Well," she said, aeons who was leading a forlorn hope, "who makes up your bed and takes care of your room ?" The youngest man replied with an air 'of truth and frankness that he roomed with a railway conductor, and an es-Pullman sleep- ing car porter took care of their room. She paused when she reached the door, and turned upon him with the face of a drowning man who is only five feet away from a life-buoy, " Miserable dependent," she cried, " who sews on your buttons ?" The youngest man on the staff rose to his feet with a proud, happy look on his face. "Haven't a sewed button on a single garment,". he cried, triumphantly, "patents every one of them, fastened on like copper rivets, and nothing but studs and collar buttons on my shirts. Haven't had a button sewed on for three years. Patent buttons last for years after the garments have gone to decay." And the woman flew down the winding passage and the labrynthine stairs with a hollow groan, while the other members of the staff, breaking through their heroic reserve,- clustered around the youngest man and congratulated him upon the emancipation of his sex:—.Burlington Ilawkeye. CO-OPERATITE Dernorawo sic ADIBBICA.—The City of Syracuse, in the State of New York,which with its environs contains a population of about 70,000, possesses a unique organisation for its milk supply. It is known as the Onon- daga County Milk Association, and was chartered and began business in the mouth of March, 1872. The stock is held by about fifty persons who were formerly milk producers and dealers acting independently, and it is apportioned at the rate of 20 dollars to each cow usually kept in milk by the holder ; the stock-book shows that the members own from seven to seventy cows each. The headquarters of the Association are in the city, where it owns and. occupies a large four-storey brick building provided with every accom- modation for receiving, keeping, handling, and distributing milk, for boarding and lodging the thirty or-more employes, and for general business purposes. The Association main- tains twenty milk routes,_with a waggon and pedlar upon each, supplying about 40,000 people through the year. The management is delegated to a president, vice-president, and nine directors, of whom five form the executive board, and the working force comprises a superintendent, cashier and accountant, milk-receiver, two distributing clerks, cheese- maker, hostler, blacksmith and helper, housekeeper and as- sistant, and twenty pedlars. The Association originated from a prosaic desire on the part of milk-producers to bene- fit themselves, and a belief that several persons who were selling milk in Syracuse, each one by himself, could econo- mise in labour and cost of delivery by co-operation. The object was to establish a central depot where the milk pro- duced by all could be received, thence distributed so far as it could be used as milk, and provision made for working the surplus into butter and cheese on joint account. The great saving expected was in the delivery to consumers; it was thought that instead of half-a-dozen waggons running daily through the same streets to furnish here and there a family, as occurred often under the old system, the cus- tomers might, by union of interests, be supplied from a single waggon. Next was the expected saving by advan- tageous use of the surplus milk; that of several pedlars being "pooled" or handled in one mass. Both of these ex- pectations have been so far realised as to give prosperity to the Association. The independent "owners" of milk routes at first looked with suspicion upon the concern but one by one have found it to their interest to join. The impression of a monopoly, likely to be at first formed, is not sustained by the facts, for the Association has opposition enough from individual sources to force it to keep up the quality of its milk and to keep down its prices, The result has really been to maintain in this city a high standard of quality and very reasonable rates.—" Dairy Fanning," by Professor

She-idO/L CATTLE FaNDING EXPERIMENT.—We have great pleasure in being ale to submit to the attention of our readers an interesting experiment made by Mr. John Treadwell, the late chairman of the Farmers' Club, to test whether decor- ticated cotton cake, malt, or a mixture of both, would be the best artificial food to give mulch cows feeding besides on hay-chaff and pulped mangels. On Dec. 3 the milk from eleven cows, which had up to then been fed on 41b. each of decorticated cotton cake, was weighed, and the evening meal found to be 1071 b. and the morning one 12311 b. The diet was then changed as regards the artificial food, 21b. of the saque cake and two pints of malt being given to every cow. On Dec. 9 another weighing took place, giving the result of 113 Alb. and 131±lbs. as the results of the two meals. Mr. Treadivell then gave four pints of malt Rel. VOW per day, and on Dec. 15 the same test was applied, with the result of 103 lb. and 122 lb. Mr. Treadwell also had the milk in each case analysed by the chemist of the Aylesbury Condensed Milk Company, and we have tabulated his state- ment below qf from cows fed on hay-thrt., and numgel pulp (A) 4Th. per cow cotton cake; (B) 218. cotton cake two pints malt; (C) four pints melt: Proportion of Water. Evening... 87.64 ... 12.36 3.02 Morning The ,cost of the cotton cake, railway frieght included, was about a per ton. The malt was from barley which had very much sprouted in harvesting, valued at 30s. per qr., to which must be added 55. per qr. the cost of malting it, when 20 qrs. of barley made 21 qrs. of malt. Making a calculation from these data, the cost of the latter would be three farthings and one-tenth of a farthing per pint, that of the cake three farthings and three-sevenths of a farthing. There would be a slight saving in cost by using malt, amounting to about 30. per day for the eleven cows, being a total outlay of 2s. 10d., against 3s. 10. when four pints per cow per day were used and no cake, and half that amount with half cake and half malt. The latter system of feeding seems by the above experiment to afford a better result than either all malt or all cotton cake, and we are not surprised that Mr. Treadwell has concluded to adopt it in future. The experiment was tried on a mixed lot of cows, some of which were forward in calf, and most of them drop- ping off their milk a little, and the produce from all cake being weighed nearly a fortnight before that from all malt would, be slightly favoured by that circumstance. We also much question whether such good results can be expecte& from malt made from barley which sprouted a good deal in harvesting, to that manufactured from sound barley. Mr.! Treadwell is not only employing malt for his milking cows,' but for other description of stock. In a letter to us he says —"I am using it for weaning calves and for all my fatten- ing sheep, the latter receiving about half a pint each in lieu of half a pound each of cake per day. They seem to do well on this with peas and roots. I also give my working horses one peck each per day."—Fanners' Chronicle.

div.head: MAKING.
div.p: MAKING.

The new year brings u-s-new-s-of -a departure in cheese and butter making wlaich will, if there be anything in it, cause a greater revolution in the dairy than anything in modern times. It comes from Germany, and consists of a new pro- Cess of making butter and cheese, by which, in the words of its inventor, "all labour is saved." Some time ago, Prof. Church told his students at the Wilts and Hants Agricul- tural College that if a quantity of cream wrapped in several folds of cloth was buried in the ground, at the end of 20 or 30 hours the water will be found to have left the cream, and the solid particles remaining will, when well washed, give a remarkably pure, well-flavoured butter. The weight of earth resting on the enveloped cream is the active 'agent in this change. Then, again, if milk is coagulated by means of rennet and the development of lactic acid, a mass of solid matter is found in the whey, and this, dried by pressure, gives cheese. These facts have been laid hold of by a Ger- man lady, who has followed them up by the contrivance of a machine " by which butter and cheese may be almost said to make themselves." We are very sorry to have to add to this charming description of this wonderful contrivance and that the accounts in the German papers deal more with the product itself than with the method by which it is produced. 411 WP are tOl4 1.4 that N 7 Madame Zieman's proaess in boater making the cream is put into clean linen bags, sur- Minded by two or three folds of coarse canvas. No pressure is employed for the first twelve hours, then weights are gradually applied in increased proportions until at the end of the second day the sack is opened and the pure butter is found free from all the butter-milk. The manufacture of cheese is conducted on the same plan, but the ultimate pres- sure must be greater. The produce is, on the authority of Dr. Petrie, a capital dairy authority, whom we met at the great Hamburgh Dairy Show three years ago, declared to be of first-rate quality, while in quantity 10 per cent, more butter and from 25 per cent. to 50 per cent, more cheese is made than by the ordi- nary method. The following is the analysis of butter as made in the ordinary way and by Madame Zieman's process : Ordinary Way. New Method. Water 15.07 _

100.00 100.00 From this it will be seen that the new system retains less water and more fat than by our present methods, and that also there is expelled no less than 1.24 per cent, of albumen. 'Phis latter is a grand point, inasmuch as, like all proteins compounds, it is very largely the cause of those changes which so quickly take place in butters, dic., on the slightest provocation by weather, A:c. This getting rid of albumen and lactic acid must have a good effect on the keeping quali- ties, while the larger proportion of fat is equally a good thing for quantity.-27te Farmer.

THE LIABILITY OF SCHOOL BOiIIDS.—An important ludgment bearing upon the liability of School Boards, was given on Saturday, by the Recorder of Hull. An action was brought against the School Board of Hull, and a pupil teacher in their service named Cherry to recover £290, damages for injuries sostained under peculiar circumstances. It was stated that Cherry was about to examine some writing done by a boy named Burrows, and while in the act of inflicting a blew upon a boy sitting close by, Cherry's pep fell from behind his ear into the left eye of Burrows, And completely destroyed the sight qt that eye. The Re- corder held that the ease came within the ordinary law affecting master and servant, and assessed the damages at &Of/ A verdict Was given for the plaintifflor that amount With costs. • • .JBBEBY DIDDLBB AT SOIITHPWIT.--41118.0, about thirty years of age, took accommodation on Friday at the Royal Hotel, Southport, but did pot sleep there that night., He, however, left a bag in his bedroom, which appeared to be well filled. On Saturday be was upstairs the best part of the morning, and came down, late to the table d'hete.• About an hour after dinner the under cook went upstrfirs to dress, when he discovered that his clothes, a watch, and other valuable articles had been stolen. He went and informed the head cook of the fact, and upon the latter going to his bedroom he discovered that his suit of clothes had also been taken, as well as his watch and other articles. Upon exa- mination it was found that other rooms had been entered. Inquiries were at once commenced, when it was ascertained that the "stranger" had taken away his bag, and left the hotel unobserved. He left behind him a brown paper parcel containing aa old pair of trousers, which would be of no use even to a rag gatherer, and two dirty shirts.

AFTAIRS IN SOUTH Arnice.—ln a letter of instructions which Sir Hercules Robinson has received from the Colonial Secretary on his departure to assume the government of the Cape, Lord Kimberley points out that the new Governor will execute the functions latterly exercised by Sir Bartle Frere, Sir G. Pomeroy-Colley remaining Governor of Natal and High Commissioner for South-eastern Africa. The proposal for a confederation is still approved, but it is deemed more convenient that any fresh movement should be initiated by the colonies. The recent occurrences in the Transvaal render it impossible to consider any arrangement for con- ferring free institutions on the Dutch settlers until the authority of the Crown has been vindicated. Referring to the Basuto war, Lord Kimberly says the late Governer was warned by his predecessor at the Colonial Office that the Cape Government must not look for assistance from Imperial troops. Instead of disarming the Fingoes and Basutos, it would have been better to form a native Fingo or Basuto yeomanry or militia. It will be the Governor's duty after the termination of the rebellion to use his influence on the side of leniency and moderation. Should it be resolved to confiscate any territory, the Governor is advised not to do so by proclamation, but to reserve it for the Queen's sanction. Shouid the Colonial Government after all be compelled to ask for Imperial troops, the revision of the system of self- government combined with self-defence, which has broken down, and the conditions under whfch native territories now ontrolled by the Cape Government are administered, might become unavoidable. Lord Kimberley urges the necessity of not extending the present boundaries of Her Majesty's possessions.

THE F acr ow atti treads nApNoni tlhVeOHnlio SPeScAreCtari7y, apco Hr tEasn tOlv deputation Anit on Saturday, to complain of defects in the administration of the Acts relating to the inspection of factories and work- shops, and to request the appointment if additional inspec- tors. Mr.llenry Broadhurst, M.P., read a memorial setting forth the desirability of increased inspeetors in order to Garry out the Act in a much more efficient manner than it WaS possible to be done 'with the present staff. There were daily violations of the Act taking place in almost every in- dustry to which the Act applied. Women and children were employed beyond the prescribed hours the places in which they worked were greatly neglected, and the Act was almost a dead letter. The memorialists did not complain of the present staff of inspectors, except that they were not suffi- cient in number to carry out the provisions of the Act; and the deputation urged that an additional number should be appointed. The most effectual way of securing the obser- vance of the law would be the appointment of a number of practical workmen to be engaged as assistants to the present staff of inspectors and sub-inspectors. But for the fear of being dismissed, many of the workmen would, when they observed an infringement of the Act, report it to the inspectors. At present they feared making reports of what they observed contrary to the law. Sir W. Harcourt said the question was full of diffculty. The Department desired to prevent the danger of the Acts being regarded with hostility by either masters or operatives. It was said that the greatest offenders against the Act were the small em- ployers; but a constant and perpetual system of domiciliary visits to the houses of small men would create,great annoy- ance and vexation. The great majority of the people ob- served the law, and what was required was to get at the minority who broke the law; and the question was, how was it to be dono ? Was it by the appointment of a great army of inspectors who should be perpetually interfering with the men who did not infringe the law, or by adopting some means to get at those who broke the law? The second was of the best course, and he suggested to the representatives not the great organisations before him whether they could receive complaints of infringements of the Act and report them to the proper quarter. They would then lee attended .to, and the fear of the dismissal of workmen wmild be ob- viated. As to the multiplication of inspectors, take care to ascertain the facts of the case as to the propor- tion of the inspectors to the work to be done. The recom- meadation that tho artisan class should be represeoted among the inspectors had Mr. Gladstone's concurrence and hie own. The right hen. gentlemen promised the most care- ful attention to the suggestions that bad been made by the deputation. One penny each allowed for Efartley's e nply 215. jars."

THE Cirs.u.nridan Won—Steady progress is being made in the investigation of the deep-sea deposits dredged up by. the Challenger Expedition. M. Renard. has established himself at Edinburgh, where in concert with Mr. J. Murray he is busily engaged in subjecting the various dredgings to chemical and microscopic analysis. In the first volume, devoted to an account of the bottom of the Ocean, will be gathered together the , facts amaseed'ildring this laborious study. It will avoid all speculation, but will contain such a body of data for the aplication of the sendinientation and chemistry of the ocean abysses as hid-never before been available. INSECTS' EyEs.—g we examine the head of a wasp or bee, we find on' the top of the head, looking toward the sky, three eyes set in a triangle,. These eyes are eimple,anfinot unlike the eyes of other creature& ;but besides these, on the side of the head, stretching almost from its crown to the javri.Theneath, are two compound eyes, which; iliTdecths miereecope, are seen to present hiliumerable six-sided spWs, Which look like the ends of the cells of a honeycomb. On dissection, each of the six-sided faces is found to be the outer surface of a double convex lens,behind which is a layer of black paint, which is comparatively thick at the edges of the lens, but thin towards the centre where a hole is left through its middle. This hole is the pupil. Behind the pigment is a cone of transparent. Matter, whose point is directed inwards, and embracing thie point isThe end of a nerve thread. The threads from eich eyelet run inwards to a sheet of nervous matter common to the whole eye, and from this `sheet other neive cords, but much fewer in num- ber than the first, ran to the'fnain thick optic nerve. The space between the nerve cords is filled up with black paint, so that each can only receive impression from its end. An insect, therefore, one would think, receiVes thousands of dis- tinCt pictures;; bar whether it so harmonises them in its common retina as-to be conscious of only one, as we are though we have two eyes, must remain a secret. The simple eyes of insects seem to be used for distant objects for if these be painted over with red sealing-wax dissolved in strong spirit, so as to blind them, the insect has no power Of directing its flight, bet towers' straight upward towards the sky. The curious compound eye' must be used, therefore, for near objects, and as they stretch round the head and look every way, they must save the, insect much trouble in turning the head as it runs in and out the bells and tubes of flowers searching for honey and pollen. Lob- sters and crabs, belonging to another order of the jointed animals, have similar eyes, but they are set on a two-jointed dem, and the Webs are square and not six-sided.—Cassele's Popular Educator. . THE EFFECT OF -nen on Itrenors.—Simple muscular Contractions indicative of fear are witnessed in larvss, pups, and perfect insects, and may result !rem touch, sight, or hearing. Caterpillars and other larvie when touched will contract or convolute into a ball; puple, when complete with flexible rings, as the chrysalides of Lepidoptera, wriggle the segments. :Many beetles on touch turn lethargic, fond- -14 'contracting legs and antennas; often into grooves of various depths, possibly habitually acquired. This is char- acteristic of the Pill Beetles (Byrrhus), and the families Rhyncophora, Coprinidie, and Coccinellidie, as of the more elegant kinds of Elateridie. The latter, familiarly termed " skipjacks?7 turning on their backs, escape when the paroxysm is past by leaping high in the air. Some contract their legs and depress their heads .either slightly, as species of Necrophaga and Malacoderma, or reeelve them int* grooves, as the weevile. The male &lime of a red and blue Clerus, frequenting Umbelliferss, appeared to me time affected, while his female sought to escape. some lemelli- corn beetles, in lieu Of contracting their legs, rigidly extend- ing them, as the common dung beetle, project the first pair and draw up the hinder as its congener Sy/vatieus, or Indif- ferently contract and extend them as the rose beetles. The active ground beetles, again, only partially recede them on I alarm; crouching down or squatting like rabbits and part- I ridges. The stag beetles, when arrested at twilight on a pathway, stand motionless as if paralysed, gaping with their mandibles, and when seized, fall theatrically on their backs. The bugs and many neuroptera on touch similarly contract their limbs; the latter, with many moths, retaining their I wings also stiff and motionless. Among the bees, the shin- ing red and blue chrysalididzei often noticed on brick walls, I involute their abdomens as wood-lice on seizure; but the bumbles and others turn on their backs, Whine, and extend the four hindee legs like a -tat on 'the defensive. These spasmodic symptoms not uncommonly result from sight and hearing. Bees also raise ,their legs and larvae jerk their heads when light is intercepted. A dark trailing cloud.' shadow passing over a colony of the orange-ringed cater- 1 pillars of the rag-weed (Callinorpha Jacobea) causes quite a I Sensation of wig-wagging while it lasts. I likewise remem- ber once, on approaching to pill-box a very minute vernal I beetle near London seeing its liras yield, when down it came, like d dust-Egot, ere I could reach it. It muet have seen my shadow! Species of other orders, the smaller moths especially, thus elude the ardent collector among herbs and grasses.—lnsect Variety: Its Propagation and Distribution. By A. H. Swinton. ELECTRIC PERFORATION OF Guss.—lf I snared the Popular belief concerning the making of fortunes by means Of patents,. I should, rush to the. Great Beal Office with a Provisional specification for &sae— sieves, and window glass ventilating window-panes, the sieves being -made of pierced with thousands of small hoick through which cor- rosive liquids might be strained, and other sifting processes e conducted. The ven- tilating extreme cleanliness .b similarly perforated a at tilating window-pane,should be , oth air might stream gently through it without .any blast or draft, and without the outside ugliness that limits the use of perforated. zinc for ventilating purposes. But the drill- ing of small holes in glass is apparently a tedious and costly b ' - process. It was so really at one time, but is not so any longer. Forty years ago, plates of glass were perforated by sparks from the Leyden jar. If the spark were passed directly upon a clean surface, the glass was liable to be shattered; but by covering it with oil the perforation was clear and without star. In those days it was necessary to do much laborious turning of the electrical machine in order to charge a jar with sufficient intensity and obtain the requisite spark. Now, by means of, the Rumkorff coil we may obtain, without any such effort, Volleys of sparks, fol- lowing each other faster than we can count them. By simply burying one of the terminal wires in a plate of ebonite, allowing its point to project just beyond the sur- face, and moving this over one side of a sheet of glass of I suitable' thickness, smeared with olive oil, each spark may, be made to punch a small hole through the glass. Very simple machinery might be devised for moving the surface of ebonite regularly over that of the glass, and thus Tsßul lating the distances and arrangement of the perforations automatically. I have used perforated zinc very success- fully for ventilation, by merely taking out 'a pane of glass from a skylight or upper part of a window and substituting the zinc. This, for the outlet of air. For inlet, a pert orated zinc plate was substituted for one of the lower wooden Pa el ds as of the -door. By these means a moderate-sized room was made ~available for the meetings of a small class, ev room was intolerable before; for, when the doors and ti i l when win- dows were closed, the atmosphere was suffocating, and opened, those who sat near„to the entering blast became shivering rheurnatised martyrs. In like manner, theatre was ventilated by substituting alarfli_l)ate of per- forated zinc for the- glass skylight, and lower openings, all of which were similarly panelled with while , perforated zinc plates. But these w wh ere very. ugly ble the perforated glass would be unobjectio, provided'theee / ah's Magazine. holes can be made large enough.—Gentm e

The porter, for which London has become so distinguished, WAR first intro- duced about the year 1750. Previous to that time the malt liquors in general use were ale, beer, and two-penny ; or eise a pint, or tankard, of three threads, meaning a third, of ale, beer, and two-penny. Then the publican was obliged to draw from three casks to serve one customer. To avoid this trouble and waste a brewer, whose name was Harwood, con- ceived the idea of making a liquor which should partake of the united flavours of ale, beer, and two-penny; this he called eutire, or entirebutt beer, meaning that it was drawn entirely fromone cask or butt. It was soon discovered to be suitable for porters and other working people, whence it de- rived its name of porter. • M. A.,ltuncorn.

div.head: 260.-RIMEDY FOR BOILS.
div.p: 260.-RIMEDY FOR BOILS.

"The Family Physician," in Cassell's Magazine, gives the following as the best remedy for beils:—" Sulphide of cal- cium, undoubtedly. A tenth of a grain should be taken hourly, or every two or three hours, or Pr. 78 maybe em- ployed. It lessens the inflammation, and reduces the area of the boil. Moreover, it liquefies the core, no that it separates mere speedily, and the troublesome little visitor is induced to take its departure. When the skin is not yet broken, and the slowly separating core not exposed, this medicine often converts the boil into a little abscess, Which seOn bursts, and the whole thing is over. If the sulphide is taken sufficiently early, the boil often dries up, the inflammation stffisides, and a hard knot is left, which disappears in a few days without the formation of a core, and without any discharge. The sulphide exerts a marked influence on the general health, removing the debility and malaise so frequently associated with these eruptions. Not only will the sulphide of cal- cium, taken in the manner we have indicated, cure existing boils, but it will often prevent the formation of fresh ones." J. HABRIS, St. Helene.

div.head: ELECTION COMMISSIONS CHESTER.
div.p: THE ELECTION COMMISSIONS CHESTER.

The Chester Bribery Commissioners met on Saturday in London. It was intimated by the Chief Commissioner that a large sum of money, which had not been accounted for, was in the hands of some one in Chester. Lord Richard Grosvenor, M.P., the Liberal "Whip," was exanuned. He denied that he had provided any money for the election at Chester, and was authorised to make the same statement on behalf of his brother the Duke of Westminster. The witness explained that an offer which he had made to Mr. Moss, the Liberal expenses agent, to provide £5OO was made after the election, and was solely intended to reimburse Mr. MOSS his own private losses, if there should be any. Mr. Moss was afraid that he would have to repay a sum of £9OO, and he went to the witness at the Treasury to ask his assistance. The £5OO was never required. GLOUCESTER.

This inquiry terminated- on Monday. The Chief Com- missioner thanked the authorities for the assistance they bad rendered, and said the guilty portion of the constituency was at least entitled to the merit of candour, for it did not appear that there was any city in which corrupt practices had taken place where upon the arrival of the Commissioners the people, both of the richer and poorer classes who had been concerned in bribery, had been so frank and so honest in telling the whole story about their misdeeds. Seveial men admitted getting bribes varying from £2 to 55., and the court then adjourned sine die.—The inquiry lasted 27 days, and during that period nearly 3,000 witnesses were examined. The number of witnesses who admitted receiving bribes was nearly 2,000. MACCLESFIELD. After an adjournment from the 23rd December, the Macclesfield Elestion Commissioners, Messrs. Mereweather, Q.C. (president), A. C: Meysey Thompson, and J. Short, resumed the inquiry on Monday. There were 120 witnesses on Monday's list, the majority of whom were examined. A publican named Crawford, it was stated, received 18s. from the Liberals and 7s. 61. from the Conservatives for his vote. A canvasser named Cotterill said he had to turn his back on many voters, because they would not go without being paid, and added," Your people will not vote bout mosey; they're good for nowt." Witness said he took 12 voters to the poll, but could not give their names.—The President said since he had been in Macclesfield he had not heard of 12 voters going to poll without inducement, and witness must give names.—The Court then adjourned. At this inquiry on Wednesday several canvassers admitted having been put "on the book" in order to secure their vote. One canvasser said all he did was to "look pleasant" by the side of another canvasser. Another canvasser said all he did for his 15s. was to "walk about with the others." John Wordem a silk manufacturer, said he was paid by the Librals as a dayman. He received 55., and was told to "wait near the Britannia Inn, and walk about." He ran up a bill of about £2 in treating. On two Liberal canvassers being called, the President complained that the Liberal can- vass books were not forthcoming. The consequence was that great delay and expense to the town was caused. A Liberal canvasser who was reticent as to names was told that he would have to attend every day until he gave them. The inquiry was again adjortrfied.

div.head: AN INTERNATIONAL EXECUTIVE.- DIJLCIGNO.
div.p: AN INTERNATIONAL EXECUTIVE.- DIJLCIGNO.

It may be profitable that the recent actian of the united fleet of the Allied Powers of Europe, in reference to the ap- plication of a joint threat to coerce Turkey into the cession of Dulcigno to the Montenegrins, should be studied by the friends of peace from their own point of view. For it is one of the most striking illustrations yet afforded of the diffi- culty of enforcing the decision of an International Tribunal against a nation reluctant to accept such a decision; inas- much as the Treaty of Berlin, with its accompanying and consequent "European Concert," was, in a certain sense, a Court of International Law, and One furnished, moreover, with a joint armed force for the purpose of carrying its de- crees into accomplishment. One of its decrees requested Turkey to surrender the port of Dulcigno to the Montene- grin nation. This step Turkey was exceedingly reluctant to take, and, in the face of united Europe, she succeeded in delaying compliance for about two years. Nor was it until the combined fleets had been for months in front of Dul- cigno and were about to proceed to active hostilities, that the Ottoman Government finally conceded the demand of the Berlin Treaty on this one point. There has been a tendency in some quartsrs, even amongst persons sincerely favourable to peace, to regard this result with much satisfaction, ae furnishing, to their minds, a practical illustration of what they would desire to see accomplished on a more general and permanent scale, namely, the adjustment of all international difficulties by means of a representative Court of Delegates or Ambassadors, whose decisions should be enforced on any recalcitrant Power, by means of the joint armies or navies of the nations forming the great central Court of Decision. A similar course has also, for many years, been advocated by occasional writers in favour of an International Tribunal, as regarded from a point of view not limited to the princi- ples of the Peace Society in reference to the objectionable character of any appeal to arms even for the maintenance of peace. But this Dulcigno experience of the Powers, when really examined in all its bearings, and regarded not in a mere scperficial aspect, but comprehensively, is a note- worthy confirmation of the very basis adopted by the Peace Society, namely, that even the decisions of an International Tribunal should rely for their execution on moral power rather than physical force. For while it is true that the vigorous manifestation of force actually succeeded in this particular instance of Dulcigno, there were many cirdutnstances which proved the great peril and grave disadvantages of such a mode of procedure. In the first place, even although the point at issue was the surrender of a single obscure town, by one of the weakest of Governments, yet that Government, exhausted and im- poverished to the very verge of collapse, was nevertheless able, by delays and one pretext after another, to baffle the threats of the United Powers for a period of two years. And it was only by the utmost tact and skill on the part of several of the allies, and of the British Government in par- ticular, that the European Concert was maintained in active union till Dulcigno was surrendered. Many other circum- stances either connected with, or suggested by, the late I action of the European Concert, show the extremely doubt- ful and perilous policy of resorting to armed force even for carrying out the decisions of an International Tribunal. If United Europe, relying ultimately on armed influence, took 1 two years to extort the insignificant town of Dulcigno from weak, wretched, moribund Turkey, what shall be said, henceforth, of the practical value of physical force as the final basis of International Law? Ear mightier is the real power of moral influence, as in the case of the carrying out of the decision of the Alabama Tribunal at Geneva. What would then have been the power, or the .results, of any attempt at coercion on a mighty Empire like Great Britain? But the quiet appeal of the public opinion of the world backing up the legal and reasonable demand of the tribunal, found a response in the national conscience and innate sense of dignity of Great Britain, and a prompt and honourable compliance with the decision of the Tribunal, unpleasant though it was, ensued. Similarly, also, in the previous case of the surrender, by the United States, to Great Britain, of the Confederate Ambassadors, Mason and Siddell, in 1881, this result was not aided, but imperilled, by threats of war on the part of England. It was conceded by the wisdom of the American Government, as influenced by the peaceful moral influence and friendly remonstrances of the represen- tatives, at Washington, of some of the other European nations. Here, also, moral influence proved a greater force than arms. And henceforth in looking to a more frequent recourse to International Tribunals for the adjustment of international differences, we must also look not to physical but to moral power as the more potent lind successful (though perhaps not universallyattainable) means for giving effect to their decisions.

FRANCE. The general result of the communal elections throdoouP.l France is declared to be in favour of the Moderate itepnb=l lican party. In Paris nrost of the outgoing councillors were re-elected, including the five Conservative members. Three' more Conservatives have also been returned. No member of the Commune or any other person who has been amnestied has IJ...en elected.

The French revenue returns for the past year show an increase in nearly all the sources of revenue, and this, it is reasonably held, shows an augmenting faith in the present institutions of the country. The Russian budget shows a deficit ef 5,4 millions of roubles, and this is not intended to be covered at present. The military budget shows an in- crease of 12 millions, in consequence of the enhanced price of all kinds if provisions and stores. The Finance Minister of Portugal in his general budget of revenue and expendi- ture for the financial year shows a considerable deficit, which, however, is less than that of last year, and the re- ceipts show a small increase,

div.head: AMERICA.
div.p: AMERICA.

NEW YORE, Jan. of the World's Fair have finally adopted Inwood Hall as the site for the ex- hibition building. The invitation to the American Rifle Association to com- pete in July next with a team representing Great Britain and Ireland has been declined.

div.head: TUE WAR IN THE TRANSVAAL.
div.p: TUE WAR IN THE TRANSVAAL.

A report was 'received at Durban on Friday to the effect that the small detachment of troops in the Potchefstroom camp had been compelled to surrender. It is stated that the Boers under arms now amount to 10,000 men, and that the number is being continually augmented. The force which massacred the detachment of the 94th was 1,500 strong, and it is not said that any casualty was sustained on their side —a sufficient proof of the statement that the 94th men were practically unarmed and defenceless. Sir George Colley reports to the War Office, from Pieter- rnaritzburgh, that the:Naval Brigade and two guns marched from the place on Sunday to meet the Boers. The General left for Newcastle on Monday. The Natal mounted police have been driven back by the Boers to within a few yards of Newcastle. Officers from South Africa who arrived in this country on Monday regret the withdrawal of tbe Dragoon Guards from the Transvaal, and state that the Boers can put into the field 10,000 men, all of whom are excellently armed. . _ . .

According to a Standard telegram of the 7th inst., the Boers made a determined attack upon Wakkerstroom, but were repulsed by the British garrison of that place. The Boers have retired from the neighbourhood of Newcastle, and have recrossed the border into the Transvaal. A military party of Boers chased a party of fifteen sportsmen,including two officers, who were out buckhunting, and killed Ave of them.

A Daily News Cape Town telegram of Monday says : The Boers have occupied Zurust, in the west of the Trans- vaal. It is reported that they entered the Baratong country, but were repulsed by the chief. The counsul in London for the Orange Free State has re- ceived the following telegram from the President, of the State, dated Bloemfontein, January 7th 1881 :—" Don't be- lieve the malicious fabrications about the Dutch. Free State only wishes peace and prosperity for the whole of South Africa, and fervently hopes that every effort will be made without the lea.t delay to prevent further blood- shed." _ _

A ckspatch was received, on Wednesday, at the War Office, confirming the report of the withdrawal of the Boers beyond Buffalo, and stating that the attack on Wakkerstroom was feeble and was easily repulsed. hiformation has reached Pietermaritkburg of the finding of Cie body of Captain Elliott in the Orange Free State, and the report that there were five wonnds on it is confirmed. An estimate which comes limn Durban states that 7,000 Boers were under arms of whom 2,000 are serving through fear. In Basutoland the colonial forces are capturing large quantities of cattle without casualties. DEFEAT OF THE BASUTOS. CAPE Towle, Jan. o.—Colonel Carrington's picquefs were attacked on January 6th by a large number of Basutos. After a severe engagement, the enemy fell back with heavy less. The casualties on the side of the Colonial forces were only trifling. The Government has received news from Potchefstroom to the let inst. The garrison had repulsed an attack in which the Boers had used "an old ship's gun," which was quickly silenced." There were stares in the fort for a month. THE GREEK QUESTION. The Diritto, of Rome, publishes a very warlike speech which was made by the Greek Premier to the French charge d' Afaires, who had strongly urged him in the name of his Government to accept the proposed arbitration. M. Con- moundouros said that Greece could not draw back from the position she had assumed. She was the faithful executor of the will of the Powers, and retrogression from the decisions of the Berlin Conference would produce confusion in the kingdon. There was no value in arbitration, because it was certain that Turkey would never voluntarily , grant the cession of Epirus and Thessaly. "It therefore became a painful but Inevitable necessity," said the Premier," to ap- peal to arms." In Paris it is said that warlike action on the part of Greece will be regarded as entirely absolving France from any further action on behalf of Greece. A report was current in Athens on Monday that the King had signed a decree calling out the reserves, but it was promptly declared to be unfounded.

Several Paris newspapers attribute the warlike speech et' Greek Premier, which was telegraphed on Sunday, to an earlier stage of the negotiations. A Times telegram from Athens, of Sunday's date; announces that the military pre- parations are being carried out most actively. Another squadron of cavalry has been formed. On the 15th of January King George intends reviewing the troops -nustered in Athens, numbering 13,000 men. "A great sensation has been created hear," says the telegram, "by the news that the Turkish press advises the Sublime Porte to interrupt the relations with Greece by sending away the Greek Minister from Constantinople and all the Greek subjects from the Ottoman Empitt." It is mentioned that this measure has been recommended to the Porte by fanatical Turkish journals. The Greek question has not entered upon any new phase. The newspapers at Athens concur in regarding the arbitra- tion proposal as virtually dead, but at Constantinople the subject is still debated in the Turkish fashion. A despatch from the Times correspondent says that the Council has no fewer then four proposals heroic it. The first is that the field of arbitration should be narrowed in such a way that Turkey should not run the risk of losing Janina, Metzovo, or Larissa. The second is that the present diplomatic efforts of the Powers should be continued until some compromise be found which Turkey and Greece could accept. Thirdly, it has been suggested that the Powers should be again required to facilitate the re-opening of direct negotiations with Greece; and, fourthly, there is the idea that there might be a new Conference in which Turkey and Greece should both be represented. None of these methods, it will be seen, are new; they have been repeatedly discussed of late, and with regard to the first it has been declared repeat- edly at Athens that the cession of Janina to the Greeks is an essential point. The Porte is still unable to discover a way out of its pressing financial difficulties, and it is stated that the Admiralty "has the utmost difficulty in obtaining even the most paltry sums for the indispensable items of expenditure.' In brief, the Sultan cannot pay for coal to fill up the bunkers of his ironclads. TURKEY. Further Ministerial changes were on Wednesday hourly expected at Constantinople. The ex-Minister Hussein Pasha is accused of having tried to secure undue perafinal influence among the military party, and though not actually under arrest he is narrowly watched. Raouf Pasha, the governor of Adrianople, haft been summoned to Constanti- nople. At Vienna the nomination of Osman Pasha as Minister of War is regarded as a triumph of the war party. Hobart Pasha has been appointed to the Presidency of the Admiralty Board, which givesihim supreme control over the fleet. The Ambassadors are about to take fresh collective steps in favour of the arbitration project. It is believed that they will support the initiative of France in recommending the Greek Government to accept arbitration. A statement comes from Berlin that no German officer will obtain leave to enter the Turkish service so long as any danger exists of a war between Turkey and Greece. ALARMING NEWS FROM INDIA. A CONSPIRACY TO MASSACRE EUROPEANS. The Bombay Gazett a publishes a very serious report from Kolapore of a conspiracy to massacre the European popula- tion, depose the Rajah, and raise the standard of revolt. Both Ilindoos and Mussulmans are said to be implicated in the plot and 27 persons are now on their trial on the charge of "levying war against the Empress." It is now stated that the first report of the conspiracy at Kolapore, exaggerated the extent though not the nature of the outbreak. It is evident, however, that there is a con- siderable amount of disloyalty latent among the Maliratta population, though no leader of mark is engaged in the revolt. A telegram from Calcutta, of Wednesday's date, states that no information of the existence of a conspiracy has reached the Indian Government. The story of the conspiracy to depose the Rajah of lade- pore and murder the European inhabitants while in church is contradicted. A despatch from the private secretary to the Governor of Bombay states that there has been no such movement either at Kolapore or elsewhere in the presidency of Bombay, and suggests that the report had its origin in the arrest several months ago, of a Dacoit who attempted to give a political complexion to a mere gang robbery. THE WAR BETWEEN CHILI AND PERU. The Chilian force operating against Lima on the land side has gained an important advantage. The Peruvians had occupied a strong defensive position at Lurin, a few miles southward, of the capital, but the Chilians, fighting with the same ardour which they displayed at Arica and other towns, assailed the position and carried it at the point of the bayonet. The fleet co-operates with the army by keeping up a bombardment of the tuts in Callao harbour. It is probable that in a short time we may hear of the in- vestment of Lima. DESPERATE FIGHT BETWEEN RUSSIANS AND TURCOMANS. The Russians admit that they are encountering a very strenuous resistance at Geok Tape. General Scobeleff has opened regular siege works against the fortress, and on the morning of the 4th instant the Turcomans made a desperate attack. The fighting was" of the most desperate and san- guinary character," and the Russians lost a general and three majors, whilst about 70 officers and men were

div.head: STATE OF IRELAND.
div.p: THE STATE OF IRELAND.

'ATTER FROM TIM Pops. An important Pontificial utterance on the condition of Ireland is contained in a letter from the Pope to the Catholic Archbishop of Dublin. The Pope expresses his confidence in the justice of the men who are placed at the head of the State, and points out that Ireland may obtain what she wants much more safely and readily if only she adopts a course which the law allows, and avoids giving cause of offence. His Holiness counsels the episcopate to direct their efforts to the end that the people in Ireland do not transgress the bounds of equity and justice. The Archbishop in sending forth the letter to his clergy gives them advice of his own. He hopes that the wisdom of Parliament may satisfy the legitimate demands of the Irish people without violating the rights of justice, and he is unwilling to give credence to the rumours in cir- culation that the Government scheme for the settlement of land question will be but a half-hearted attempt to grapple With the evil. A sufficiently drastic remedy is suggested in ene of the Archbishop's closing sentences, which runs as follows :—" Health and security can never be restored un- less the cancer which has been eating away the life of the nation be cut oat to its last fibre." The Cork Land League on Saturday investigated a case between landlord and tenant, and the proceedings were of a remarkable character. Two brothers, who were the land- lords, appeared before the League, and they were asked if they consented to that body arbitrating in the matter. One of the brothers replied that the members of the League had taken Cie matter Into their own hands, and he merely at- tended in order that the public might form a judgment on the facts. He charged the League with prejudice in inves- tigating the matter. After a scene of violence the landlords withdrew, and the League resolved that the case was one of hardship, and requested the landlords to make some abate- ment to the tenant. The members of the Loughrea Land League declared that Mr. Mitchell-Henry no longer represents the feelings of the people of the county of Galway, calls upon the hon. mem- ber to retire from the representation. Later in the evening a party assembled on the fair green, and amidst groans for Mr. Mitchell-Henry and the Government burned a portrait of the member for Galway. At a magisterial inquiry held in West Cork a Roman Catholic priest said that the local police administration had failed to prevent the commission of atrocious outrages in the district, and an idea was held by the people that the police were the authors of these offences. He suggested that the Government should have an inquiry made as to the ground for such suspicion. The magistrates and the sub-inspector of police approved of the suggestion, and a memorial on the subject is to De sent to the Lord Lieu- tenant. The Council of tlaeßallinasloebranch of the Land League have passed resolutions in which they call upon Mr. Mitchell Heory to resign his seat as member for county Galway, and denounce the " hon. gentleman's accusations against the League as " foul and malignant falsehoods." NEW YORE, Jan. Ilth.—Mr. Redpath has delivered another violent lecture on the Irish question, in which he virulently denounced the Irish landlords. The Rochester branch of the Land League has sent a total of 3,800 dollars to Ireland. _

About four o'clock on Tuesday morning a mail cart running between Limerick and Tralee was plundered of its contents by a party of armed men. The driver was not in- jured. No arrests have been made. The Lord Lieutenant of Ireland has commuted the capital sentence passed Cal Bernard Nolan at Armagh for the mur- der of Michael Boylan, at Crossmaghen, to one of penal ser- vitude for life. At the weekly meeting of the Land League on Wednes- day Mr. Egan, hon. treasurer, announced that this week the I League had received for organising purposes the sum of I £2,986. The League had also received for the defence fund £1,074. This brought the total receipts for the wek to £4,180. Mr. M‘Gough, who represented a deputation of com- mercial travellers presented amidst applause a subscription of £l2O from that body. He said that in giving this subscription to the Parnell Defence Fund the commercial travellers 'of Ireland bore their testimony to the efficiency of the action of the Land League in promoting the prosperity of the country. As to what had been said about outrages aud the disturbed state of the country, he (Mr. McGough) had been on the road for 30 years, and he could bear testi- mony to the unusual peacefulness that prevailed at present. —Mr. Clancy, another commercial traveller, said that the 120 subscribers to this £l2O represented 120 business houses, who drew together an incomeof about £12,000,000 a year from Ireland, and that was anything but an evidence of capital being frightened out of Ireland. AGRARIAN OUTRAGES IN IRELAND IN 1830.—A Parlia• mentary return was issued on Wednesday, giving particu- lars of outrages reported to the Royal Irish Constabulary Office from 1844 to 1880 inclusive. The number of agrarian outrages reported last year was 2,590, the figures for each month being as follows :—January 114, February 97, March 83, April 67, May 88, June 99, July 84, August 103, Sep- tember 168, October 269, November 561, and December

On Wednesday morning a force of 100 constabulary pro- ceeded to assist process servers on Lord Granard's estate at Drumlish and Ballonamuck, county Longford. Over 3,000 perains assembled, armed with scythes, dic., and surrounded the h0u525, placing women in front, One of the process servers narrowly escaped with his life. The magistrate, Mr. Rogers, in order to avoid bloodshed, withdrew his men, and a larger foe will be sent. a STATE TRIALS.

• At the Land League- trial in Dublin on Monday, further evidence was given as to the language used by Mr. Sexton, M.P., and other of the traversers at meetings in different parts of the country; and an attempt was made to connect them with the publication of certain placards, manifestoes, and more especially with the notorious " Pandeen O'Rafferty's Ten Commandments," of which a large number of copies were printed at the instance of the League Execu- tive. An unexpected announcement made by Mr. Serjeant Heron, one -of the leading counsel for the Crown, in the course of the day that the case for the prosecution would probably close on Tue.day was received with considerable satisfaction. The trial was again adjourned. No evidence of special interest was given on Tuesday. Several shorthand writers were examined, but the facts elicited, as to speeches made by the traversers at land meet- ings, were very similar to those previously recorded. Before the Court adjourned the Attorney General intimated that, with the exception of one witness who was then on his way to Dublin, the case for the prosecution was ended. The leading counsel for the traversers, Mr. M'Donogh, Q.C., being unable to attend the Court through illness, the learned Judges consented to an adjournment until Thursday. In the Lar.d League trial at Dublin, on Thursday, Mr: M‘Donogh, the leading counsel for the traversers, opened the defence in a speech of some hours' duration. The crime of conspiracy, he contended, could not justly be imputed to the traversess, for that which they had done had been done openly, its object being to resist oppression and benefit the Irish people. As for the remarkable utterances of Mr. Nally, he ridiculed the idea of their being regarded seriously, that gentleman being notoriously "one who thought more of a pretty lass and a glass of whisky toddy than he did of the British Constitution." The indictment of Mr. Parnell and his colleagues was nothing more than an Irish landlords' indictment against the tenant farmers of Ireland. He indignantly repudiated the charge that the traverser!' had preached "contention, con- fiscation, and communism," and, as to Boycotting, it was practised under various names—as " black-balling " and "sending to coventry "—in every grade of society. He argued that the crime alleged to have taken place had for its cause the excessive misery of the Irish people, and not the action of the Land League, an organisation which, Started as a means of relieving distress, afterwards aimed at a permanent amelioration of the tenant farmers' condition by constitutional and lawful means. It had done that which the Land Act of 1870 aimed at but failed of accomplishing —it had practically put a stay to evictions. At the close of the learned gentleman's speech the Court adjeamed.

MR. GLADSTONR AND IDS TENANTRY.—The rent audit of the Hawarden estate took place on Tuesday, at the Glyn Arms Hotel, Hawarden, when captain Vickers announced that a communication had been received from Mr. Glad- stone to the effect that a remission of 10 per cent. would be made on the half-year's rent to all the tenants on the estate. The grounds upon which the reduction is made as that the season of 1550 has not been so satisfactory as to recoup the formers for their severe losses in the extremely bad season of 1879. This half-yearly reduction of 10 per cent. follows upon a reduction of 15 per cent, made at each of the two pre- ceding half-yearly rent audits. THE ANNEXATION OF THE TRANSVAAL.—Mr. COURTNEY, amid some laughter and ironical cheering, said, in reply to Mr. O'Donnell, that he had no present intention of 'stinging in a motion condemning the annexation of the Transvaal. He had so often stated his opinions on the subject that the House was already in full possession of them. Several private members had notices on the subject, and he trusted that no diffidence on the part of Mr. O'Donnell would prevent him from adding to the list if he thought proper. THE LICENSING Laws.—The PREMIER informed Sir Wil- frid Lawson that there was no likelihood of the Government bringing in a Bill this Session dealing with the licensing laws. TURIEY AND GREECE.—Mr. GLADSTONE was not able to add to Sir H. Drummond Wolff's information with respect to the relations of Turkey and Greece beyond the statement made in the Queen's Speech. THE DEBATE ON THE ADDRESS.—In a full and attentive House Mr. Suety resumed the debate on Mr. Pamell's amendment to the Address. In a speech of great modera- tion he speaking for the large number of the Irish people, said they were not entirely satisfied with what was going to be done on the land queedon. The Speech from the Throne might mean anything, "But the Speech from the Treasury Bench the other night does not," he added, amid'some cheer- ing from below the gangway on the Ministerial side," mean what we want." These cheers were renewed and taken up all over the Ministerial benches when Mr. Shaw added, "I have not yet given up my belief in the Prime Minister." He believed that the Bill, when its clauses were mad- known, would be found to be not so bad as was feared. But he would say that it would be better not, to touch the ques- tion at all than to touch and not settle it. As a practical contribution towards such settlement, he threw out the suggestion that there should be established a tribunal which should fix the rent as between landlord and tenants.—Lord RANT:imam Crrcncrutt, who on rising was loudly cheered by Sir H. Drummond Wolff, offered some remarks on the situaiion. Lord Randolph had discerned "a simmering on the benches opposite," which led 'him to the conclusion that if a division were taken on the question of coercion, the Ministerial Whips would fail to recognise in the lobby the faces of some of their most ardent supporters. If there had been a few more murders, or if Mr. Gladstone had only had the good fortune to bring about an armed rising in Ireland, he might have counted on the support of iittled found L i breerda le e tptoanr t yin. tAh es eiotniwtoarst, t hLaotrd supportßandforloptnh Cthheurcuhn other quarters placed the passing of the Bill beyond con- troversy. A little later in his speech he departed from these general terms, and announced that for himself and his friends near him they would support the Government in the endeavour to deliver them from the fanaticism of hon. gen- tlemen below the gangway. This delicate reference to the party of whom the noble lord is one of four leaders, was re- ceived with loud and general laughter.—Mr. CHARLES RUSSELL, as being strongly opposed to coercion, declared hi intention of voting for Mr. Parnell's amendment, and spoke distrustfully of the Labd Bill. An observation to the effect that the Land Bill, as sketched by Mr. Gladstone, bore on its face marks of compromise intended to cover differences of opinion in the Cabinet was a proposition that seemed to amuse the Premier, who was an attentive listener.—The debate was continued by The O'Donoghne, Mr. Bradlaugh, Mr. Fitzpatrick, Captain O'Shea, and Mr. Litton, who made a strong appeal to Mr. Gladstone to go beyond the indication already furnished of the objects of the Bill. The appeal was joined in by Mr. Richardson, another Ulster Liberal.--Mr. THOROLD ROGERS, speaking after 11 o'clock, when the House had refilled, called forth some laughter and ironical cheering from the Opposition by his emphatic denunciation of Sir Stafford Northcote's alliterate phrase (" force, fraud, and folly ") as the wickedest and foolishest words he had ever heard.—Mr. PLIINKET, in an occasioaally eloquent speech, described the addresses of Mr. Shaw and Mr. Russell as an attempt to "Boycott the Whigs." Their remarks were addressed, not to the resolution before the House, but to an attempt to force the hand of the Government on the land question. Mr. Pluaket's announcement of his inten- tion to vote for the Coercion Bill and to give the most candid consideration to the Land Bill was hailed with ironical cheers by his fellow-countrymen below the gang- way. The right hon. gentleman, in illustration of Mr. Par- nell's popular plan of campaign, very effectively quoted the passage from Shakespeare in which Jack Cade tells his fol- lowers that under his regime seven halfpenny loaves shall be sold for a penny, that every three-hooped can shall have seven hoops, and that it shall be made felony to drink small beer.—On the motion of Mr. MITCHELL HENRY, the debate was at ten minutes past twelve, adjourned. was, IN THE NAVY.—Mr. TRETELYIN brought in a Bill for the abolition of flogging in the navy, and the other orders disposed of, the House adjourned at half-past twelve. HOUSE OF LORDS—TUESDAY. ANSWER TO THE ADDRESS.—The answer to the Address to the Speech from the Throne was brought in. DISORDER IN lints:Nes—Lord DUNSANY moved for series of returns illustrative of the disorder in Ireland.— Earl SPENCER declined to grant the returns, on the ground that before the information could be collected the session would be over.—Their lordships adjourned at six o'clock. HOUSE OF COMMONS-TUESDAY. Sir WILFRID LAWSON gave notice that on the earliest possible day he will submit a resolution calling upon the• House to put into action the resolution in favour or Local Option agreed to on the 28th of June last. QUESTIONS..—There were comparatively few questions on the paper, and those related chiefly to Ireland. In accor- dance with the understanding arrived at last session, by which the obviously useless custom of reading out printed questions which are in every one's hands was tabooed, mem- bers as a rule are content to refer to the number of their question when putting to the Minister. Some of the Irish members, however, perceiving in the breach of this custom an opportunity of prolonging the preliminary proceeding, insist upon reading their questions —Mr. SAXTON taki9g this course last night with respect to a long question relating to "the head master of the Parsonatown Model School," the House made a remarkable and ingenious demonstration against the deliberately vexatious proceeding by refitting papers, so that the hon gentleman was not heard. Never- theless he occupied the full measure of time, apparently reading out the question. THE WAR IN TETE TRANSVAAL.—In reply to Mr. Serjeant Simon, Mr. GRANT DUFF was understood to admit the ac- curacy of a telegram published in the Daily News yesterday, which stated that the Boers had advanced to Zeerust, in the west of the Transvaal; and also to confirm the report of the receipt of the friendly telegram from the President of the Orange Free State. But the right hon. gentleman was so indistinctly heard that this version of what he might have said is not put forward with confidence. A "SCENE "—A question from Mr. Biggar, addressed to the Prime Minister, with reference to certain witnesses at the State trial in dublin, led to a scene.—Mr. Gladstone pointed out the unusual character of the question, as dealing with proceedings in a court of law still pending ; and was not sure that the departure from custom was better or worse because Mr. Biggar was personally interested.—Mr. 1310GaR not being satisfied with the answer, rose again and promised to" conclude with a motion," an undertaking received with loud cries of disapprobation from the House. An appeal from Mr. Pease to the Chair brought out the fresh fact that on the previous day Mr. Biggar had taken his question in the usual way to the clerk at the table, and had been ad- vised that it could not be put. He had then communicated directly with Mr. Gladstone, and gone 'beyond the Speaker's authority by putting the question. This disclosure drew forth a fresh storm of indignation, in which Mr. Biggar stood unabashed, calling out amid the lulls, "Mr. Speaker, Sir." At length he sat down, promising, amid some laugh- ter, to recur the question when the Estimates were brought forward.

I wish to make one remark more, if you will forgive me. It is in defence of the Guardians and in defence of the Relief Committee of the Widnes district, over which I have the honour to preside. We are told on all hands that we are spending the ratepayers' mo,ley. These gentlemen, who simply look for their amusement to the reports of the pros ccedings in the newspapars, little know what the committeeS have to contend with. In Widnes we are payinv an average of £3O a week in relieving families, the heads of which are temporarily disabled, and employed at these works. We have had cases this morning (and nearly at every fortnightly meeting) of this eort,and one of my brother Guardians tells me that 4f only the normal poor were considered his own I rates would relieve these poor people. What is the result? ,The employers of labour who have brought these men, and who enrich themselves by their labour, do not do hilt they ought to do. If they did what they o-aght to do in times of -sickness they won.d help the men, and not send them to the Board of Guardians. (Hear, hear.) £3O a week, gentle. men ! Barnacle; Messrs. Meadows, Gerrard, Buckley, Ranson, Swift, Paris, Dobell, Kenwright, Lowe, Leatherbarrow, Syder, and Tyrer. THE PROPOSED NEW CHAPRL. At a meeting of the Building Committee, heldon the 6th January, the Clerk produced a letter from Messrs. Weeks and Hughes, architects, asking for plans of existing drain- age at workhouse, to be informed of the proposed site of new schools, and other information. Resolved that Messrs. Weeks and Hughes complete plans of schools as if they were to be erected on land connected with the workhoftse, and that they have access to the general and other plans of , the workhouse. It was understood that if the Clerk received ' the plans completed before Thursday next he would convene a meeting of the committee for that day at 10 a.m. The Rev. Mr. Chambers introduced the question of the erection of a new chapel, and submitted a plan prepared by a local architect of a proposed chapel in the district of St. Helens. Upon the motion et the Rev. T. Chambers, seconded by Mr. Leatherbarrow, it was resolved to recommend that Mr. Gandy, architect, St. Helens, be requested to prepare plans if terms can be arranged. The CHAIRMAN : Can any of you gentlemen interested in the chapel say whereabouts this building has to be placed. Rev. T. CHAMBERS: The chapel must be made as easily accessible as possible. That would be a question to be raised and spoken of afterwards. I have a plan g me by Mr. Pigot of a mission church about to be erehcn- tits St. Thomas's parish, St. Helens, to hold 400 people cost is estimated at people, and t given to to he L 1,079. I would ask the peron of the Board to facilitate matters by not advertism plans, but for 4 , but simply ask Mr. Gandy to reduce the quantity from 00 to 200, and the cost of course would be reduced only in lthing y e propor- tion. £7OO will cover the whole thing. I' want to know is whether tha proPesed chapel in St Helens is to built of brick or iron. Mr. BUCKLEY : I think it is to be builtteon, I h of brick. Rev. T. CHAMBERS :that this matter be pushed forward as speedily Oh, very well, a h s. possible. I don't see why we are bound to Messrs. Weeks and Hughes as architects. Mr. RANSON : I should like to know whether the chapel 18 to be one to be used by both Protestants and Catholics; or are there going to be two chapels? Rev. T. CHAMBERS: I this r. Ransom, it was clearly NI laid down in what I said to the Board that it was to be one chapel, for the use of both Protestants and Catholics. Mr. RAN.9•OI: I quite understood that. Rev. T. CH.4.10311113: But I do not think Mr. Fidler .aid anything to the contrary. I would suggest that we have a commodious vestry with two closets—one for holding the requisites of the Protestants, and the other for the Catholics. This could be easily done, and we could have the altar draped to snit both Protestants and Roman Catholics. We could work together very nicely, but to have two chapels would be going into a different sort of action. I took very great care myself to write to the Walton Workhouse, and the same system is carried on there very harmoniously. If this was decided upon there should be a vestry large enough with two &olds to hold the vestments of Protestants and
