The. question of dealing with a strons hand with I corrupt practices at elections, which' Hr., Watkin I Williams, who has recently been raised to the judicial bench, brought before the House of Commons last session, has been taken in hand by the Government; and the Attorney-General has subraitted.to Parliament a most comprehensive and stringent measure for preventing a repetition of the disgraceful practices which the inquiries of Election Commissioners have in several cities and boroughs brought to light. When the Ballot Act was adopted it was confidently believed that it wOuld not onli be a protection to.voters in the discharge of their electoral privileges, and put a atop to that rowdyism which was formerly the 'associate of a parliamentary contest, but that it would stem bribery and corruption. It was felt that as the voting would take tame in secret, strong political partizans, who had only too often purchased the votes of electors by money and beer, would be chary in running the risk of being cheated at the ballot box by those whose lack of integrity and manliness made them a prey to bribes. But the disclosures in the courts of the Election Commissioners have gone to prove that in Many constituencies bribery has been carried on wholesale, the dispensers of bribes preferring to sun the risk of being "sold" in the polling booth to miss- ing the chance of their corrupt practices securing votes for their party candidates. The evidence adduced at. the Election Inquiries has demonstrated that the party "wire puller." *ho have engaged in this risk have not been far wrong in their calculations. It is true that there are voters who have accepted bribes from one party and Voted for the opposition candidate, and that there are others who have taken bribes from both political parties and then voted for the candidates ivith whose political views they seriously coincided with; but the majority of the bribees have been true to their promises to those for whose wealth and beer they engaged to sell their birthrights to. 'Every honest politi- cian must agree: with us that it is high time some stringent steps were taken to strip our representative system of such baneful associations, by making the law governing elections a terror to evil doers of what- ever social degree or status. The bill introduced by Sir Henry James, the Attorney-General, is calculated to do this. Its provisions are undoubtedly of a most stringent character; but where the disease it a malignant one strong remedies are required. The scheme which the Attorney General unfolded to 1 the House of Commons, in the early hours of Satur- day morning, strikes at nearly all the oorruptions which have fastened themselves upon our represen- tative system, the imperfections of which, notwith- standing our boasting of its excellence, have come to be recognised and unfavourably commented upon by foreigners whom we have regarded as living under leas satisfactory institutions. Sir Henry James in pointing out that the absurdly extravagant and lavish expenditure which pervades the great majority of elections throughout the country compels men of great mental capacity and of political worth to yield places of honour to men of less mental calibre and energy, but possessing longer purses, put a weapon into the hands of those who agitate for the payment of representatives, and we doubt not they will make 1190 of it in the future. This lavish expenditure, as the Attorney General observed, calls into existence a set of people who, without political enthusiasm or convictions, regard an election only as the means of making so much money, and natarally throw their weight and exertions on that side from which they are likely to receive the highest payment. This is, as he re- marked, the worst kind of political strength, and an effort ought to be made to substitute for it the volun- tary efforts of men honestly moved by political con- viction to exert themselves in order that their views may be carried into effect. To prevent extravagant expenditure, which gives birth to corrupt practices, the Bill proposes, with certain exceptions, to abolish the present system of employment during Parliamentary contests. The excertions are one election agent, who are to be brought into existence for an important purpose, one personation agent in every pollling sta- tion, and one clerk and one messenger—who are not to be electors—for every polling district in counties and for every soo electors in boroughs. The bill also pro- hibits within like areas the use of more committee- rooms than one, which is not to be in a licensed house. It also prohibits any payments -for the conveyance of voters to the poll, both in counties and boroughs. Other expenses, such as payments for exhibiting bills or the use of boards, are likewise prohibited. To avoid the doors of corruption being opened by any ingenious devices on the part of election agents in the shape of providing " employment" for voters in large numbers to carry out any party scheme which the Bill does not specifically prohibt, it is pro- posed that the limit of expenditure for all purposes shall be fixed in a schedule, such expenditure graduating according to the size of the con- stituency; and that no cmtract or payment shall be made except by the election agent. Every claim must be sent in to him within ZO days after the return; every payment made within 40 days.; and a detailed statement of inch payments must within 60 days be published and sent in to the returning officer. This return must also state the amount received by the agent and from whom it has been received. The Bill also makes it an illegal practice for anyone to pay or provide any money for the election except to the election agent. The statement of expenses and receipts so made must be accompanied by a declara- tion made before a justice, and on which perjury can be assigned, by the candidate or his agent, stating that no payments have been made or moneys received beyond those shown in the return, and that no further payments will be made. Any breach of these provi- sions amounts to an illegal practice, and the seat is vacated ,thereby. There are saving clauses, which give protection to persons prevented by unavoidable causes from complying with the provisions just described. As distinct from acts which the Bill prohibits as illegal, there are provisions for dealing with corrupt practices, and some stringent regulations affecting petitions. Should the Bill become law it will be a misdemeanour to enter into any agreement whereby for money, or for the vacating of a seat or for other consideration, a petition is to be withdrawn. The representative of the Publics Prosecutor is to be present at the trial of every election petition. If there is sufficient evidence of a person having been g uilty of a corrupt practice, the representative of the Public Prosecutor is to summon him before the Judge, who is to try him summarily and have power to sentence him to six months' imprisonment. The accused, however, may elect to be tried by a jury, in which case the trial will take place at the Central Criminal Court, and so avoid the partisanship of the locality. Hard labour is added to imprisonment, and and in cases of corrupt treating or of keeping open house and supplying liquor without payment, whether to voters or non-voters, the licensed victualler is liable to have his license suspended for two years. A pub- lican will, therefore, be bound to receive payment for all liquors he sells at election times, and will not be permitted to chalk up "drink shots" to Mi. Anybody who may arrange to see to his bill being liquidated when the contest has ended. Another alteration pro- posed is that whilst a voter is now entitled to vote after he has been proved guilty of corrupt practices he shall bode prived of electoral privileges for 10 years. A collision occurred on the Nantyglo railway, on Wednes- day, between a mineral train and some trucks. A fireman was killed and the drivers of the trains were injured. The serving of processes on Lord Granard's estate in county Longford was carried out on Thursday. The Riot Act was read, and the police force of 350 men is said to have driven back the crowd with bayonets.

• FIRE AT WIDNES RAILWAY STITIOR.—Aperat Dive o'clock on Saturday morning, a fire °courted at the London and North-Western Railway Company's station at Widnee. A pointsman at the station first found out that a small wooden hut on the east end of the down platform was in flames. Hetave an alarm, which was responded to by a number of Messrs. (hakell and Deacon's men, who put out the fire. It was with difficulty that it was prevented from spreading to the main portion- of the station premises. Damage to the amount of about £lO was done. The cause of the fire is unknown.

Miss Airy Dor Ix Rtowonzr.—Miss Amy Dot, sister of Tom Thumb, gave two entertainments in the Public Hall, Runcorn, on Monday and Tuesday evenings. The young lady is stated to be a native of New York, 15 years old, and only 26 inches in height. She was very well received by the audiences, which were very fair as regards nuMbers, and her humorous observations caused much amusement. Captain Austin (under whose management the entertainment is) is a very good ventriloquist and a fair conjuror, and his contributions to the proceedings were much applauded. Miss Annie Wynne, another of the company, is a ballad vocalist of considerable power. A number of presents were distributed amongst the audiences.

HALTON MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY.-011 Monday evening, the Rev. J. Nowell read a paper to the members on "Mental Culture." The Rev. J. Bateman (I)resident) occu- pied the chair. The paper has been previously printed in The Examiner, therefore most people of this district know of the valuable hints and instructions contained in it as to the cultivation of the mind. The essayist said there was as 'great danger in overstocking the mind with knowledge as there was in eating too' much food. So much time should iv set aside each day to mental Cultivation and strictly observed; notice should be taken. of the old saying," What is worth doing at all is worth doing well." The following gen- tlemen spoke :,--Messrs. A. E. Davies, S. Barrow, T. Miller, R. Hughes. The rev. gentleman was heartily thanked by many of the members for hie valuable information and in- struction. Theli-Wir a—goOd ittendane-e.---Com. MILL-Bnow Rump &nom, Ruscom.=-In.connec- tion with the• Sanday school attached to Holy Trinity Church, which is held each Sunday morning and afternoon in the Board School, Mill-brow, a tea party was given to the scholars, to the number of 130, and several of the atten- dants at the mission services held on Sunday evenings in the same building, last Friday week, in the Trinity schoolroom. The management of the proceedings fell on Mr. Rogerson, who ably carried them out. After tea, addresses were given by the Revs. W. Preston and W. Robinson; and readings by Messrs. Rogerson, Hankinson, and Dawson. A portion of rthe Trinity Church- choir, under Mr. Ravenseroft, enlivened the proceedings with singing, accompanied by the harmo- nium. The evening was brought to a close by all present singing, "Onward, Christian soldiers," and the pronouncing of the benediction.

CAPTURE OF ALLEGED FOWL STEALERS AT RUNCORN.._ I At the Runcorn Police Court yesterday, before Mr. Charles Reynolds; George Haves, and Joseph illayes, 18, and 20 years of age, respectively, were charged with breaking into a cote and stealing four hens, the propedy of Mr. Thomas Horsetail, cashier to the firm of Messrs. Occleston and Son, tanners, on the night of the 14th inst. Sergeant Handford stated that in consequence of a number of robberies of fowl having taken place in the neighbourhood, he was sent to watch in Irwell lane. He afterwards went, as the result of what, he saw, to the house were the prisoners live. He found they had four hens in their possession; two of which they had killed and were plucking. On taking the men in custody, they made no reply.—Mr. Horsefall was called and he said he could identify the fowl as those formerly in his possession.—The prisoners were remanded until Monday.

WIDNES PAR= CHUB= ENTERWIMENTS. The eighth of these popular entertainments was given in the schoolroom, Waterloo-road, on Monday evening. The Vicar presided, and there was a large audience. The entertain- ment was entirely musical. Three glees," May Day," "The laughing chorus," and "Auld Lang Syne," were given by the Widnes Glee Class, under the leadership of Mr. Imison. These were well received, especially" The laughing chorus," which was provocative of considerable merriment. Two in- strumental performances, "The blue bells of Scotland "and "Grand march," were decidedly features in the evening's entertainment. These were given by three young gentle- men from St. Helens, Master Alfred Gardner, violin; Master George Gardner, flute; and Master Harry Gardner, violon- cello. The selections chosen were capitally executed, and the young instrumentalists gained the warmly expressed admiration of the audience. Mr. T. Davies, in his two songs "What an Englishman is made of," and "Moods and Tenses," was encored, as were Messrs. C. and J. Pownall in their et "All's well." A similar compliment nas awarded Miss Jane Gardner, of St. Helens, for the rendering of "Merrily, merriiy, over the snow "and "The lover and the bird." This young lady also gave a pianoforte solo, "Ivy green," with much taste. Mr. Charles Pownall met with a good reception in his song "Annie dear, good-bye." The "Death of Nelson," by Mr. John Pownall, was well re- ceived, as was Mr. Holt's rendering of "Give me the man of honest heart.' The Chairman having thanked the ladies and gentlemen taking part in the entertainment, the pro- ceedings terminated with the singing of the National Anthem. , WIDNES SIINFEWILD AND ItIIDLAND UOMMITTEE'S WORE- YEN'S ANNUAL onnem—The annual dinner took place on Saturday evening, at the Central Hotel, Widnes. Mr. I. S. Patten, the station master, occupied' the chair, and Mr. VV. Holt the vice chair. The loyal and patriotic toasts were proposed by the Chairman and Vice-chairmaw.—Mr. Wat- son gave "The Sheffield and Midland Committee," and re- marked that it was scarcely necessary for him to make any lengthened ebservations on the subject, as the toast was one which would at once commend itself to their notice. He was glad to be able to state that the company were doing an extensive and rapidly developing business in Widnes, and this in the face of the existence of a very powerful com- petition in the shape of one of the oldest railway companies Mwr.ll'iatwtean. n —The Chairman, in responding. said the workmen of the drunk with cwoiathritrmy.usicaille choounpoluerds, wthiteh name etooafst, tne company had to thank the several manufacturers it Widnes for the capital dinner with which they had been provided that evening, in one of the leading, if not the leading hotel in the place. He was always glad to sees good muster at their dinner. In conclusion, he proposed "The town and trade of Widnes."—Mr. Haney acknowledged the toast, and dwelt briefly upon the advantages which had in many cases accrued to the tradesmen of Widnes from the Sheffield and Midland embracing the district within their operations. He was of opinion that the trade of the town was gradually improving, and that they had left behind them the extreme wV hi Coem-t h he ei r nahaand g ha ao,oen" Ts ohrieushienarletdh os of int he e Clshaiorrm ain6, dulness characteristic of business some 18 months ago—The "y we airtsh. - He paid a high compliment to Mr. Patten's business ability, tact, and courtesy. The toast was drunk with musical hononrs.—The Chairman said their first annual 'dinner took place,s9me four or five years ago • and year by year the number of those in the employ of die company appeared to increase. Might their motto still be "Forward."—Several other toasts were drunk, including "The press." During the evening the following contributed to the nonviviality by songs .&c.:—Messrs. J. Walters (Penketh), John Lea, James Burke, H. Moss, W. H. Davis, J. Russell, the Vice- chairman, Williams, Upward Graham, Nugent, and Rolphe.

CAPTURE OF A GANG OF ALLEGED LEAD STEALERS.— At Widnes Police Court, on Thursday, before Mr. F. Gossage Julia Tobin, Mary Tobin, Mary Ann Kenna, Ellen Hunt, and Mary Clarke, all women, were charged with stealing 2k cwt. of lead, value Ll. 145., the property of Messrs. T. Snape and Co., of the Phcenix Alkali Works.—Paul Kerley, marine store dealer, Cholmondley-street, was charged with receiving the lead, knowing it to have been stolen:; and he was defended by Mr. Swift, jun.—A foreman at the works, named James Hunt, said the lead produced in court had been stolen from Messrs. Snape's. On the sth instant he saw the prisocers Kenna and Julia Tobin, at about eleven o'clock in the forenoon, near the works, with sacks in their possession, and on running towards them, they made cif. He found the sacks to contain lead, which had been stolen from the premises; it belonged to a cistern in course of re- pair.—P.C. Clarkson stated that on the previous day, in company with Sergeant Eastham, he went to the shop occupied by Kerley, and they asked him if he bad bought any lead that day, and he said " No," and added that he bad none upon his premises. He offered to let them search, and whilst he and 'Kerley were doing so upstairs, the sergeant shouted him to go into the cellar. He went there, and saw that Eastham had discovered about 4i cwt. of lead in a dad; corner under the stairs. They examined the book kept by, the prisoner, in accordance with the Act of Parliament, but they could not find any entry of lead having been bought, for above a week. He {witness) next apprehended Mary , Clarke, and charged her with stealing the liad then pro- duced in court.—She answered that she sold a little of it, but had no hand in stealing it. At the time he charged Clarke, the prisoners Hunt and Kenna were present. Hunt said she never sold any or took any away; but that Clark and Kenna sold it. On the way to the police station, Hunt made an observation to the effect that "she ate some of the lead" (meaning, it is supposed, that she partook of what was bought with the proceeds).—P.C. Pitt apprehended Kenna, and, in answer to the charge said she took none of, the lead.—On the application of the Inspector, the magis- trates remanded the prisoners until Saturday.—Mr. Swift applied that hall might be granted to his client, but the application was not granted. div.p: TOWN TAM,

The meetings of Board of Guardians are often the scenes of what are, in the language of the populace, designated "storms in teapots ; " for one of these has within the last few days taken place at the Runcorn Board. It is only fair to say that, as a rule, the members of this public body are not given to making therriselves conspicuous by their extraor- dinary discussions, but they generally pursue the even tenor of their way like good men and true. Their usual calm has not been broken in upon by any strange vagaries on the part of some of their officials; and I can only express the hope that no careless reader—one apt to take things fqr granted will think I.am speaking of. another similar assembly across the water, who have for some time past been making themselves famous. Neither has the almost lake-like still- ness of the proceedings of the Runcorn Board been disturbed by Mark Twain's "friend the tramp." The wow was not owing to another Oliver Twist asking for "more," and hav- ing had his future fortune predicted by, some modern Bumble; nor to the revelations of another "Amateur ; Casual." Nothing of the kind.. The storm has arisen owing 'to a pony having eaten some potatoes!' The reader my feel . incredulous but what I say is nevertheless a fact. Most of us who have reached manhood remember how the great 'Sepoy mutiny was caused by greased cartridges; and how the floating of various plants on the bosom of the Atlantic caused the famous Genoese to consider the possibility of the existence of a continent beyond that mysterious and unexplored sea. lam not, however, going to write anything after the style of Jules Verne's "Mysterious Island," but deal with the doings of the Workhouse pony, which will, I suppose, be famous in future history. A pertain worthy Mr. Lowe—l am sorry I have not the gentleman's acquaintance—has dis- covered the hidden mystery as to the potatees,and all honour to his name. Mr. Lowe is apparently of an inquisitive dis- position, and he does not like anything to pass before' him around which there is any mystery. Eleeis as big a foe to what he cannbt understand as the most advanced naturalist. It seems this worthy man happened to go, to a late Board meeting a little earlier than seine of the other Guardians— probably on the principle that the early bird catches the worm—and there was a slight possibility of his finding a key to certain mysteries that had haunted the chambers of his active brain for the previous few days. He was "putting his horse up,"—there is nothing of the proud man about Mr. Lowe—and he saw one of the Workl,onse men taking a feel to the master's pony. Probably being pretty well posted' on Biblical subjects, he had in his mind the beautiful cup ,by which Joseph divined, which was found in the sack of one of his brethren—amongst the corn. He found no cup, but he discovered what ex- cited his wonder almost as much—a number of potatoes. He appealed to one of the old members of the Board— Mr. Thomas Norman—apparently thinking that gentleman would be able to give him some explanation, but my worldly wise friend- "Told him net to make such a noise about it, as he had had some potatoes as well as the pony." Here was another mystery which Mr. Lowe was as anxious to ffnd out .as Edgar Allan Poe was to know of the raven sitting on the bust of Pallas, whether "within the distant Aidenn he should ever clasp a sainted maiden, named by the angels, Lenore." Cautiously proceeding with his en- quiries, he discovered that the members of the Assessment Committee were provided with a capital dinner on the quiet, and he poor soul was not even allowed a potatoe like the pony. Against, this treatment he loudly protested at the last Board meeting, on the ground that he had come eight or ten miles in order to get to the workhouse. The awful conduct of the quadruped given to eating potatoes—probably as fond of them as a native of the green isle—was carefully investigated ; but, on considering the evidence, there appears to have been false swearing in the "court " on the part of some one. Mr. Jones, the master of the house, stoutly maintained that what my hero thought were potatoes were only peelings. Now it is hardly to be supposed that a gentleman with such strong powers of observation and knowledge of the world as Mr. Lowe, would not know the difference between a pots- toe and its peeling. The beloved partner of Mr. Jones is said iv Mr. Lowe to have admitted that potatoes had been boiled. A man was questioned, who said there were two and a half potatoes; a woman who graphically describes them as "two and a handful," (which is very like the say- ing "as large as a piece of chalk), and the chair- man (Canon Barclay) appears to have said that the people called before them "all agreed that there were a little over two potatoes." The last definition would be a some- what puzzling sum, even if expressed as an algebraic quan- tity. What is "a little over two ?" That "little" might be a great deal in the mind of Mr. Lowe. Then Mr. Norman charged that gentleman with having come up to him chok- ing with rage, looking perfectly wild, "even wilder than he looked then, and that was bad enough ;" white with excite- ment, and shouting "I have found it." It is quite evident to me that Mr. Lowe is a well read man, and he he was thinking of "Eureka" (I have found it), which is said to have been the exclamation of Archimedes, the Syracusian philosepher, when he discovered how to test the purity of Hiero's crown. Mr. Norman concluded by making some further reflections upon Mr. Lowe and the number of times he attends the meetings of the Board in a year. That gentleman had, however, better keep a sharp look out, for he may rely upon it that Mr. Lowe, who has ev.idently con- siderable qualities of mind fitting him for a place in the detective department of Scotland Yard, will not be: easily hoodwinked or bamboozled.

There must have been a good deal of electricity In the air on the day when the gentlemen constituting .the above Board met, for I find that at another of their 'gatherings, over which Canon Barclay presides with his 'usual tact, a quarrel ensued between two of them on the discussion of the lielsby drainage scheme. Mr. Challoner said "the ratepayers were all at sea with respect to the matter," on which Mr. Midwood replied that if he went there to speak untruths he (Mr. Midwood) did not. Their differences were only settled by the interference of the Chairman, who very properly, as an ecclesiastic of the Established Church, took the part of the peacemaker. May he have the blessing mentioned in the Beatitudes!

The meeting of the Widnes Local Board this week was in some respects, a rather tame one, considering the stirring times the public have had of late in perusing the delibera- tions of this local Parliament. Major Cross again broke a lance with the members of the Widnes Property Owners' and Ratepayers' As.,ociation, and came off victor. It appears that the members of that body have forwarded a communication to the Chairman, asking him to call a meeting of the ratepayers for the purpose of considering the advisability of dividing the district into wards. A resolution was then passed by the Board that the members of the association should be asked to forward their reasons for requesting that such a course should be adopted, and until they had done so, nothing further should he done in the matter. Major Cross seems to have stated that upon considering the law in rela- tion to the question, he found he was bound to call a meet- ing to consider the suggestion, and he had written to the association stating his willingness .to do so on receipt of a bond guaranteeing the expenses incident to holding it, and the cost of a poll, should one be demandectl When Greek meets Greek then comes the tug of war!: Mr. Brunner has again been elected chairman of the west district of the Widnes Liberal Association, which is doing a good work. At a meeting on Tuesday evening, the General and Executive Committees were elected; and Mr. Brunner made a short speech— Gloria in Excelsis on the result of the last general election and the return of Mr. Rathbone to a Liberal Parliament possessing such a large working majority. The speaker spoke in eulogistic terms of the way in which the members of the Liberal party in Widnes worked at the last contest. PLACCUS.

WIDNES PAELLI.=TART DEBATING O=TY —The House re-opened on Wednesday night, but no busin..ss was transacted through the non-atten4ance of a sufficient number of members, and there was an immediate count out.

ODDIPELLO49B' BALL AT RUNCORN.—The fifth annual tea party and ball in connection with the Loyal Wright's Pride Past Grands Lodge Independent Order of Oddfellows, M.U. was held on Thursday evening in the Public Hall, About three hundred persons were present. After tea a short meeting followed, which was briefly addressed by the Revs. Canon Barclay, M.A., and the Rev. William Robinson. The meeting was brought to a close soon after eight o'clock, when dancing commenced. Wood's Runcorn Quadrille Band had been engaged, to the strains of which dancing was continued until about three on the following morning.

RUNCORN BURIAL. BOARD.—A monthly meeting was held on Wednesday afternoon. Mr. Norman presided, and there I were present Mr. Briscoe, Mr. Coleburne, Mr. Rhodes, Mr. I Littler, Mr. Whittaker, and Mr. Salkeld, secretary. The Secretary reported that the total number of interments since the opening of the cemetery to the 25th December, 1880, was 5,339, including 2,77 Church, 2,725 Dissenters, and 437 Roman Catholics. A plan of the proposed mortuary to be erected in the cemetery was submitted by the Clerk. It had been drawn by Mr. N. Barker, and the estimated cost was £.200. This was considered too large a sum to be ex- pended on the erection of a mortuary, the Board being of opinion that a building compatible with the cemetary could be erected for a less sum. After a little discussion on the matters of detail connected with the proposed building it was decided, on the motion of Mr. Littler, seconded by Mr. Briscoe, that Mr. Barker be asked to prepare plans on a less costly scale to be submitted at the nest meeting. The other business was unimportant. RUNCORN BRUNSWICK lIIUTUAL IMPROVICHVNT SO- CIETY.—After a brief recess, during the Christmas holidays, this society met on Wednesday evening, at the class-room, Brunswick-street. Mr. Simister occupied the chair, and there was a large attendance of members. Mr. J. Craig, principal of the Collegiate School, gave a lecture on "Scottish Life and Character," in which he recited a num- ber of the Scottish anecdotes contained in Dean Ramsay's entertaining book entitled "Reminiscences of Scottish Life and Character." The audience listened with great interest to the lecture and showed their appreciation of the jokes and witticisms by repeated applause and laughter. The saying quoted by the lecturer was approved by all present, day night," •' A little laughter now and then, Is relished by the wisest men." Mr. Craig's really fine rendering of Burns's " Cotter's Satur- day a pleasing variation in the proceedings. A Tao of thanks was cordially passed to the lecturer.

div.head: LOND N AND NORTH-WESTERN EMPLOYES SUPPER AT WIDNES.
div.p: LOND N AND NORTH-WESTERN EM- PLOYES SUPPER AT WIDNES.

This annual supper was held at the Grosvenor Hotel, Widnes, on Wednesday evening. A numerous company, representing the coaching, traffic, goods, permanent way, locomotive, and other departments, sat down at half-past nine to a repast which was well served by Mr. Sankey, the proprietor of the hotel. The after proceedingd were pre- sided over by Mr. Bansom, the station master. Mr. Carter, the traffic inspector, occupied the vice-chair. The usual loyal and patriotic toasts having been drank, the aricn-Grearnroar said he had much pleasure in proposing "The Town and Trade of Widnes, coupling with the toast the name of Mr. Billington, statioe master, Hale Bank." Mr. BiLlaworoar, in reply, said it had been his pleasure for a number of years, to watch the advance which the town and its trade had made. It had seemed to rush into existence like a mushroom, but unlike that luxury it was of durable growth. Each succeeding year found it more pros- perous than its predecessor, and it was his earnest hope that successful as 1880 had been, 1881 would be productive (ft even better results. (Bear, hear.) Mr. Reales, station master, Appleton, then gave a song "Under the British flag," which was well sung. This was followed by "Beautiful girls," given with good effect by Mr. Carver, traffic inspector's clerk. • The Vice-Cstarnarezt then proposed the toast of the even- ing "Health, and prosperity to the London and North- Western Railway Company," and called on Mr. Sansone to 'respond. Mr. Senecas said that at a gathering like that, so full of the railway element, his remarks would not perhaps be altogether out of place if they did "smack" something of steam and locomotion. For they knew these were essential to theie business, and that it was owing to the invention of the former property that it had been found necessary to brace the land from end to end with powerful girders, which were beet known to them when described as the "iron road." It was their privilege to be engaged in one of the most tre- mendous enterpises of which it was the great good fortune of the country in which they lived' to be able to boast. If they had ever imagined themselves on a pinnacle sufficiently elevated to disclose to their view the enormous railways, and the immense traffic that was continually going on (night affording no respite) to and from all centres of the land, they would have seen something that would have astonished and amazed them supposing it had been their custom not to look beyond the locality in which they found actual em- ployment. He thought there fees something in this great machinery—in which, be it remembered, every one of them hurried an item of more or less importance—which was calculated to awaken their enthusiasm, and cause them to be proud of the work in which they were engaged. (Hear, hear.) The ready means they bad' for conveying hundreds of thousands of tons of goods from the seaports to the interior town?, and from the interior towns to the seaports, and in such a brief space of time, compared with the tedious journeys thathad to be made some time ago, either by road or canal, must have made the merchandise, of which be spoke, very much cheaper than it used to be, for the carriage of 'it was undertaken at a reduction of cost equal to the difference between the old and the increased rate of speed. Perishable goods, too,were freighted by them late at night, and run through the country a distance of 200 miles, or more, into the London markets by break of day, and in the case of fish, why,they are sometimes landed in Billingsgate alive' so that the Londoner might !at for. hill southern breakfast to-day what yesterday was sw:mming In the sea off the northern coast. Then with regard te the passenger traffic there was no Monday, Wednesday, and Friday work with them, but every day a number of trains run right away through, from east to west and north to south, so that a traveller might go where he would almost when he Pleased. The speaker then gave a graphic description of the journeys made by the Company's "expresses." He said a loaded train would leave Lime- street for Euston, at a given hour, the guard was there, and the driver, who always carried under his rough pilot coat a lion's heart, and was withal the most quiet un- assuming man on the train, stood to his engine—the passengers were all seated—the clock pointed the hour, and the shrill whistle gave the signal—" right away!" In a moment the wheels were in motion, and away they rushed. Through the tunnel at Edge Hill, parts of which never saw the light of day. There was no time to parley, for 200 miles must be accomplished in less than five hours. Arrived at the great bridge at Runcorn (to drew the plans or design the structure of which would bare driven your ancient engineer stark mad), they do not pause, for the foundations are sure, but ehoet across like a swift arrow, and make haste to leave Lancashire and Cheshire behind. They paused to take a breath at Crewe, and then puff, puff, puff, through cuttings, the banks of which were some of them mountains high—now under the very hills themselves, dart- into the tunnels at one end and out at the other like a lightning flash piercing a rock! Away she scuds, through valley after valley, and hill after hill. Villagers on the platforms of road-side stations are warned to stand back for the " express " is due to pass, and she comes careering through at such an amazing pace (a flying squadron of coaches) that they are scarcely seen ere they are out of sight —away! away! Darkness comes on, and on dashes the train, not fearing to be obstructed in its course by the old enemies of the stage coach, highwaymen or rough weather; and when at last the engine steams into the terminus to the nich of time, it is not at all distressed, and seems to say I have done wonderful; these performances are quite natural to me: I could have tra- velled much further, and in much less time. (Cheers.) Now, while this train had been running between the two points named, a multitude of others had been pursuing different directions. So great is the weight of goods, and so large the number of passengers and parcels, that during the last year their receipts had made a near approach to, if they had not actually exceeded, ten millions of money. What a heavy responsibility the management of so gigantic a con- cern must be! Arrangements had had to be made durintt the year that had gone for conveying no less than 30,000,000 tons of merchandise, 48i million of passengers, and a power of parcels. So that a moment's reflection would be sufficient to convince them, if anyone entertained a doubt on the sub- ject, that their lives were being spent in an important, use- ful, and honourable occupation. It was his (the speaker's) duty some time ago to weigh daily the tickets which • had been issued to passengers travelling over the company's line and sent to the audit department, after collection, to be checked, and he found that the record of these daily weights, at the end of twelve months, amounted to nearly forty tons. Then the railway acted as tell tale clock, indicating the state (of the country—if times were bad their receipts went down, if commerce flourished quite the opposite was the case. A heavy weight of care lay always at the manager's door, but he thought nothing could cause them so much pain and anxiety as acci- dents through collision, which were attended with loss of life. They knew these had been rendered almost impossible by the complete state to which the appliances for the work- ing of the traffic had been brought, if every man did his duty; and he felt sure all present would remember with gratitude, that out of a long string of accidents which occurred a short time ago, the great company under which they served escaped with a slight casualty or two which did not, he believed, involve the loss of a single life. (Great cheering.) Sorely this fact reflected credit on both officers and men. Moreover, every one of them might do something to keep the company in its presentetate of efficiency if they possessed the legitimate ambition to do their work well, and he ventured to say that no one could dispute the fact that it was fairly, within the province of all of them to aspire to be good servants of the company —(hear, hear)—and he believed that if a man was really anxious to make his home and his life happy, there was no better, no surer way to success in this parti- cular than a conscientious and careful discharge of the obligations he was placed under, with regard to the work from which he derived the means to establish the happiness of which he spoke. This conduct would enable them to contribute more, much more, to the health and happiness of their officers, and to the general prosperity of the Company, than complimenting them with all the toasts in Christen- dom possibly could; and the same means would as certainly win for them the increased esteem and patronage of the public, whom they served. (Loud cheering.)

a The -toast was followed by ‘" When these-Old clothes were new," rendered in splendid style by Mr. J. Howard, traffic department. The CITAIRMAN then proposed the "Donors." Inspector CARTER responded. He remarked that it was very encouraging to them, as public servants, to know that their humble efforts to please had met with the ap- proval of the good people of the town to whom they were all indebted. The toast was then drunk with musical honours.

Mr. CARTER then entertained the company with a whim- sical whistling solo, which was much enjoyed. A vote of thanks was proposed to Mr. W. Ashton, the chief booking clerk, for the admirable manner in which he had carried out the arrangements connected with the supper. Mr. ASHTON, in response, said it always afforded him great pleasure to contribute what he could towards making his colleagues happy, and he was more than pleased to find that his efforts in this direction had met with their appre- ciation.

Other toasts and songs followed, Mr. Newton (Wigan), Mr. Billington (lisle Back), Mr. Gibson (Widnes Loco.), and others obliging. A very pleasant evening's entertain- ment was brought to a close atone a.m., the whole company singing "Aukl lang syne."— Corn.

THE WIGAN ELECTION.—The writ for the election of a member of Parliament to represent Wigan, in the room of Lord Lindsay, elevated to the Upper House on the death of his father, was received by the Mayor of that borough on Tuesday. The nomination has been fixed for to.day (Satur- day), and the polling for Tuesday. Both political parties are working with great activity, and a close contest is expected ; but the feeling is increasing that, with united action on the part of the Liberal party, yet another defeat will be added to Mr. Powell's already extensive list, and that Mr. Lancaster will be returned. On Tuesday evening Mr. , Lancaster addressed a crowded meeting of the electors in the I Public Hall, and a vote of confidence in him was passed with enthusiasm. Two crowded meetings of working men were held on Thursday evening at Wigan in support of the candidature of Mr. John Lancaster, who is contesting the representation of the borough in the Liberal interest. Speeches were delivered is gr. Lancaster, Mr. W. E. Briggs. MAI, Mr. H. Broadhurst, M.P., and other gentlemen, and resolutions expressive of confidence ia Mr. Lancaster were passed. div.p: LATEST TELEGRAMS. &c.

Ma. GLADSTONR.—Mr. Gladstone slept much better on Thursday night. His cold has almost left him. TWELVE FISHERMEN DROWEED.—TweIve fishermen have been drowned off the Caithness coast by the upsetting of their fishing boats.

Robert Hume, charged with the murder of Annie court in St. John's Wood,was discharged by the Marylebone magistrates yesterday. The Union steamer Nubian sailed from Plymouth yester- day for South Africa, having on board Brigadier-General Sir Evelyn Wood and staff. The Muster of the Rolls yesterday granted interim injunction restraining publication on the doors of Prestbury Church of the sentence of deprivation passed on the Rev. Bagshot Dela Bere. An action was concluded in the Sheffield County Court, on Thursday, in %hich a clothes dealer named Murphy sought.to recover £25 as damages from Police-officers Hopkins and Hogged, of the borough force, for assault and false im- prisonment.

At the Central Criminal Court, on Thursday, John Sulli- van, a boot closer, waf sentenced to seven years' penal ser- vitude for stabbing a married woman with whom he bad cohabited. l'he woman had threatened to leave him and go back to her hasbann.

At the Central Criminal Court, on Thursday, Sarah Jane Swann, aged 25, an unmarried woman, was charged with the murder of her female illegitimate child. The jury found the prisoner guilty of manslaughter. The judge sentenced her to five years' penal servidude.

. - RITUALIST APPEALS.—The hearing of the appeals of Mr. Dale and Mr. Enraght was resumed Yesterday morning, when Mr. Wills continued his arguments in support of the promoter's case. Be submitted that Lord Penzance acted within his powets in committing the applicants to prison for contumscy, and that there was no informality in the issuing of the writs which would vitiate the proceedings. THE MURDER AT SOLITIULL—SUPPOSED CLUE TO THE AssAsa/J.—A telegram which was received on Thursday, from Dublin, stating that the police knew the name and birthplace of the Solihull murderer, and that the crime was the result of a dispute between two branches of the Fenian organisation in England, has caused considerable sensation in Birmingham and district. A description of the man has been circulated among the Irish police, but up to the present without succ( ss.

ALLEGED MARDER AT GLASGOW.— Yesterday morning, an elderly man, named William Baslen, who walks with the asfistance of crutches, was remanded by Stipendiary Gem- mell, at Glasgow, on a charge of assaulting a woman named Leslie with his crutches, from the effects of -which she ex- pired on Thursday. It is likely that a serious charge will be preferred against the cripple, as the woman, according to medical testimony, must have been brutally assaulted. A BOY'S FINGER FOUND IN A SAUSAGE.—The purcha- ser of some sausages in Liverpool had them cooked, and when about to eat them found that there was a human finger in one. Suspecting a mystery, he informed the police, who made inquiries, and report to the health department that a boy, while mincing meat at the machine, had his finger cut off, and it was carelessly left lying about while the last was taken to the hospital. The finger was accidentally tiikde up in the sausage as discovered. SHOCKING DISCOVERY IN A WOOD.—OIi Thursday, in the Dockwell Wood, near Llanwern, about three miles from Newport (Mon.), two men out shooting found hanging from a tree tke body of a man perfectly naked. A short distance from the tree were found the man's clothes. It is believed to he a determined case of suicide. The man is a perfect stranger in the neighbourhood. He appears between thirty and thirty-five years of age, was five feet five inches high, with sandy hair, whiskers, and moustache. He had on moleskin trousers and vest, brown tweed coat, laced boots, grey worsted stockings, Welsh flannel shirt, and hairy cap with flaps. THE GREAT STRIKE IN THE LANCASHIRE COAL ,
TRADE. PROBABLE SETTLEMENT OF THE DISPUTE.

The number of colliers now on strike In South Lancashire against the proposals of the masters that they should contract themselves out of the Employers' Liability Act is daily increasing, and there are now abont 40,000 men away from work. The men on strike held meeting. on Thursday at Mosley Common, Worsley, and at Radcliffe and Westhoughton. At tke meeting on Mosley Common about 7,000 men were present, a large proportion of whom had marched together from Pendlebury. At the close of the meeting about three thousand of them proceeded to two pits in the neighbourhood owned by the Bridgewater Trus- tees, and at one pit they compelled forty men, who were working under the Act, to terminate their labours, asserting that the best means to obtain a victory over their employers was a general cessation from work. The men at the Atherton Collieries, which usually employ nearly 2,000 hands, have been withdrawn from work. The same course has been taken at several other pits in the Tyldesley district. The coal proprietors of West Laneashi re held a numerously attended meeting in Liverpool yesterday in reference to the present strike of 40,000 miners. Resolutions were passed to the effect that as the raen did not wish to be under the new rules which it was proposed to substitute in piece of the Employers' Liability Act, the masters could not object to the !nen withdrawing from the arrangement, but the masters withdrew their offer of extended support to the permanent relief society, and must further consider their position in respect to any contribu- tions thereto ; that there was, no such improvement in the state of trade since the subject was last conside.ed as to justify an adrance of wages, but the masters were willing to consider the practicability of a sliding scale with the prices and wages of 1877 as a starting point; and that the masters did not think weekly payments would tend to the increased safety of the miners. A co.nanittee of the masters afterwards had a meeting with a deputation from the men, and a long discuscussion took place. Ultimately it was agreed that a committee should be forraed for the purpose of adopting a sliding scale and the masters' committee also undertook that the subject of weekly payments should be further considered. The repre- sentatives of the men stated that they would recommend the mento re-commence work on the above undertaking. THE MINERS' CONFERENCE.

At Thursday's sitting of the Miners' Conference in Man- chester, Mr. Macdonald, M.P., declared that the men in Lancashire who arbrefusing to contract themselves out of the Employers' Liability Act and have left their employ- ment are being subjected to " unmitigated coercion" at the hands of their masters. The working classes throughout the country had under the circumstances an opportunity afforded them of showing their appreciation of the benefits of the Act by making representations to the Government in the matter and offering aid to those who are engaged in the struggle now going on. A number of resolutions were adopted with the view of giving greater protection to work- men in mines, including one in favour of the entire pro- hibition of blasting by powder or any other dangerous ex- plosive substance where explosive gases are known to exist, the prohibition to remain in for until the manager pro- nounces the mine to be in a safe condition.
LAST NIGHT'S PARLIAMENT.
HOUSE OF LORDS.-LAST NIGHT:

PROTECTION OF LIFE AND PROPERTY IN IRELAND.— Earl FORTESQUE gave notice that on Monday he would ask whether the Government would introduce into that House bills for the protection of life and property in Ireland. TrrE AUGMENTATION BENEFICES BILL was read a second time. . .
"-TRE BURIAL Acrs and Judicial Committee Bills were passed. THE POPE'S LErrna.—ln reply to a question, Earl GRANVILLE said the Pope's letter to the Archdeacon of Dublin was authentic.
The House afterwards adjourned. lIOUSE OF COMMONS.—LasT NIGHT. Tss PENSION LIST.-Mr. BRADLAUGH presented a ber of petitions praying for an enquiry regarding perpetual pensions.

IS THE HOUSE OF LORDS A. NECESSITY ?—Mr. LIDOU- CHERE gave notice that that day month he should propose a resolution with regard to another place, of which he had already given notice. (Loud laughter.) TitE LANDING OF BRITIEDI TROOPS. Sit CHARLES DILKE, replying to Mr. R. Fowler, said there was no foun- dation for the report that the British Government had asked the permission of the Portugese Government to lend troops at Dilagoa Bay. There was no intention of making such application. THE CREW OF THE SANDFLY.— Mr. SHAW-LEFEVRE said that the reports published in the newspapers of the murder of the Lieutenant, in command of her Majesty's ship Sandfly, and his crew, in the Pacific, had been con- firmed by the reports received at the Admiralty. Sub- Lieutenant Bradford, who had acted with bravery on the occasion, had been promoted, and Captain Maxwell had been directed to follow up and punish the murderers, but he had been directed not to burn villages, and to reward natives giving him assistance. Mn. BIGGAR Hnstonocs.—Mr. BIGGAR, pursuant with the private notice he had given, asked whether representa- tions had been received by Her Majesty's Government from foreign Governments, or the United States, as to the condi- tion of Ireland, caused by the oppression and tyranny of landlords, and whether the Sultan of Turkey had sent his fleet to cruise off the Irish coast. (Laughter, and "Oh !") —The SPEAKER informed the hon. member that his question was not in proper order. (Cheers.)—Mr. Broaan said he would repeat it in an amended form on another occasion. THE ADJOURNED DEBATE ON MR. PARNELL'S AMEND- MENT to the Address was resumed.—Mr. SYNAN contended that sufficient reason had not been shown to justify the Go- vernment in suspending the Habeas Corpus Act in Ireland. —Mr. DiLiwaw said his vote that night would cause him great pain. The Government asked for additional powers to stop the outrages in Ireland, and, having confidence in them, was prepared to give them the power they required. He pointed out the difference of Mr. Parnell's speech in the House from those delivered by him in Ireland. His addresses to excited mobs were direct incentives to outrages. Mr. Dillwyn then alluded to the murder of Lord Meuntmorres, and said friends of his had seen Irish peasants trampling in the blood. (Cries of "Name.") He declined to give name, as it was not safe to do so.—Mr. PARNELL rose to order, and asked the Speaker if the hon. member, on anonymous authority, was in order in calumnia- ting the Irish naticin. It was English soldiers, not Irish peasants, who did what the bo. member, described.—Tie SPEAKER said the hon. member was not out of order.—Mr. DlLLwru insisted that what he had described had been dote by Irish peasants, and he concluded his speech by saying be should vote against the amendment.— [Ln-r SITTING.]

STRIKE OF CIIENICAL MEN AT Sr. HELENS.—The men employed at the salt cake furnaces of the Ciloke Alkali Company's works have determined to remain out OD strike for a short time, all events, in consequence of the pro- posal made by the firm to rduce their wages. The price paid at these works is and has been from the commencement of the works 3s. per ton, and the men think it a most un- justifiable action on the part of the firm he reduce the price to 2s. 6d. The men, therefore, numbering about 200, are at present out on strike, and a subscription fund has been opened for their support. They appeal ad i ppeenal engaged othen wchoermkiinegami wenalokfa,Sto a t. Ha at ° s especially to ta as are fighting a battle which they e set,hee saps while con- sider has been thrust upon them by the employers. From the information we have received from tke men themselves, who waited upon us at the Examiner Office, we are enabled to state that the price of 3s. per ton is the lowa paid in any chemical yard in tke town; and in some yards it is as much as 3s. 4d. per ton. All the men at these works are not out on strike, as the reduction does not affect the contract men, who are at work as usual. The strike has been taken advan- tage of by the firm, who have engaged mechanics to make some necessary repairs. BAD ICE ACCIDENT AT Sr. HELENS.—The low tem- perature of the weather which has caused the various ponds in the neighbourhood to be covered with ice has induced lovers of skating to indulge in the exhilarating exercise peculiar to this season of the year. We regret to have to record a death by drowning which occurred under the foi- -1 leaving circumstances:—A boy, named James Davies, ten years of age, who resided with his parents near Ravenhead Colliery, Sutton, appears to have left his home about half- past nine on Monday morning with the intention of taking a pair of boots to be repaired, but Instead of going with the boote deceased gave them to his sister, and went with three other boys to slide on the dam near Grace's-row, Sutton. He had only been sliding a few minutes when one of the boys named Cunliffe called to the deceased to come back. The fell, and the ice broke, deceased being riemmeedrsisedteliyn the water. He shouted for help, and Cunliffe calle.d for assistance, and John Mort partiallyw then deceasedi "o t hn sank. men succeeded in getting deceased to the surface, he being then quite dead. He was taken home, and no medical officer was called in.

TETE "TWO WONDERFUL LETTERS." ' Sir,—Your " faithful egg and butterrnan," most favoured of mortals, has had the pleasure of dining in the Blue Olympus, and sipping nectar with the Cerulian gods, and greater gratification still of participating in the post prandial "feast of reason and flow of soul." Now, although lam not prepared to assert that the speeches thereat delivered were remarkable for profundity of thought, still they were pregnant with the materials for thought. What a picture of contented happiness was the gallant chairman, the pro- poser of the "great toast." Unappalled by the immense amount of the national substance annually wasted to support this "greatness," and unregardful of the toiling millions sobject to the customary mulct to uphold this graciousness, he finds a pleasure, and thinks it an honour, to propose his "great toast." Now I mentally transferred the contented chairman back over a few centuries and found him in the reign of an unlimited monarch again proposing his "great bout," and expressing his belief that there was "no desire for change." Verily, there are those who being born in Hades would have wished to be reared there. And so "the inhabitants of India are pleased to call our Queen their Empress" are they? Let them thank heaven that so little contents them. The gift of being pleased by cheap pleasures is a valuable one. Let them make the most of their joy and be grateful to its creator Benjamin. Ah ; but even that rose is not without its thorn, for ke was also the creator of the necessity of certain disbursements in the Afghan affair. Alas how the bitter and the sweet get mixed in this world! But if tlaey, the aforesaid inhabitants of India, do take a delight in this titular gingle, I hereby make over to them all and several my interests and joys (if any) in said titular gingle, with the sole provisio that they do take to themselves to have and to hold (and the faster the latter) any the first Emperor of India who lsy mischance may be found in our midst, and may God give them joy of him ! In these days of all round mutual admiration and universal testi- monial giving, it is refreshing to deal occasionally with the staked truth. Mr. John Bright has been taken to task by the Lord of Carnarvon, in that he has been more thoughtful of his duties as popular representative than of the follies and fictions of a sham Monarchy. Indeed, I think Mr. Bright must, as a lover of truth and straightforward dealing be occasionally ashamed of his enforced part in the great national farce of government by proxy. To a man of Mr. Bright's feelings and temperament it must be a great trial to be compelled to keep up the fiction, that we. a self-govern- ing people, require the addition, over the head of the actually governing body, of a sovereign, who by an antiquated fiction is supposed to rule. Now the fiction would not be a very great grievance were it not accompanied by the un- welcome fact of the enormous expense required to support it. This cumbersome and absurd Governmental fiction is a clog and an embarrassment to the action of parliament, immoral in its tendencies and unjust in the incidence of its attendant taxes. It is a very cheap .kind of loyalty which strives to maintain its idol by enforced contributions of those who do not worship it. I should have not the slightest objection to giving up all claim to this idol, if the worthy chairman and his co-thinkers would take and maintain it; though I question if there be a man in England out of a lunatic asylum and not a candidate therefor who would voluntarily contribute to keep up this antiquated anomaly. Monarchy in England has long since lost the reason for its existence and now clings round the body politic as a useless inornate parasite, imped ng its vital action, and strangling what it clings to. I believe that this system of sentimental an traditional government is tottering to its fall and will ere long be replaced by the government of common sense; that is, our present representative form of government with the premier at its head, but without the regal incubus of a sovereign who is paid enormous sums to rule and then for- bidden to do it. This, sir, is one of those peaceful revolu- tions to be effected in the not remote future. Can any sane man doubt for a moment that it would be better to devote the sums incidental to the maintenance of a pseudo- sovereign, to the far higher and nobler use of educating the people? That the present iniquitous anachronism shoald terminate with the present reign should be wished and worked for by every man who has the welfare of his country at heart.—l am &c., JOHN PEERS. Buttermarket-street, Warrington.

As to who is to blame for this neglect of the people I shall not at pre- sent stop to enquire; but that it is a fact I only need point to the "theatre," left to itself or chance, the want of a pub- lic art gallery or museum, schools of science and art, and also a park for the people. I may say in that I have had in my time many day dreams of a park for St. Helens, and yearningly, wondered where it would be situated, and how would it come into our possession. Would the Council rise to the dignity of the occasion and provide one at the public Cost? Or, pleasing infatuity, which of our brewers, chemical manufacturers, glass merchants, or colliery proprietors, would ba the generous donor; but never in the extravagant wt my "airy visions" did I imagine that the beautiful park at Ecclestone, which has just been offered to the town by Mr. Taylor, would be so tangibly and unexpectedly brought within our reach; or that, if the offer were made, there would be found two contrary ideas as to the advisibility of accepting the gift. Now, sir, let us examine some of the objection's to the acceptance of this magnificeut park, and I Will venture to assert—to reasonatle people—they will at asfee dissolv% into "thin air," or, vulgarly speaking, idle our. To be brief, any park, no matter whore situated, would require a wall building round for its protection. It would also require draining. Any sheet of water to be orna- mental would require to have its banks kept in repair. Any park to be used for the benefit of the people, recreatively, mild not be allowed to be let off in building, plots. And I presume that Mr. Taylor, in bestowing a park on the town, has not the desire, for that reason, to go into his own honse by the back door. But there is another objection besides the reservations: it is in the wrong place. And this, sir, is enough to make one lose his patience. Thatto Heath? Bah! 'Tie an impossibility; money could not do it. Let that pass. Another place is Denton's Green lane, on the right hand side. Again. this would require walling and draining, reservoir to be made, and kept in repair. Besides, the land wants buying; and even then it is too near to the gentry tcf Cowley Hill to be palatable to the people of Sutton, from some dog-in-the-manger point of view. Take the left hand side of the same lane—a dull, dreary, lifeless wilderness, from which every vestige of vegetation is fast disappearing, and past which, seven days a week, may be seen winding tiaeir dismal way, sad add mournful processions; or, worse still, some unsightly and abhorred scavenging cart, with the pestilential contents of some ash-pit; besides the same drawbacks of walling, cowering, kc., as the other, and then too near te some body, and too far from the unfortunate sojourners in Parr, Haydock, &c., to be enjoyed, and on whose side of the town it is impossible to grow anything' but colt's foot, which, as the poet says,— Seldom droops, chilled '33, the blight of neglect. . . _ . .

As to Ecclestno Hall, or Taylor's park, it is a Ruskinincia aroadia, compared with the above places. The situation is at once verdant and healthful; in fact, the only piece of land suitable for a park contigmous to St. Helens; and in the views which it gives, will be found the only bits of pleasing landscape to he seen in our neighbourhood, and past which will be rolling in a few months the tram car, bearing its load of pleasure, recreation, and health seekers from every part of the town. Yet, sir, there are those "vulgarised Philistines," who carp and wrangle, and " pull up the sluizes.of their stupidity," and pour forth a flood of cankerous rubbish for the mere sake of p indering to a mor- bi I vanity; or perhaps it may be only a tynochondrical madness, which will not allow them to enjoy th,se smiling landscapes, intended for our hours of ease, which nature tells its are so essential to a happy and healthy existence. But I trust the Council, who are invested with the powers and responsibilities of our borough, will he found to discharge its functions worthily. I cannot but hope that no sugges- tions of parsimonious selfishness or false economy will be saffered to stand in the way of this magnificent gift and boon to the pecple --Yours truly, St. Helens, January 10th, 1881.

(Applause.) He had noted the signs of Word for the re- their success with unalloyed pleasure and gratification eand the evidence of their great liberality which had been given that-night was not only highly creditable but full of hope for their future success, which depended on their own pluck and energy.. (Applause.) He believed there was ample room for all the Christian agencies which were at present at work, and there was ne occasion why any of them should envy others. (Applause.) There was a vast amount of spiritual darkness which needed enlightening, spiritual death in need of spiritual life; and all religions, more or less, were in need of intellectual improvement. He had been told that last Sunday was the most drunken Sunday that had been seen in Warrington for many mouths. This was a lamentable fact. Working men, it would seem, hailed the return of prosperity by drinking; and it was the duty of the churches to remedy this state of things. He had before expressed his opinion that secession from the Church of England was the only honestco They coarse for people of evangelical convientntio;era, belief. and and , 4t, could not remain except by n evident tqAti th.st in matters of, religatnr:- epeepremi'Must bese would ", not suffi,ce., , (Applaoe.)
