'hoping tea leirej their presence and the influence of 'evangelical faitVand doctrine. That was hopeless. In fact, the opposite was generally the case, and in his experience he bad known many who had come under the influence of Ritualism, protesting at first, but eventually sitting down with it quietly and con- tentedly. Those evangelical laymen who had children were incurring great responsibility by allowing them to remain to be taught principles subversive of their own faith and the teaching of the Lord Jesus Christ. He firmly believed that the movement they had begun had done much good in the town. It had called the attention of the Church people to what Ritualism was doing in the country, and it had exer- cised a quiet influence on the town itself. (Applause.) He was convinced that if it had not been for the movement there would have been a stronger development of Ritualistic feeling and practice than was to be found in the churches of the town, and therefore he thought their church had done good. Referring to the imprisoned clergymen, he said the course they had taken was snore effective than imprisoning the men who had practised Ritualism in their churches, and those men had no right to go to prison in the garb of martyrs. (Applause.) He was glad to have had the oppor- tunity of making the acquaintance of Mr. Lane, and he hoped that Wycliffe Church and Emmanuel Church might work hand in hand for long years to come. (Ap- plause.) The CHAIRMAN then called upon the Rev. J. Warnock to address the meeting. He said it was gratifying to know that the different evangelical churches in the town were working , hand in hand, and giving to each other mutual support. (Hear, hear.) The Church of England wielded, as she ought to.do, a great power in the country, and he gave to the es- tablishment the credit of doing much good. But the various Dissenting bodies were doing quite as good a work in the face of a great many discourag,ements and much opposition, for which they deserved credit. After giving the tenets on which the Church with which he is connected and the Emmanuel Church were agreed, he remarked that they had found nothing new. It was their duty to arrange old truths, to teach and preach them. The Bible, and the Bible only, was the religion of Protestants, and it was the duty of Christians to give a loyal and loving obedience to the word of God. There were two classes of law-breakers in the country at the present day. One was the Ritualistic clergy of the Established Church, and the other was the Irish peasant, who had suffered deprivation fora long number of years, and who was driven to the verge of despair in order to obtain food and shelter for his family. He would leave them to judge which was the greatest sinner of the two. (Applause.) Bishop GREGG, D.D., said he had been greatly cheered by the presence and support of those ministers of religion of different denominations. Ile congratulated the members of the Reform Church on their success, the result of the united efforts of their minister and themselves. In speaking of the work of the Reformed Church of England he would have to speak of the Established Church, audit was his desire to say nothing that was unworthy either of a gentleman or a Christian minister. It would be his duty to speak of the service book of that Church, on which was stamped the word "compromise." In the reign of King Edward Vl. (applauPe)—one of England's greatest monarchs, in the year 1549, certain prayers were drawn up by certain golly men, and the first prayer book was formed. In 1552 a great im- provement was made in the book, the most Protestant Prayer Book that had ever been in the Church of England. Queen Mary then ascended the throne, followed by Queen Elizabeth, who made a further revision in 1559. And here came in that wondrons spirit of compromise, which, so far as he could see, was the basis of that I ementab'e schism which was rending the Church of England to pieces. (Ap- plause.) Further revisions were made in the reigns of Janice I. and Charles H., of whom he could sc ircely trust himself to speak. Further compromises were made, over 600 changes were introduced, which, with the exception of the , first prayer book, was the most Romish prayer book that had ever been in the Church of England, and it existed to-day. Could they then be astoniohed to find that seeds thus sown produced what they regarded as priestcraft and Ritualism, which had driven some in the Public flail of Warrington that night from the church which they had so truly loved? Almost immediately on the publication of that prayer book, in 1662, there was passed that iniquitous Act of Uniformity which demanded conformity to every doctrine and dogma contained in the ,service book as issued from the hands of Charles H. That Act drove out from the Church 2,000 of the most noble and godly spirits that had ever lived in this country. Thus they had the first exis- tence of that great Protestant body the Nonconformists of England. (Applause.) There was no hope forthe main- tenance of Protestants iu the Established Church, except there were eradicated out of her service book the seeds of schism which were producing to-day a sacerdotalistic crop in their churches. (Applause.) He thanked God that that noble man, Lord Eubrey, was about to introduce in Parlia- ment a Bill for the revision of the book of common prayer I of the Church of England. Were such a prayer book as they had in the Reformed Church introduced as the prayer book of the Establishment, no one would deplore more than he would the continued existence of their body, and no one . would eejoice more than he would in having the privilege of leading to their old mother those persons who had joined with him in seceding from the Establishment. (Applause.) They saw in the Establishment to-day a body known as the Church Association, and another known as the Church Union, representatives of different sections in the same church. Looking at the results which followed from tha existence of these bodies, they had authority greater than human for saying "that a house divided against itself cannot stand." (Ap daue.) What, then, was the position ' which the Reformed Church assumed? Tilt, said they did not like Secerdotalism, andthneiort edxepsei cr fruitwd to maintain the Protestant religion and the liberties of England. (Applause.) They could from that which they regarded as evil. Consequently, in- stead of trying to explain away and make compromises with their consciences in receiving the emoluments of the Ch urc of England they went out of the Church. (Applause.) There were three points on which they differed with tin. Established Church. They did not believe in what was called "Baptismal Regeneration," nor that in the Lord's Supper was there a sacrifice of any kind whatsoever. He would far rather believe that, as one gentleman had said,
ineorn,
sth January.

Jonas swallowed the whale; than that out of any amount of grain there was any sacrifice to the Lord God Almighty. (Applause.) They could not believe that any man, priest, or prelate had any right, authority, or power to absolve sins, which could alone be forgiven by the great High Priest above. They had done to-day what the Church of England did 300 years ago to a certain extent. They had endea- voured to complete the eraiication of Romish doctrines from the Church of England prayer boek, and before that Church could accuse them of schism they would first have to justify the action of that Church three centuries ago. There had been a good deal said about union. There might be false conceptions of union, but he did not think that union existed or consisted in a man giving up his own honest con- viction on a question of ecclesiastical polity. The Bishop then gave an outline of the work they had accomplished in South End, Essex, since they had commenced in 1877, and concluded by saying that if any persons in this town who were suffering from Ritualism were convinced that the Reform Church would meet their need, he was certain that other towns would be convinced of the same thing. Lan- cashire was the pulse of England, and if they convinced Lancashire they had convinced England. (Applause.) Mr. HALL proposed a vote of thanks to the choir and all the office bearers for their services during the past year. They had, he said, about 200 scholars on the books, and an average attendance in the afternoon of 140, but they were short of teachers and they would be glad if some of those present would kindly give them a helping hand. It was well known why they had left St. James' Church. A gentle- man had tried to vindicate the placing the cross at the east end of the church, and the candlesticks on the communion table, quoting from a book supplied by the Church Associa- tion. He felt indignant that St. James Church should have been put to such a use as that—(hear, hear,)—and he was perfectly astonished at the way in which the services had been conducted. If those present would go and see the way in which they of the Reformed Church conducted their services they would find them carried lon as they used to be in St. Jarites' church. (Applause.) Mr. GALLOWAY briefly seconded the :motion and the pro- ceedings terminated.

the valley of Jezreel ; went on for eight or nine miles ; then over part of Carmel: on until he stood by the side of the great sea—the Mediterranean—and saw its blue waters dancing in the sunlight; on, until he came to Tyre with its merchant princes, and its sellers of purple, who took very little notice of him. His poor feet were sore, but he had another fifteen miles to go in order to reach Zarephath. At last he came to that place and found the woman who had to sustain him gathering sticks with which to bake a cake, that she and her son might eat it and die. This woman was a widow, and she looked rather "faded ;" and on seeing her no doubt Elijah said "This is rather a bare pasture." He told the widow to bake him a cake before making one for herself and son. She would no doubt look at the prophet and say to herself "You are a very healthy looking man. You appear as if you could cleat the barrel of meal up yourself." (Laughter.) But she did not reason in that manner, or say that a bird in the band was worth two in the bush. The barrel of meal did not waste, the widow gave many a neigh- bour a good butter cake, and she could have fed a whole vil- lage with it. (Laughter.) The prophet remained two years with the widow, and then went to show himself to Ahab. What a change the land presented! Everything was barren and bare; for three years there had been no beautiful woods, no blossom in the spring time. The men had almost grown so lean that they could have lent them- selves out as stove pipes; they had hollow eyes, lantern jaws; and the tailor had to alter their clothes for them, and out of the alterations he got enough to make a suit for his family. (Great laughter.) The lecturer next described the meeting of Elijah, the uncrowned king, with Ahab. With his eagle eye he looked the wicked king in the face; and a real man could always look a shoddy, shabby humbug in the face. (Applause.) Ahab charged Elijah with being he who troubled Israel, on which he answered "You are patting the saddle on the wrong horse: look at home, sir." (Laueb- ter.) Then came the contest between Elijah and the hostile prophets on Carmel, a beautiful mountain covered with flowers and shrubs, from the brow of which the blue Medi- terranean could le seen as it rolled in; the valley of Jezreel, on to Lebanon, rnd Hermon, the hoary headed chieftain of the mountains. In describing the satirical appeal to the prophets of Baal, he said that Elijah told them their god was possibly, asleep, the hot weather having overcome him, and he had one eye open; he had perhaps some cotton in his ears; perhaps he was on a journey; perhaps he was chasing some Bashi-Bazouks—(loud laughter);—perhath he was with some great explorer looking for the north pole; were they aware if he had takea a return ticket or not. Mr. Mackenzie concluded by describing the descent of the fire of God; the flight of Elijah to Horeb; and his subsequent translation to Heaven. Ahab, Jezebel, and the ivory palace had passed away, but the name of Elijah lived and would do so to the end of time. Babylon was a habitation for dragons, but the name of Daniel lived; Felix and Agrippa were almost forgotten, but the name of the poor prisoner, Paul, was remembered ; Charles the Fifth was dead, but the name of Martin Luther was a powee to-day. (Applause). When Christ was transfigured, Elijah sras on the mount, with "not a grey hair in his toppin." (Laugh- ter). His presence on Pisgah proved the immortality of the soul. Might they see the prophet of Horeb in the life everlasting; might they follow his glorious example by waiting patiently to the end, and doing their work until the Master called. (Loud cheers.) Votes of thanks were passed to the Lecturer and the Chairman, the movers and seconders beim! the Revs. J. Nowell, Henry Valentine, Edmunds, J. Billington, and Mr. Mackenzie; after which the proceedings terminated. The proceeds will be given to the Weston Day Scl,nol.

div.head: REV. PETER 111A.OKENZIE ON " ELIJAH," AT RUNCORN.
div.p: THE REV. PETER 111A.OKENZIE ON " ELIJAH," AT RUNCORN.

On Thursday evening week the Rev. Peter Mackenzie, the popular lecturer, spoke at the Runcorn Public Hall, his subject being " Elijah. There was a good attendance. Mr. John Simpson presided, upon the platform were the Revs. J. Nowell (superintendent), Henry Valentine-Edwards, J. Billington (Methodist, Ellesmere-street, Free Church), and Mr. Thomas Norman. The Cataluna/a said he would not occupy their time by any remarks, but simply call upon Mr. MacKenzie to give his lecture on Elijah,—one of the most interesting and ex- traordinory characters in the Bible. The LECTURER, who was enthusiastically received, said the chairman had referred to the greatness of Elijah, who was certainly one of the most remarkable, marvellous, and romantic individuals the Hebrew people ever produced. Nothing was said in the Bible about his history previous to the time when he was introduced to their notice; nothing of his ordinary pursuits. He was introduced to them at once as " Elijah, ' who was of the inhabitants of Gilead ;—that wild and romantic region where Jacob wrestled by the brook Jabock, where its rapid torrent, came down from the moun- tains of Gilead. They would remember the struggles of the patriarch at the time when he was going to meet the brother he had so grievously injured. The spirit of the Lord came upon Jepthah at Mount Gilead. When David sought shelter from the unnatural treason of his son, who clutched at his sceptre, and who had stolen the hearts of the people, he sought a refuge in connection with the same mountain. From the summit of this mountain the shepherds as they tended their flocks, could look into the terrible and torturous tossings of the Jordan-3,000 feet be- low! When God sought to heal the heart of the daughter of His people. the calm came from Gilead. When God wished to find a man upon whom He could lay His hand to free_Palestine from its ills, He found one who "was of the inhabitants of Gilead"—a man who had graduated in atsture'e college; not one from the hierarchy, with the pres- tage of hereditary office, but a man mailed in the panoply of virtue and inspiree'Vrith the spirit of Jehovah. Forth ato came', in altble Crilo,ssal manhood—a prophet of fire .—a bu'nin.and' 'sliding light in one of the darkest 11e,11.0e of bun-Imi hist9ry,: was eminently qualified (or the work Co whieh' tfi 'Mister had called him, by the :strength of his faith, the force of his character, and the Varleisness of his disposition; one only fitted to stem the .t6rt4ial 6f rgodless age. It was generally supposed that he was tall and wirev, bronzed, and browned with the sun of Syria; that his frame had been strengthened by the moun- tain stoma and wet with its dews. He had long shaggy locks hanging over his shonlders—indicati tg that he was a Sam- son from the mountaine of Gilead. On his shoulders was a mantle of sheep-skinn, and he had a leathern girdle about his loins. What the rod was to Moses, the mantle was to Elijah. With the mantle he smote the waters of Jordan, and they divided; with the mantle he cevered his face as he stood in the presence of the Master at Hareb ; and his gar- ment fell to his honoured successor, as the prophet climbed the heavens and went home to the test which remaineth for the people of G,d. The prophet was introduced to him in the Bible with significant abruptness, as speaking to King Ahab and saying, "As the Lord God of Israel liveth, before whom I stand, there shall not be dew nor rain these years, but according to my word." The lecturer briefly described King Ahab as one who would not allow his people to follow pastoral pursuits, but sought to make them a commercial nation. Ahab improved upon the projects set on foot by King Solomon. He need not refer to the possessions of Ahab in the trading city of Damascus, or the ivory palace in which he lived. Ile was great in peace and great in war, but with all his power Ahab was a worthless apostate from the faith of Israel, and did more to grieve God than any king who had gone before him. Jeroboam, the son of Nebat, who made Israel to sin," was a bad one, but Ahab was a worse. (Laughter.) The King built a temple at Samaria, and it was such a gor- geous and immense structure that when the whole nation was called together by the bellman, at the command of royalty, they could all find a place in it, together with Mar- wood and Calcraft, who were there to finish those who did not attend. (Laughter.) Ahab led the nation away from the living fountain of water and caused them to hew out for themselves broken cisterns in which there was no water. Jezebel, the queen of Ahab, had 400 chaplains for the worship of Ashtereth, and she had also 450 priests of Baal. She was not satisfied that the house of her god was secure, and that Samaria was the centre of the civil power and the idolatrous worship, but she decided to get rid of all the pro- phets of the Lord—to extirpate and finish them. She was a foolish woman, with a rouged face. God made the very object of her worship the instrument of her punishment: and this was what He often did in the case of those who set up various idols in their hearts. Probably the meeting of Eli jab with Ahab took place upon a state occasion, when the King was seated ,on his throne with Jezebel by his side, and homage was being done to Baal. Elijah presented him- self without being sent for or announced, and in a voice of thunder delivered his awe-inspiring message. If Elijah had stopped there no doubt Ahab would have sald, "Lay hold of that man; and if the rain does not coins I wdl have blood. I will dock him below the ears." (Laughter.) Bat the prophet proved rather a slippery eel; and he gave the King what the Scotch called leg-bail, no doubt believing that distance would lend enchantment to that particular view. Elijah absconded. (Laughter.) The prophet next received the command, "Get thee hence, tmd turn thee eastward, and hide thyself by the brook Cherith, that is before Jordan. And it shall be that thou shalt drink of the brook ; and I have commanded the ravens to feed thee there." That was a very remarkable statement when they considered the difficulties in the way of such a promise being fulfilled. Some good men, in their interpretation of this particular Scripture, said that the ravens no doubt meant Arabs who went to the brook to get water for their cattle, and Elijah being rather a prepossessing man, and one whom they would like tit make a friend in case of a' shindy', his person was held sacred, he having broken bread with them. Well, it did not matter much if this "travelling preacher" found himself comfortably circumstanced in the Cherith circuit,— (laughter)—where they would remember he was stationed six months. He (the speaker), however, believed in "the black gentlemen," "the black footman," when a lad, and he had not altered his opinions since. (Hear, hear.) Look at the difficulties. First, it was said that the birds were not fit to feed the prophet owing to being unclean according to the Levitical economy. Well, they were at least as clean as Abigail's mules, or donkeys,—(loud laughter)—and they did not prove unclean carriers. Then another objector said that these birds never carried anything to their nest during the period of their incubation ; but then that time was a very long one, as it occupied six months. Another objection was that these birds lived on carrion,—that which a Nazarite, a Italy man of God, durst not eat for his soul. He was pre- pared to admit that the ravens were "rather aristecratical " in their notions of food—they preferred it rather gamey, with a rich flavour. (Laughter.) But, as the Scotch folks said, they were not over particular, for they had a crop for all sorts of corn. (Much laughter.) They would help themselves to a chicken, and they would not stick at a duck! He should not have liked to have had to look after Ahab's poultry yard at that particular time, for in the morning the manager would have asked where one chicken or goose after another had gone, and on his telling him the ravens had taken them, he would probably have said, "Oh, ravens your grandmother!" and uttered awful threats of what he would do. (r atwitter.) He should not be surprised if Elijah had duck, minus the green peas, to his dinner at times. (Laughter.) He had the brook for his musical box; he could see his God in the blighted verdure, in the blazing sunsltine. in the stars that gleamed in the blue canopy over- head, and in the brook where his face was mirrowed. Elijah was no doubt a happy man, for had he not the promise, "Thy bread shall be given thee, and thy water shall be sure?" (Applause.) By and bye the brook gave indica- tions that it was drying up by becoming more and more like a thread of silver. Some of those present could sympathise with the prophet, for their nests were empty; they had got daug.hter married, or their son had gone to Australia or New Zealand, and the Cherith of their temporal resources had dried up. Elijah next received the message "Arise, get thee to Zarephath, which belongeth to Zidon, and dwell there: behold I have commanded a widow woman there to sustain thee." Now if the prophet had been a cantankerous "brother," on the look out for a better circuit, he would have said 'Shetland a second time ;"—(much laughter)— but he had more sense than to find fault, as he knew that his God was too wise to err, and too good to be unkind. Elijah started to cross the Jordan, and soon reached the mountains of Gilboa, made memorable as the place where Saul and his sons met with their death. He plunged into

div.head: EMPLOYMENT OF COLLIERS.
div.p: THE EMPLOYMENT OF COLLIERS.

IMPORTANT CASE AT ST. HELENS. A case of great interest to miners, inasmuch as it affects the employment of colliers, was heard at the St. Helens ' County Court,on Wednesday, before T. P. Thompson, Esq., and a jury. Mr. &gar, barrister, Liverpool, appeared for the plaintiffs, who claimed £3 7s. 6d. for wages due, and £4 39. 4d. for damages for wrongful dismissal without proper notice and for breach of contract to employ the plain- tiffs as coal miners. The defendants, who were represented by Mr. Swift, put in the following counterclaim: Damages for that the plaintiffs, being workmen under a contract by service with the defendants, wrongfully absented themselves from and qnitted the said employment and neglected their work, £9 135.; carting coal for plaintiffs, 3s. 6d.; sharpen- ing picks for plaintiffs, Is. 6,1.; club money paid over, Is. 41.; fine, 2s. Bd.; total, £9 18s. 10d. Mr. Sessar, atta opening the case, said Edward Jones and George Hayes were the plaintiffs, and Messrs. Bournes and Robinson were the defendants. This was an actien to recover wages, and also to recover compensation in conse- quence of the defendants not having given the plaintiffs work for the fortnight commencing on the 3rd or 4th Nov., in accordance with a contract which the plaintiffs and them- selves made. It appeared that in August last the plaintiffs, who were colliers, went to Mr. Williams, the under-looker in the service of the defendants, who were colliery pro- prietors, and induced him to take them on work at the mines, The plamtiffs worked as mates, that was to say, they were to get certain wages, which were from time to time to be divided between them. The first work they did was called "ribbing." For this work they were paid something like 9d. a ton. When that was done they had to make a "level "- that was, making a passage through ths coal fer the purpose of working the mine. For that the wages they were to receive was 2s. 101 per yard, and Is. 2d. per ton. That work lasted for about six weeks, and at the end of that work they got paid. They had afterwards to commence making a level apparently down brow, at any rate, it was called "driving down brow." There seemed to hove been some danger of water in connection with that work, and they were to receive ss. 10d. per day for cutting a gutter, in addition to the 2s. 101 per yard and Is. 2d. per ton. There could be no doubt as to the figures being accurate, because the defen- dants themselves had given a wages sheet upon which they had given plaintiffs credit for those sums; but they said the plaintiffs were not entitled to any remuneration at all, be- cause on the 4th November the plaintiffs left their employ- ment. The circumstances under which the plaintiffs left their employment were most important for the jury to con- sider. On the 3rd of November the particular work of "driving down brow" was over, and Williams, the under- looker in the employment of the defendants, said the new work-they were to be engaged upon was of an entirely dif- ferent sort. It appeared to be work at the "pillar," and 'Williams said the plaintiffs would only in future receive 2s. 2d. per ton, but 4s. additional would be given to them for every ten tons of coal they got. These terms the plaintiffs refused to accept. Williams then offerA them Is. 6d. a day extra, but still the plaintiffs de- clined and said it was not a reasonable offer. The plaintiffs said they would take their tools away. Williams expressed himself satisfied with the work they had done, and there could be no doubt whatever they were entitled to the wages unless the defendants made out they were entitled to pay the plaintiffs nothing for that fortnight in consequence of their not having a fortnight's notice. It seemed there was a custom that there should be a fortnight's notice on both sides, unless there was some special arrangement between the parties. Defendants said plaintiffs were bound to give a fortnight's notice before they left on the 4th November. Plaintiffs said, on the other Land, defendants ought to have given them a fortnight's notice before they altered the terms upon which plaintiff's were working, and that they were en- titled to continue working at the colliery at the rate of 2s. 101. per yard and is. 2d. per ton for the fortnight com- mencing on the 4th November. With regard to this part of the case he admitted he had some difficulty in asking the jury to give him a verdict, because in the very nature of things colliery owners could not guarantee they would always have levels to cut, and gutters to make ; and although it was quite true that as long as that particular kind of work was going on each party was entitled to a fortnight's notice yet when that job was done he was very much afraid that those for whom he appeared were wrong to say that they were entitled to a fortnight's notice: He therefore withdrew that part of the claini, and raised the question as to whether the plaintiff's were not entitled to be paid a fortnight's wages, according to the wages sheet, and upon that .he thought there wavao doubt whatever as to his getting a verdict. He called George Hayes, collier, Thatto Heath, who said he and Edward Jones went in August last to Mr. Williams, an under-looker for defendants, and he took them on. They never made any arrangement as to notice. The first work they did was " ribbing " at 9d. a yard. Nothing was said about price in the first instance. After" ribbing" about a week they commenced to dive a " level " which they were paid for. Before they commenced that work Williams said they would be paid 2s. 10d. per yard and is. 2d. per ton. They agreed to the terms and finished the level in about six weeks. They commenced to "drive down brow" on the same terms for a fortnight when they completed the work. The "down brow" was finished on the 3rd November, and the following Thursday they got a wage note produced. They saw Williams, who said when the "down brow" was finished they would have to start on fresh work at another price. They again saw Williams and tried to arrange a price for the new work, but he would not come to their terms. The new work was taking a piece of coal eight or nine yards wide and throwing it up to the level. Williams said they would cease having a yard price, but they were to get Is. 2d. a ton, and he would give them 4s. for every ten tons they got. That was not as much as they got before. He afterwards offered them Is. 6d. a day extra, hut he (witness) and his mate thought it was not enough. Wil4iams said it was a different style of work altogether to that they had been doing. They said they would take their tools away. He said they must not do so, but see Mr. Turner, the manager. They told him they would not do so, as he (Williams) engaged them, and they left. They went to the colliery for their wages, hut Mr. Turner said he would not give them their wages until they had served 14 days' notice. They afterwards got the wages sheet (produced) from the colliery.-Mr. Segar said if Mr. Swift abided by the 14 days' notice, he could not possibly give up his second item of claim.-Cross-examtned by Mr. Swift, witness said tnheer al ceunsthoemd dt on not Williams willaisamnoattoa general m was. A collier could please himself about working at a re- ivteelll thday'e m their Whenrk duced price without 14 days' notice. They did not promise to return to work at the price they had offered them.- Edward Jones confirmed the evidence of Hayes.-John Cross, formerly coll'ery proprietor and now miners' agent, id he would find plaintiffs "down brow" work equal to the le level to serve their notice in, and he said he woul net. said he went with the plaintiffs to Mr. Turner to ask him if When a job was finished, if the parties could not agree, they were not bound to work. Mr. Swift, for the defence, said the plaintiffs worked at n colliery where there were about 1,000 men, and they knew when taken on they were taken on at the same terms as the other men. There wss no special bargain made in any way. The plaintiffs went to the

r colliery and asked if they would give them a job. They were sent to the foreman who took them to a place. Their first job was "ribbing," for which they got Rid. per yard, and is. 2L per ton. The prices at this colliery were 911. per yard and is. 20. per ton for "ribbing," !f men were work- ing at " stret " they got 2s. 10 per ton, and if they were working at " wide " work then the scale price was s. 2d. per ton and 4s. extra for every ten tons. The men entered the colliery upon the ordinary terms prevailing not only at the colliery but all through the district. Having done the " ribbing " the plaintiffs arrived naturally enough at a block of coal. It did not require as much labour to get at that coal as it did in working on the level and the price was reduced accordingly. When the plaintiffs found that the " stret " work was finished they wanted to keep on as they preferred it, and they kicked against doing "breast " work at the colliery prices. Their remedy was to say "Well, we don't like that work, and unless you find us another job at stret ' work we shall give you 14 days' notice." It had been 'suggested that every time a man's job was changed they had a different contract. It was nothing of the kind. Th ei)nly contract was to take them on, and the contract was to do the lawful work of their masters, and to be paid for it at the colliery prices. The plaintiffs having refused to perform their contract they forfeited by the rules of the district the money in hand, and rendered themselves liable to pay damages to their employers.

Thomas Williams, underlooker at the defendants' colliery, said the plaintiffs were turned ever to him by the manager. He did not remember engaging the plaintiffs. They came to him and said he was to find them a place. Nothing passed between them as to prices. He handed the men over to a foreman and told him to set them on. Witness chose the place where they were to work. After the measuring he sat down in the working-place and said, "After to-snorrow do you know the conditions of this working-place." They said, " No, what is it ? " Witness said, " The yard price will be knocked off and you must " breast " the coal oat before you. The allowance is 4s. for every 111 tons you send up." What be told them was in accordance with the usages of the colliery. The plaintiffs alluthd to the extra width, and having to throw the coals up brow, and they asked him if he would allow them day wages. Witness said he could not do that, but as long as the place kept over 8 yards wide he would allow them Is. dd. a day to throw the coals up brow. They said that would not do for them; they would leave; and he said they would have to serve notice. Plaintiffs replied they would not serve notice, and he told them they would not get their money if they took their tools away. He never told the men they would have to start at fresh work when the "Down brow "was finished.

Richard James, fireman, said be set the men to work, nrhen they both sat down and asked the prices all through. He told them the prices before they commenced work. It was the rule at the colliery that the men must give 14 days' notice before they left. Robert Turner, manager of the colliery, said the men came to him for work, but he referred them to the undef- looker. It was the rule for the men to go to the work that was set them. The usage at the colliery was to give 14 days' notice on either side, and if a man did not fulfil his contract he was to forfeit the current fortnight's wages. The defendants estimated the plaintiffs lost ten days work, which, according to their calculation, meant £lO damages sustained through the defendants absenting themselves.

Francis France, certificated manager of the St. Helens Colliery Company, Limited, said he bad over 1,200 bands under him. The custom was that when a man started work he began under the custom in force at the particular colliery. Benjamin B. Glover, colliery proprietor and agent, said it was the custom for the men to be put on fresh work without notice being given. In the St. Helens district if a man left without notice the wages of the previous fortnight were detained, or the money due at the next pay day. Isaac Billing, certificated manager, employed by Mr. Glover, James Baines, manager, John Harrison, under- looker, gave similar evidence. Mr. Swift and Mr. Segar again addressed the jury, and his Honour having summed up the evidence, the jury gave a verdict for the plaintiffs for the amount of wages claimed and also upon the counter claim.

_ The fortnightly meeting of this Authority was held in the Boardroom, at Dutton Workhouse, on Tuesday. Present: —The Rev. Canon Barclay (in" the chair), Rev. J. W. N. Tanner, Messrs. J. W. Ashton, J. Highfield, W. Pickering, J. Weir, H. Lowe, J. Challoner, J. Mclntyre, J. Dubyshire, J. Midwood, J. Smith, aen., J. W. Baguley, W. Wilkinson, Linaker (clerk), and W. H. Linaker (deputy clerk).' FRODSHAM WATER STYPLY. The Frodsham Water Supply Committee reported that they had carefully considered Mr. Bancroft's scheme for supplying water from Five Crosses, and also Mr. Timmins' scheme for a water supply from well at the gas works. Mr. Bancroft proposed to bring the water from Five Crosses by gravitation, the yield being, as ganged by Mr. Bancroft in 1879, 41,910 gallons in 24 hours and estimated to cost 41,902, supplying Church-street, FLin-lane. Main-street, to Vrodshaitt Bfldge, the Quay, Coladen-streeti-Ship-street, and -130t4r-atrest. - Mr. fritinnins 4prApotid- to ,pump, the water, qrakt well and lsette hole at HIS gas tverks to a. reservoir 'alsoVe MOtl4lll Pleasant arid-supply Main-street ts FrOdsham -Bridge; the Qthry, Ship-street, Clurreh-serret, to Police Station, 'Flain-datte, CO cottage-above: 'South ,Bank. Cobden-street and Book-street weed take theit shippty, from • the' nearest pillar'wen to- sich'street. The'yield'of-itater was esti mhtsd at 24,000 gallbris pev4 hours, atid the cost £2,188 75.,6d., in addition to which there would be a payment to the Gas Company for use of well, and the weekly expense for fuel, and engineer wages, and wear and tear of engine. In , neither case was cost of land or way leave for pipes calcu- lated. The first cost of each scheme was practically the same, and considering the annual cost for pumping and water charge in Mr. Timmins' scheme, the Committee were of opinion that Mr. Bancroft's scheme was the most eco- nomical, as there would be but a small annual charge for turning the water on and off at the reservoir, and it would embrace a larger area and yield a greater supply of water than Mr. Timmins' scheme. Mr. ASHTON moved that the report be adopted, and steps taken to carry out Mr. Bancroft's scheme. Rev. J. W. N. TANNER seconded the motion, which was , carried.

THE NEW HEDICAL OFFICER'S QVARTSRLY REPORT. Mr. J. G. BRIDE, medical officer, reported that during the quarter ending 31st December, 1880, the registrar's returns recorded 150 births, and 74 deaths, in the three districts comprised in the Runcorn Union. Of the births 79 were males and 71 females; of the deaths 38 were males and 37 females; 18 were under 5 years of age, 13 of these being under, one year, and 56 were five years and upwards. During the corresponding quarter of last year there were 144 births and 88 deaths. The new medical officer called the attention of thre authority to the low death rate of last year which compared favourably with that of the corresponding quarter of last year there being 13 deaths less: The births were six over the number which occurred during the corresponding period of last year. The district since his appointment had been almost free from zymotic diseases. Typhoid fever ac- counted for one death which occurred in the workhouse. There had been another case, but death did not result. Bronchitis accounted for 13 deaths, and this he attributed to the changeable character of the weatar during the winter. THE HELSBT SEWERAGE SCHEME Mr. MIDWOOD moved that the resolution which the Board came to a month ago, to carry out the scheme for the s-werage of Helaby be rescinded, and that the ratepayer's scheme, which was explained to the Board in the memorial read at the last meeting, be adopted in its stead. Mr. LOWE seconded the motion.

AT. t. Mr. Midwood then laid a plan before the Authority, and explained what.the ratepayers' scheme was. It was con- sidered at some length by the Board, and eventually Mr. Asifrox moved an amendment that the carrying out of the scheme of the Authority be deferred for three months so as to give the owners of property from which the nuisance arose an opportunity of abating the nuisance with- out the intervention of the Authority. Mr. Mchrricus seconded the amendment, which was carried unanimously. Mr. MIDWOOD agreed to withdraw his motion, Mr. CHALtorrEn remarked that the ratepayeri of Helsby were all at sea about the ratepavers' scheme. Mr. Mrovroma protested against Mr. Challoner making rthy such remarks, as the ratepayers were not at sea. Every ratepayer had been seen, and the whole thing explained to them as clear as it could be; and how Mr. Challoner could make such statements he could not Tinderstond. Mr. Crrattoxam : He wants to make it appear that I am speaking untruths. The CHAIRMAN : I did not understand what you said in the face of the memorial which was signed by 123 rate- payers. ' Mr. CrtartolcErt : There are more than 123 ratepayers. What has become of the rest? What do others say? More than one, or two, or three have been to me about it, who had never been asked to sign the memerial, and some who have signed—if they had had the thing properly explained to them—would never have done so. If Mr. Midwood speaks untruths I do not come here to speak untruths. - Mr. Mtnwoort explained that what he said was, be did not know what Mr. Challoiser could say in the face of a ' memorial signed by 123 inhabitants in a little village like Helsby. He did not say that Mr. Challoner had been saying what was not true. The CHAIRMAN thought Mr. Challoner might have heard one or two complaints, bnt forgotten that the memorial had been sieved by 123 ratepayers. Mr. CHALLONER was still of opinion that many rate- payers knew nothing of the scheme. The subject then dropped, and the meeting terminated." div.head: STRANGE ROBBERY BY A T. HELENS Walt! AN.
div.p: STRANGE ROBBERY BY A T. HELENS Walt! AN.
ALLEGED KLEPTOMANIA.

On Monday, at the St. Helens Police Court, before Messrs. W. Pilkington and H. A.- Bright, a respectable-looking woman' named Mary Ann Taylor, residing in Barrow-street, near the Town Hall, was charged with stealing a pair of horns from a beerhouse in Parr, and some merino from a shop kept by a Mr. Shields.—Mr. Johnston said there were eight cases against her, but they would only proceed upon two. The aggregate value of the whole of the property she bad stolen amounted to £7 Bs. 6d. The horn produced had a snuff-box Constructed in the middle.

Ann Jane Allen, barmaid for Peter Jackson, beerhouse keeper in Parr-street, said the horns were safe in the house between four and five o'clock, and she missed them between five and six o'clock. She saw the prisoner in the house at about half-past five, when she had a "small gin." She did not see her go away. P.C. James Lindsay said he found the horns produced in the house of the prisoner, and he took her into custody. At first she pleaded not guilty, but afterwards admitted that she took them.

Jane Shields, wife of William Shields, draper and grocer, said the piece of French merino and cotton was her.hus- band's property, and was worth £1 19s. The merino was stolen from her husband's shop on Monday last, and the cotton was stolen last Saturday three weeks. Thomas C. Kennerley, Church-street, draper, said the satin produced was worth 305., and was stolen from his shop about a week ago. Prisoner: It will be four months ago. Witness: It may be; I missed it a week ago. Herbert Lockland, assistant to Mr. Henry Martin, Church- street, said the ulster produced was worth I9s. 9d., and was stolen from Mr. Martin's shop three or four weeks ago. William Bradbury, an errand boy for Mr. Edward Wood, ironmonger, in Parr-street, said the clock produced. was Mr. Wood's property, and was worth about Ss. t3d. It was safe in the shop at five o'clock last Saturday night. Alice Ashurst, a milliner, working for Miss Murphy, Shaw- street, said the crape produced was worth us. 3d., and was stolen about a fortnight ago.

Margaret Laman. a servant at White 'fart public-house, said the two tablecloths were the property of Mr. George Ripley, and were afolen a few days ago. Richard Rigby, tailor and draper, residing in Oxford- street, said the window curtains produced were his property, which he missed from his shop on Tuesday morning last. He saw the prisoner in the shop a few days prior to Taesday. Mr. Swift said one hardly knew what to say in such a case. The woman had been labouring under some mania. She had borne the character and occupied the position of a respectable woman. She i 4 also respectably connected, her father, who is named Bridge, having been a gamekeeper, but who was now employed at Mr. Pilkington's brickworks. She was married, and had been a great many years- She bad seven children living, the eldest of whom was seventeen ' years old, and the youngest, which she held in her arms, fifteen months, and she was expecting another. Their wor- ships had heard of cases of that kind before in which women , in a certain condition had been affected by mania of this description; and great numbers of women bad been dis- charged from offences of that kind because of that mania. Although the woman had pleaded guilty, be did not want to detract from the legal effect of that plea, but, taking into account all the circumstances, he did not think their wor- ships would think it necessary to send her to prison. It was quite clear she had made no use of the stolen things, with the exception of the window curtains. She had done nothing whatever with the other things, had not turned them into money, and had not secreted them. Mr. Johnston: Yes; half of the merino is gone. Mr. Swift: There is no proof she ever bad it. Prisoner: Oh no, sir; it is just as I got it. Mr. Swift: She has pointed out the things stolen, and stated where she got them from, so that the police had no trouble whatever. She gave them every assistance she could. Mr. W. Pilkington :Where does your husband work?

Prisoner: For'Mr. Webster, sir. Mr. Johnston: She said that it was through poverty she had stolen the goods. They formerly kept a shop, and having a lot of money out she was tempted to do this. Mr. Swift: She lost a lot of money by shopkeeping, but she has not converted this into money. They were found intact. Mr. Bright: Have you anything to support your pre- sumption that she was not in her right mind when she , stole these articles? Has she been guilty of it before? Mr. Swift: No, your worship. The longest date alleged against her is that one--three weeks last Saturday. Mr. Kennerley spoke to last week, but the witness said it was four months. That was only her statement. Everything comes from the 23rd December down to to-day, Mr. W. Pilkington : She does not seem to realise her position. Mr. Swift: That is a very strong proof in support of what I respectfully submitted to you. If your worships would impose a fine instead of sending her to prison the people , would have thfir property back, Mr. W. Pilkington : How have the goods been taken? Mr. Swift: She appears to have gone to the shops for ' gs home, and kept them there. something, taken the thin Mr. W. Pilkington : No attempt to pawn? Mr. Swift: Not at all, sir; it is simply a mania to get possession of the goods. Mr. Johnston: I could have given fuller evidence had she not pleaded guilty. She said in the first inttance that , the horns were in her possession two years ago. Mr. Swift: I don't think that detracts from the truthful- ness of the observation I made a short tithe ago. Mr. W. Pilkington : The question is whether she is in her right mind or not. I don't think she can be. Has there been anything against her before? Mr. Johnston: Never anything, sir. Mr. W. Pilkington : You see we have only the stubborn fact before us that she has taken them. The Bench, after considering their decision, said it was a very serious offence, but they wished to give her the oppor- tunity of paying, and she would therefore be fined £6, or ' £3 in each case, or two months. The money was paid. Mr. Gladstone on Wednesday received a deputation from . his constituents in Midlothian asking him to present a pet tion in favour of legalising marriage with a deceased wife's sister. The Premier informed them that in the present state of of public business it was impossible to give any pledge a English or Scotch business, but he would do all in his power to promote their object.

NEWTON IMPROVEMENT COMMIS- SIONERS, The monthly meeting of thie Board of Commissioners was hild at Newton, Town Hall, on Monday last. Mr. W. Win- ston*, presided,,and there were present (101. McCorquedale, Messrs. J. W. Emmett, J. FAiroloUgh, J, rardey, Foster, Wood, J. HeWoreley _(law-elek), R. Brierley (surveyor), and Dr. Wathies (Medical officer), • . • HIGHWAY, PUBLIC ,WORIS; AND SANITARY 0014MITTEE. ' At a-meeting of the Highways, rublic Works, and -Said- tary.,conimittee, held on tho 20th -December, the committee having again discussed the responsibility for ,the removal of Tomlinson's two children to the Infectious Diseases-Hospital at Warrington, resolved that the same be again considered at a special meeting iof, the Board (in conimittee) on Monday, 13th ITinuary, in the presence of the law 'clerhi and medical officer. Or. Watkins read his report upon the mortality front diarrhea fer the quarter ended 30th September last, en- quired for by the Local Government:Board, and it was re- solved that the clerk forward a copy of the- report to the Local Government Board., . Communicatiees dated 27th November, 1880,, from Messrs. Charlewood. arid Aspden, on hebalf of kr. Williams, New 'Hey Farm, and -from Mr. Stone, of Newton. Park, dated 6th December, 1580, complaining of the pollution of Newton Brook by Messrs. Gillespie and Mason were read. Dr. Watkins, medical officer of health being present, reported Olathe and the surveyor had in- spected Newton brook and were of opinion that the refuse ' from Gillespie and Mation's works contained nothing of such a noxious nature as to be dangerous to the life of cattle., 'The committee :therefotelionsidered the Board was not in a position to interfere in the matter. It Was rescilved that when the medical' officer- certified the necessity for isolating or removing infections patients, Mr. Brierly be authorised to makta arrangement for their removal and acceptance at the 'Warrington Infectious Hospitall • MT: nearer moved, and Mr. Foirenn 'seconded the adop- tion of theminutes, which was carried.. GAS AND WATER COMMITTEE. A meeting of the Gas and Water Committee was held on the 20th alt., when an application was read from Mears. IMcCorquodale and Co. for a 3 in pipe to be Laid from the main in Southviorth toad to their warehouse to supply the gas engine. It was resolved that the same be laid at their cost from Southworth road is private property. A letter was read from Mr. W. Hughes, Holegliton-street, renewing his application for gas meters to his two houses. Resolved that the possession of the meters having been made more secure, the application be acceded to on the understanding that Mr. Hughes provides his own dry meters, and bears the expense of altering the service pipes, as well as all responsi- lity for accidents or damage to any portion of the gas sup- ply. On the motion of the Cnernmew, seconded by Mr. Ex- am, the minutes were passed. ' FINANCE COMMITTEE. - At a meeting of the Finance Committee, held on'the 20th December, accounts amounting to £479 is. Bd. were ex- amined and cheques signed for payment. Mt. Emmen. moved the confirmation of the minutes of this oommittee, • which was seconded by the CHAIRMAN, and carried. - The minutes of the School Attendance Committee, which contained nothing of public interest, were also passed. THE ALLEGED POLUTION OP NEWTON BROOII. TIRi SURVEYOR read the following letter from Mr. Thomas Stone :—" I received a letter from your Board, dated Decem- ber 7th, ' saying that the Sanitary Committee, would take into consideratioh the grievances I complained of against Messrs. Gillespie and Mason, paper makers. A month has now passed since I wrote you, and I have heard nothing of the matter.- Will you be good enough to let me know what has been done by your Board that I may know what steps to take?' Colonel McConiarronarm t The letter will be answered by Mr. Brierley in due course,' by sending a copy of this minute of the Sanitary Committee. Mr. Pliznar asked the Medical Officer how he same to the conclusion there was nothing injurious, and did he make an analysis. Dr. WATKINS : No. The CHAIRMAN asked if it was the opinion of the Board that the matter should remain in abeyance. It was a very serious matter, and there was no question with his mind that it would ultimately result in the Board having to carry their sewage to the Sankey Brook. Mr. Pardey said there was only one :course open to the Board, and that was to send a copy of that minute to Mr. Stone. Colonel MCCORQUODILII said he recollected many years ago, some time after the works were started, there was con- siderable noise by their net boxing in the steam. He called tile attention of Messrs. Gillespie and Mason to that fact, and they very promptly boxed it in and stopped the nuisance. He was not present at the last meting when the subject was brought forward, but he had a little talk with Mr. Gillespie, and he led him to understand that if anything required to be done he (Mr. Gillespie) would have the greatest pleasure in doing it. If the chimney:was;wanted a greater heigbt than now he would not hesitate to raise it; and as regarded purifying the brook, if it required doirfg, and it was in his power to do it, he would only be too glad to de it. Having seen several mills and being connected with several, he (Colonel McCorquoditle) had a little know- ledge of what had been done in the country. It had been found an advantage to paper-makers to have as little pollu- tion as possible. He alluded particularly to Scotland, where the Duke of Buccleuch prosecuted the paper-makers on the river Esk. The Duke prosecuted one or two for some years, but he believed now everything had gone;on satisfactorily, and settled down, because the paper-makers exerted them- selves to do what was necessary; and he felt sure Messrs. Gillespie and Mason were prepared to do the same. Mr. Gillespie did not admit there was' anything wrong at pre- sent, and he did not think there was anything wrong. There was a little noxious smell at times. Dr. WATaram : That has considerably reduced since.: Colonel MCCORCNTODALE said occasionally when the wind was blowing from the west when he opened his ball door the smell was very obnoxious indeed; and he believed silver was damaged to a certain extent by it. He fancied that arose from St. Helens, and a good deal might be laid to Messrs. Gillespie and Masons' charge that possibly belonged to St. Helens. However, he felt sure whatever was wrong, Messrs. Gillespie and dason would put it right. Mr. PARDRY asked whether the proposals or offers made were to be considered sent to that Board, otherwise they could not take notice orthera. If they were to be accepted as proposals from Messrs. Gillespie and Mason to the Board he was very glad. Colonel McCown/oaten explained that he was speaking of a conversation he had with Mr. Gillespie, and that he had ventured to give his experience of other parts of the country, and to say if anything was wrong Messrs. Gillespie and Mason would rectify the matter. Dr. WATEINs said the only thing he had not got consent to was the great question of settling tanks—a vbry exten- sive arrangement of settling tanks. That they looked upon as a question of expense directly between the Board and themselves. The smell had been considerably abated lately by the new process .if taking steam from the rag boilers into the chimney. Colonel MCCOEQUODALE said he was not authorised to, bring any message from Mr. Gillespie. He was merely stating a conversation that took place between them in a railway carriage, and thereby mentioned it to show the desire he had to put matters right supposing they wens found to be wrong; but as before stated he understood the doctor to say there was nothing in connection with the mill coming within the Board's province. Mr. WOOD: IS it not a matter between Mr. Stone and Mr. Gillespie? The CHAIRMAN: If it is a public nuisance it is the duty of this Board as a sanitary authority to see that it is abated, but, acting on information given by the medical officer of health, the committee decided that in the present state of the case it was not at all incumbeet upon the Commissioners to interfere. • The subject then dropped. STATION ACCOMMODATION AT EARLESTOWN. Mr. FAIBCLOIJOR drew attention to the want of station accommodation at Earlestown. Passengers heti to wait there half an hour before the train arrived, and there was nothing to protect them from the weather. He thought if the matter came to the notice of Mr. Shaw they would get the neces- sary accommodation. The 'emulous : I thought they' had built a shed. Mr. FAiRCLOUGH said not on the left band side. ry " on

I meeting of the Warrington Guardians, to come across a heading "Dispute With the Newton Commissioners." The Clerk's letter was read. Mr. Winstanley, a commissioner, who was present at the last meeting, and to his recollection made no objection to the letter being sent, *sa reported, in his capacity of Guardian, to have said "that morally the Newton • Commissioners ' were responsible." lie was also further reported to have said "He had spoken to members of the Newton Board, and.he 'believed they would agree to pay half the charges." When Mr. Birley mentioned this matter at the Sanitary Commiltee, Mr. Winstanley said he ,had been Incorrectly reported. With that of course he had -Rating to de; and be eonld'otily say thatthe Newton pub- lic judged of their representatites by the reports they saw in the newspapers:. His objeotion to Mr. Winstanley's con- duct was that he had in the first place no right to repudiate at a meeting of the'Board of. Guardians what he had virtually ,agreed Mat a Meeting of the Commissioners. In the second !plebe it was ri extremely improper thing M canvass' some members of that Board, and say ' He believed they would pay half.' The Comniissionere eitker owed the account, ,or did not. . The Law Clerk said they were not legally respon- sible, which he took ittniant they did .not °welt. He ob- jected to an offer,'on behalf of the ratepayers, to pay 10s. in the Z; and he dincerely trusted that such'an expression 01 epinidn by thelnembers of the 'Board on this affair,— which he looked -upon ab an insult to the Chairman, to their Clerk, and to his brother Commlasioners;—as would prevent Mr: 'Winstanley, or any one else, practising the same tacties." - • ' 4

The Cumin/AN was exceedingly sorry Mr. BirleY was not preterit thaeday. If he had been her would 'probably have heard something that would have enlightened him upon that subject. At all-events he would have given Mr. Birley his opinion very clearly oh the matter he had referred to. It !was utterly incorrect from beginning to end, for any gentle- 'man who was present at the meeting Mr. Birley referred to must remember that he (the chairritan) contended that the Board were morally responsible, and, if the, Commistioners got out of the payment it would be by a legal quibble. He maintained also that the moral responsibility of supporting those children rested upon this Board. In reference to what I took place at the Board-of Guardians ond the report that , had appeared it was certainly very incorrect. What he did I state was this: The Clerk made nee of some very strong ' I language indeed, and he stopped him. Another member of the Board—whose name he was not going to mention—made use of vary strong expressions indeed with regard to that Board of Commissioners, and he told him he had no right to use such expressions in reference to gentlemen yaw were superior to himself. (Laughter.) But be (Mr. Winstanley) said this: "Now, as there appears to have been a mistake lii this matter, perhaps the best way would be to settle the matter amicably by dividing the expense. Understand me," I said, "clearly. I have rib authority whatever for making such adoffer, but from a conversation or two that I have had witluome of the members, I think it possibly might be agreed to." That *as the sum and substance of _what he said at the Beard. The 'Commissioners must bear in mind he was not there as a Commissioner—he was there as a mem- ber of the Board of Guardians, and had a right to take part in:the discussion and express his opinion. He thought as the matter had reached thus far, it was the Commissioners' bounden, duty to go into the question and inform themselves as to the exact position of the Cage, and he thought they would come to the conclusion that it was a mistake—a very grave mistake—that those children were ever sent to the Workhouse. . Mr. FAIRCLOUGH : I think, Mr. Chairman, it would be well if we were to leave this matter uiatil Mr. Birley is present. The CHAIRMAN: Well, I should be very pleased. I should like him to be present. Mr. FAIRCLOUGH: I think it would—be much more,satis- factory to yourself and Mr. Birley it he was present. The CHAIRMAN: The letter is uncalled for in this way: I gave him this explanation before he wrote thie,letter. Mr. PARDRY said the Chairman had mihiaderstood the letter. Mr. Bide', said, "legally responsible," and the Chair- man used the words, "morally responsible." . The Cnhanmax : There is a yery strong reflection upon me. _ _ _

Mr. RanDnv : Our Law Clerk advises us there is no legal responsibility. Upon that adviee we cannot pay it. The CHAIRMAN: Yes; and in reference to that we have had further information of a very important character, and it was the desire of the committee that the matter should' be gone into in the presence of the Clerk, so that he would hear the evidence that was given before us since. Mr. PARDEY : I ahonld like to ask, was it after the Board met tkat you had your conversation with the members of Board when they suggested we might pdy half? The CHAIRMAN : They suggested nothing of the kind. / suggested that possibly it would be a good way to settle the matter without getting into any litigation if we could each pay half. • Mr, PARDEY: I think you spoke to some members of the Board. . I

The Cluing/1/4x : Well, I did speak to some members of the Board. I had a reason, and I will tell you what it was. There were two phases of the case, as it appeared to me. One was the support of these children in the hospital nnd the other the medical attendance, and I thought we could arrange it if the Guardians would pay for the food and we paid for the other attendance. Mr. PABDEI: I think it is most important that the busi- ness of the Board should be done at the Board's meeting; not that we should pass resolutions of anything, and then afterwards members et the Board should meet and say we are ready to upset the resolution. The CILLIRMAN: If I was of opinion that yea had got into a fix, and that it would lead to litigation and great loss —and I really was of that opinion—l think I had a right to talk in private to members as to the best way of avoid- ing it. Mr. Etintarr ultimately seconded Mr. Fairclough's pro- position, which was carried.

div.head: lIOSPITAL ACCOMMODATION.
div.p: lIOSPITAL ACCOMMODATION.

The SURVEYOR -7;d the following letter, from the Clerk to the Haydock Local Board, on the above subject:—Sir,— Adverting to your letter of the 16th ult., I am instructed to say the members of this Board are quite willing to confer with your Sanitary Committee on the question of hospital accommodation for both townships._
A committee consisting of Messrs.Wmstanley, Fairclough, McCorquodale, and Birley, was appointed to meet the Hoy. dock Local Board. -

div.p: TITS DEATH BATE.

Dr. WATKINS was ve;;lra—pl;y7C.;;;;;- that although 25 per cent. of the deaths in the township had taken place in the two months of November and December the death rate from all causes was only 14.98 on the estimated population. Of course his report would be before the Board at the next monthly meeting. The CHAIRMAN: But the death rate is rather more than the average. Dr. WATKINS said when they had two, sickly mouths as during the last two months of the year, to produce 25 per cent. of the whole he thought it was not .alarming. Mr. PARDSY : ?think 14 very low indeed. Dr. WATKINS said in is report the Board would have two very serious things to weigh. One was the adoption of some means to ascertain the existence of infectieus disease im- mediately on its outbviak, and the other was the provision of a burial ground for Newton—a matterovhich.they could no longer delay. The meeting then terminated.

MEETING OF LIBERALS AT WIDNES. The annual meeting of the members of the Liberal west division of Widnes was held on Tuesday evening, at the Sinam's Cross Board Schools. Mr. HENRY BRUNNER presided, and, in opening the pro- ceedings, said that since they held their last annual gather- ing for the purpose of electing the General Committee, they had passed through a very exciting time. Above all other things, they had had a general election; and they could congratulate themselves upon the victory which the Liberal Party had won throughout the country. They might, per- haps, not be satisfied with the result of that election in their own division of the county of Lancaster. However, as far as Widnes itself was concerned, he was sure they polled every possible man, and nearer three than two to one, as compared with the votes recorded by the Con- servatives. They might also be well pleased that Mr. Ratlabone, who fought such a gallant fight in that con- stituency, had found a place in the present Parliament. (Hear, hear.) The Liberals of that division of Lancaster would have felt very glad if they could have had the honour of returning him to Parliament, but when he was defeated they felt convinced it would not be long befere a con- stituency would be found for him. He was sure they must all feel glad that Mr. Rathbone was in the House of Com- mons during such an important session as the present one was likely to be, as he would be able to assist in the settlement of the various difficult questions likely to come before it. Mr. W. BERRINGTON JONES said that before they pro- ceeded any further with the business of the evening, ho had to propose a vote of thanks to the chairman for the valuable services he had rendered to the Liberal cause during the last twelve months. He could speak from experience as to the hard work Mr. Brunner did during the election. Mr. Jonm TAYLOR had much pleasure in seconding the motion, which was put and carried unanimously. Mr. BRUNNETZ. said he was very proud if anything he had been able to do during the past year had been of service to the Liberal party, and if his services in the office which he held had given satisfaction. For his own part, he wished to thank all those who worked so warmly and heartily with them during the general election. He did not think there was one member of the committee who did not at that particular time show that his heart and soul were in the work. The CHAIRMAN proposed, and Mr. WILLIAMSON seconded a motion, which was passed without dissent, appointing the following as the General Committee for the ensuing year:— Messrs. George Hesketh, E. Loines, T. Robinson, W. Hosker, D. Hirst, J. Bennett, J. Bray, J. Latham, T. Hughes, J. Daynall, J. Powell, T. Seed, G. Saxe, S. Owens, J. Newell, G. Gentles, Dr. O'Keeffe, P. McKinley, Jos. Ander- son, W. B. Jones, W. Sadler, W. Doward, Jas. Morris, B. Brown, T. Sadler, T. Jones, S. B. Stringer, John Pve, J. Egan, T. Elwell, George Newns, Michael Dodd, and W. C. Eccles. The Executive Committee were elected as follows, on the motion of Mr. J. Taylor, seconded by Mr. Dodd:— U. Brunner, T. D. Elwell, Lawrinson John Taylor, F. H. Hinkhurst, J. Williamson, Joseph Anderson, R. Webster, S. Sadler, and W. Sadler. Mr. V. BERRINOTON-JONES moved that Mr. Brunner be elected chairman for the ensuing year. The motion was seconded by Mr. MORRIS, and passed with acclamation. On the proposition of Mr. Joule TAYLOR, seconded by Mr. WILLIAMSON, Mr. T. D. Elwell, journalist, was appointed secretary to the division. Mr. Er..wem. briefly acknowledged the compliment, and the proceedings terminated.
RUNCORN POLICE COURT.
MONDAY.—Before Mr. William Banks (chairman,) and
Mr. Charles Hazlehurst.

Lan AND JEALOUSLY.—TRE GALLANT YOUNG SOLIDER. —Annie Santley, a fair looking and well-dressed young woman, with red hair, was summoned for assaulting Martha Wilding, another young woman. Mr. Lake (Day and Lake) represented the complainant, and said the case was one arising out of jealously. Having briefly detailed the alleged facts, Mr. Lake said there was no vendictive feel- ing against defendant, but they wished the magistrates to bind her over.—Complainant stated that she lived in Halton lane, and on the previous Thursday morning,between eleven and twelve o'clock, she was shaking carpets, when the defen- dant came up to her, used very disgraceful language, struck her twice in the face, and threatened to tear her liver out. She said that if she could not have her rever.ge during the day, she would take it at night time. Alice Clare, about le years of age, stated that defendant struck complainant in the face thrice. In cross-examination, she said she did not hear any one say "if any one is locked up, it will be red "un."—Defendant stated that the complainant had made lime grossly scandalous language about her to a young soldier, who had left Runcorn and gone to Birkenhead. She went to ask the girl about it, when she repeated the statement, and said that her mother, who was a poor widow woman, kept men in the house. She never struck complainant, and the case simply arose out of jealously. Complainant charged her with "wanting the young man, and she did not want him at all." —(Laughter.) She had never had any comfort since "she left the young man off," (laughter,) which eventoccurred about three years ago.—The Chairman said the bench were convinced the defendant bad committed the assault. They could not allow her to take the law into her own hands, and she would have to pay ss. and the costs, 12s. 6d. Defendant paid the money. DarrtutENNEss.—Mary Cawley, and Harry Harrison, a butcher, had each 10s. and 9s. 61. costs, to pty for drunk and disorderly conduct on the lot and 2nd inst. BEGGING.—James O'Brein was sent to gaol 14 day's, with hard labour, on the evidence of P.C. Bassons, for be2glng in Bri ,ge-street, on Saturday eight, after being warned to desist.

div.head: RUNCORN CASHIER IN COURT.
div.p: A RUNCORN CASHIER IN COURT.

Mr. Thomas Done, cashier to the Bridgewater Navigation Company (who has been in their employ some years), was then placed in the dock. Superintendent Williamson said that about a quarter-past nine on Saturday morning the prisoner came into his office and asked to see him. On his going out to him he said he had come to give himself up. He had been the cashier at the Bridgewater Navigation Company's offices at Rnncorn. He had been doirg wrong, and had been drinking. His books were wrong, and be thought it would be the best thing for him to do to come and surrender himself. It was his intention, he further added, to assist the officials to the utmost of hts power to make a full disclosure of his offence. He thought the amount he had embezzled would be about £l3O, as he had been going wrong for the past 12 months, In consequence of prisoner's statement he sent an officer for the Bridgewater Navigation Co.'s agent at Runcorn, Mr. Meadowcroft. That gentleman came to the office and told him they were then auditing and examining the accounts, but, so far, they had not been able to discover any defalcations. He had not seen Mr. Meadowcroft since, and that morning he had wired to the general manager of the company at Minchester, Mr. Collier. He had not yet received a reply. Mr. Meadowcroft had stated that he had not been instructed to prosecute. Prisoner had given himself up on a charge of felony, and he (the Superintendent) had no alternative but to see that the case was thoroughly investigated. It might ultimately become a case in which he might have to com- municate with the Public Prosecutor. He therefore asked that the prisoner might be remanded until Wednesday, in order that in the meantime he might hear from the Naviga- tion Company authorities, and communicate with the Public Pr.osecutor.—The magistrates accordingly remanded the prisoner until Wednesday. He was admitted to bail, him- self in a surety of £5O, and Captain E. Davis and Mr. Henry Coward in sureties of £25 each.
On Wednr.sday the prisoner was again brought up, before Mr. John Brundrit.

Mr. Lake: I appear for the defence of the prisoner. Superintendent ;Williamson haying repeated the evidence he gave on Monday, stated that he had made all possible enquiries in the case, and there did not appear to be any charge against the prisoner. His only course, after having thus laid the facts before the Bench, was to ask them to dis- charge the prisoner, and should anything transpire justify- ieg such a course, he could be reapprehended. Mr. Johnson (Deputy Mag-strates' Clerk): There is no e'ne here to represent the Bridgewater Navigation Co.? The Superintendent: No, nobody at all. I saw Mr. Meadowcroft yesterday, and at that time he said they bad sot found anything against the prisoner. Mr. Z.,' filen you have no evidence to offer against him?

The Superintendent: None whatever. hir. Johnson: Do you wish to say anything on the pri- soner's behalf, Mr. Lake r Mr. Lake: No, sir; what Mr. Williamson has said fully explains why Mr. Done gave himself up. There is really nothing at all against him; and the case is evidently one of delusion, arising from the effects of drink. Mr. Brundrit (to the prisoner): Under the circumstances, there is nothing for me to do but discharge ym. You have brought this trouble upon yourself; whether there is any Cause for it or not, you know best; it is not for me to judge. .at the same time, I may re nark that it is evident you have been addicted to drinking for some jafiel, and that has no doubt been the cause of you giving yourself up to theL police. I bope it will be a warning to you not to get into each trouble in the future. You are discharged. Mr. Done: Thank your worships. Mr. Done awn left the ennet le;th 11 mber of his friends. On Thursday the directors 01 the bank of England raised the rate of discount to 3i per cent. Two German noblemen fought a duel on Tuesday, near kankfort. The challenger shot his opponent dead on the Riot. "Family matters" caused the daplorable encounter.
