div.head: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The usual meeting of the Runcorn Board of Guardians was held at Dutton Workhouse, on Tuesday,the Rev. Canon Barclay presiding. There were also present the Rev. J. W. N. Tanner, Messrs. J. Ashton, T. Norman, G. S. Hazlehurst, J. Chaßoner, J. Righfield, J. Mclntyre, W. Pickering, H. Lowe, J. Weir, J. Midwood, J. Darbyshire, J. W. Baguley, J. Smith, sen., W. Wilkinson, H. Linaker (clerk), and W. H. Linaker (assistant clerk). THE ALLEGED EXTRAVAGANCE AT THE WORKHOUSE : MR. LOWE MAKES A "SELLER EXPLANATION." Mr. Lows said be thought after the report that had gone forth of what he said at the last meeting, he should be allowed to make a fuller explanation of the matter. He did not think he should have received the treatment he did or he certainly should have given a fuller explanation last Board day. He though, he should be allowed to explain more fully. The Caernmax: It is a question that fairly arises out of the minutes. Mr. LOWE proceeded to state that he was putting his horse in the stable when a man came with a tin under his arm. The man was a little bot:aered in opening the door, and when he lowered the tin he saw the potatoes. He met Mr. Norman in the hall, as he thought coming from dinner, and Mr. Norman said, "Now, come, hold your noise, and say nothing about it. You have had some." He said, "You have had beef to yours, I suppose ?" and Mr. Norman re- plied, "Yes, I have." He was not to be hoodwinked by that, and when Mr. Norman saw he was not to be hood- winked, he said he would see Mr. Jones. He (Mr. Lowe) made enquiries whether dinner was provided for Guardians who came early, and he was told it was for the Assess- ment Committee, and nobody said anything about it. He said he came seven or eight miles, and if there was a dinner he knew nothing about it. Mr. Jones came in, and he dis- tinctly denied there had been potatoes boiled. [A Member : For the Guardians or the pony? (Laughter.)] Mr. Jones said they were peelings, but he said they were not; they were potatoes. When he brought the matter before the Board Mrs. Jones was called, and she said at once there had been potatoes boiled. It had gone forth he had made a complaint against the Master, but it was against the man that he made the complaint. Mrs. Jones said there bad been a trap set, but he thought the trap had been set for hitn,The woman, who was called, admitted there were two potatoes and a handful. What could a big woman take in her hand? Then the man Huxley was called. As he (Mr. Lowe) told the Board the man he got as a witness came from Mr. Ben- nett's, and he had no authority to keep him two or three hours. The man Huxley said there were 21- potatoes, and the woman said there were two and a handful. The Chair- man went against him, and Mr. Norman said "hear, hear;" and they tried to make it out he was telling a lie. Would he go there to tell a lie? He thought when they came there , and saw anything going wrong they were to speak about it. (Hear, hear.) He thought Mr. Norman made remarks when he left the room about his (Mr. Lowe's) attendance there. Mr. Norman prided himself on his attendance, but he had formed his opinion as to his attendance. He thought it was irregular to provide dinner for any committee. He had never dined there, and as there were poor people in the parish who could not get a dinner, he thought it wrong for Guar- dians to dine there. In his opinion the man who fed the horse should have been cautioned. But he went out of that room without any caution, and as if he (Mr. Lowe) had been telling a lie. The Chairman did caution Mrs. Jones, but the man went out of the room as if he had done right, and it was made out by Mr. Tanner and Mr Norman that be (the speaker) had told a lie. The CHAIRMAN thought Mr. Lowe was mistaken about that. He did not remember that anyone accused him of stating a lie. It was a question of opinion. Mr. Lowe said there was a dishf nil of potatoes, and the man said there was n. That was a mistake between two persons. Anybody might make a mistake. Mr. LOWE stated that his witness was a man who was loading straw. The other witnesses were paupers, and he would bear all the blame rather than throw it upon the paupers. Mr. WILKINSON thought it was very wrong for any of the members to hold with the paupers. He would take Mr. Lowe's word that what he stated was correct. He was sur- prised that Mr. Tanner and Mr. Norman held with them. Mr. DARBYSIIIIIE did not think anyone doubted Mr. Lowe's word. They brought evidence, and it was against Mr. Lowe. If he had had his witness there to prove— Mr. LOWE : I distinctly told you the man had gone borne. The CHAIRMAN said Mr. Lowe brought a charge and he said the circumstances justified him Cu making it. Then three persons were called, Mrs. Jones, the woman in the kitchen, and the man who fed the horse—and they all agreed that there were two potatoes and a bit. What could they do when there were three persons giving evidence against one ?
Mr. LOWE : But the woman admitted there were two pota- toes and a handful.

Mr. NonataN: No; she never admitted that. There were 2. The CHAIRMAN: Of course; you are quite right. She said she srcaped the cullender out. Mr. MIDWOOD believed every word Mr. Lowe stated. Mr. NORMAN* was Vary pleased that Mr. Lowe had come that day to make such a vicious attack upon all of them by stating they had charged him with telling untruths. No such thing was stated, and what he said to Mr. Lowe in the lobby was certainly a joke. The man was raging, and he came through the door stating " I've found it out! I've found it out! There's horse keeping! I've found it out!" He looked whiter than he did now, and that was bad enough ! But if Mr. Lowe thought he came there for his dinner, thank God he had got plenty of dinner at home ; and if he had not, perhaps he could go to Manley and get one at Mr. Lowe's house. Mr. Lowe would not turn him out, would he? [The CHAIRMAN: I think not]. If be did not know Mr. Norman he would know him before he sat down. He never undertook a public duty without ful- filling it. He would not be like Mr. Lowe, who came once in 12 months. That was not the position for a Guardian to be in. He ought to attend more than twice in 12 months. He thought Mr. Lowe ought to attend there and see the re- lief administered. As to the potatoes, what he said to Mr. Lowe was did he think Mr. Jones kept men in that house to peel potatoes for the horse ? Were these potatoes purposely peeled and boiled, and taken into the stable and given to the horse ? The woman distinctly stated that in shaking the cullender two potatoes fell out, and then she scraped the bottom of the cullender, and that was all that went in that horse's meat. Was it not better to give the horse two pot toes and the scraping of the cullender than to throw them away? Mr. Lown: What are the pigs for ? Mr. Nommx: Do you think anybody would run to the pig stye with two potatoes? He quite agreed with Mrs. Jones if Mr. Lowe would only maintain the position be had taken up that day, attend the meetings of the Board, and attend to the business the same as Mr. Norman and other people did, he would find something more to do than to talk about two potatoes. They were engaged from the time they came there to the time they went away—at least he was. And it was not for the sake of anything he got there. If he could not attend to the business as a gentleman he would never sit as a Guardian. He thought it wrong for Mr. Lowe to have mentioned the matter again. He had better let it

drop. The CHAIRMAN : I must say he is perfectly justified in bringing the thing forward. He thinks he has been charged with a falsehood. Mr. NORMAN : No one did accuse him. The CHAIRMAN: No, but he thinks so. Mr. Lowe said the deputy-clerk told him dinner was provided. Mr. NORMAN: We were here from 10 o'clock until half- past 4 or 5 o'clock. Mr. LowE : Do like the Chairman has done to-day,— bring some sandwiches. The enernwew : That is a reflection upon me for eating them before the Board; only I have no time. Mr. NORmAN : You attend here weekly and then you will do well.
Mr. LOWE: I have not been as well entertained as you, air!

Mr. CHALLONER asked, did any Guardian think it right or reasonable that Mr. Norman or anyone else should be there attending committees from 10 o'clock in the morning until 5 or 6 o'clock at night and get nothing to eat or drink?
—••••• • Mr. Low: That is the law. Mr. CHILLLONER The law wants altering then, and the sooner it is altered the better.
The CHAIRMAN: I think we must go in, gentlemen. THE CHAPLAIN'S SALARY.

The ASSISTANT CLERK read a letter from the Rev. Ed- I ward Marsden, which stated that the stipend of the chaplain of the Workhouse was scarcely sufficient, as the duties had Of late very much increased. More than one third of the stipend was spent for conveyance every Sunday, and he applied for an increase of salary. It was decided that the Clerk write to other Unions to ascertain what they paid their chaplains. THE HOSPITAL ACCOMMODATION. Mr. Dansey, inspector of the Local Government Board, attended the Board with reference to the proposed altera- tions to the infirmary. The Local Government Board had had the plans before them, and they had been considered by their architect. In Mr. Smith's original ieport he objected mainly on the ground that there would be no proper cross ventilation in the wards. Even if the Board spent more money there they could only have accommodation for seven extra beds on one side and seven on the other, making a total of 14; and if ever afterwards it was necessary to ex- tend the hospital it wonld not be done on that side. Suppos- ing their numbers went on increasing no further extension would be sanctioned on the ground that it would com- pletely spoil cross ventilation, and that was the reason why the Local Government Board put the subject before the Guardians as to whether it was worth while spending MOO or £4OO in putting up a building which would be useless. The Local Government Board had bad the amended plans before them and the architect, in his notes, said .the objections to the new fever wards were remedied by Im- proved staircases, but as recarded the other defects, which were more serious, they remained unaltered. It was a ques- tion whether the Local Government Board would consent to the alterations at all. lie had to point Out to the numbers there had increased very much during the last four years. He saw by his reports, which he had sent to the Local Government Board in 1876, the number then in the House was 104. That report was dated June, 1878, and in Decem- ber, 1876, there were 106; in 1877, there were 110; in March 1878 the numbers had gone up to 136; in February, 1879, they had gone up to 154; and last year in June, 1880, they had gone up to 161; 80 that the numbers seemed to have kept on increasing during the last four years. But 161 was not the highest point they reached in 1880. He saw the numbers in March, 1680, were 174 as against 168 now. So

that the Board might take that the numbers had kept on in- cieasing for some years, and they would see by the Master's journal that the parts of the house most full had been the infirmary, and the men side—particularly the able-bodied men and old men. Practically there were no able-bodied men in the house. There were sixteen beds. for old men and fourteen occupiers, 15 for able-bodied rren and 16 occu- piers, for women and children 22 beds and 29 occupiers. If they took the books for the last three or four years they would find the Workhouse had been very full of these par- ticular classes, and the question arose whether it would not be necessary for the Board very shortly to provide further accommodation for those classes. He remembered when he was there with the architect of the Local Government Board a few months ago, the master said he had so many cases he did not know what to do with them, and under that pressure people had to be put in the fever ward as a temporary ar- rangement. Not only was the infirmary becoming full, but the men's side particularly got fuller ever year, and was quite full now. As the Local Government Board pointed out if the Guardians spent £4OO or £5OO in doing alterations which they could not but regard as unsatisfactory. It was I for the Board to consider whether they would I go to a little expense or whether it would be better for them to defer the matter at present with a view to taking the whole matter into can-. sideration and finding out exactly in what classes space was insufficient, and where they needed further accommodation. If the Board built a separate ward hospital the present hos- pital would be mainly available for old infirm men. It was a very large question, and though he did not think the LoPal Government Board would absolutely refuse to allow the Guardians to spend the money they proposed, they would put to the Guardians those facts, and very likely the Guar- dians would be throwing their money away. The CHAIRMAN : Do I understand you the alternative is to erect a separate building? Mr. DANSEY : The Local Government Board architect does not see any other way in which the infirm iry could be ex- tended so as to secure cross ventilation. Mr. NORMAN: This house was built to accommodate 200 inmates. Mr. DANSE'v said that might be, but they could not mix up the classes. Mr. Nonusx thought the Guardians' architect would be able to extend the present buildings so as to secure through ventilation. As to through ventilation, he had his opinion on that subject, and whatever the Local Government Board's architect might say bethought it was not a good thing. He believed it was quite possible for the infirmary to be altered for £2OO or £3OO so as to suit their requirements for 15 years, and he did not think the Local Government Board, if the Guardians made accommodation, had any right to refuse' to sanction it. Mr. DANSEY They are bound to see that the accommoda- tion is proper accommodation, and would not be fulfilling their duty in sanctioning it. Mr. NORMAN: I grant that; but if they give us permission we will see that proper accommodation is made, and you shall inspect it if you like. (Laughter.) Mr. DANSEY said he was bound to take the opinion of the Local Government Board, and if their medical officer and architect said it could not be done in any other way he was bound to take that opinion. Mr. Mcltrrynn I thought there was provision wade for extension. Mr. NORMAN: So there Is; but Mr. Dansey is throwing cold water upon it because their architect says so and so. Mr. DANSEY : I am surprised at you after the able way in which • - argued about the horse.. (Laughter.)
you k. Mr. Lowia
: Mr. Norman likes it all his own 'ay.

The matter was referred to the Visiting Commitiee, and The CILAIRMLN thanked Mr. Dansey for his attendance, remarking that the recommendations would receive every consideration so far as was consistent with the purse of the public, which was just now rather sensitive.

div.head: WIDNES POLICE COURT.
div.p: WIDNES POLICE COURT.

afoxpay.—Before Mr. F. H. Gossage. MISCELLANKOIIS.—Thomas Sexily was fined ss. and costs and John O'Donnell 2s. 6d. and costa, for drunkenness.—A tramp, giving the name of John Pemberton, was sent to gaol seven days, for begging. . TUESDAY.—Before Mr. George Pilkington. BREAKING A MAN'S Jaw AT WIDNES.—Peter Walton was charged with unlawfully wounding and doing grievous bodily harm to one Jeha White. The persons in the case are both chemical labourers, in the employ of Messrs. Sul- livan, Moss Bank. Complainant stated that about one o'clock on the morning of the 31st December, he and the prisoner were working together in the ash shed, and he complained to Walton that he was idling his time. The prisoner said he would not be "gaffered over" by him (White), to which he replied that if Walton made use of that remark again "he would stick his head in the furnace." He also gave Walton a push, when he (witness) turned round to see the foreman about the matter. The prisoner then hit him a blow with his fist on the right cheek, which was of so savage a character, that he became "dazed." He I could not say what took place after, but ultimately they were separated. He afterwards went on with his work, but he was in great pain, and went, away from the works at six in the morning. He went home to bed, and whilst there he found that he could not speak, and had to call attention to his condition by knocking. A doctor was sent for, and Dr. O'Keeffe's assistant came, and was afterwards followed by that gentleman. They examined the man, and found that his jaw was broken.—Dr. O'Keeffe gave evidence as to the serious nature of the complainant's injury, and said it must have been a very severe blow to do such damage.— The statement of the prosecutor was corroborated by John Dare, labourer, and John Hagerty, machine clerk. These witnesses said they saw the assault committed. Dare stated that the prisoner struck complainant five or sixtimes.—P.C. Strickland proved apprehending the prisoner on the after- noon of the Ist instant, and in reply to the charge he stated that the complainant struck him with a shovel, and what he did afterwards was in self defence.—Prisoner, on being charged before the magistrates, said be had nothing to say, and ,he was committed to the Quarter _Sessions for trial.

WEDNESDAY.—Before Mr. W. Earle, and Mr. George Pilkington. A TWENTY SECOND APPEARANCH.—Catherine Matthews was charged with having been drunk and disorderly.— Sergeant Eastham said that about half past eleven on Satur- day night, he found the prisoner in Queen-street, drunk and exceedingly disorderly.—The Inspector said this was the 22nd appearance of the woman, and when last before the Bench, she was sent to gaol for one month, with hard labour. —Prisoner was again sent to prison for one month, with hard labour.—Matthews (to the chairman) : Thank you, sir. THE TOPER'S LlST.—Thomas Burke was fined ss. and costs for drunkenness, in Sutton's-lane, on the let inst.—Another man also named Thomas Burke, who had been convicted before, was fined 15s. and costs, or 14 day's imprisonment.— Patrick Quinn, drunk in Pleasant-street, on the Ist inst., had 7s. 6d. to pay; and Owen Jones, and Mary Rawlinson had each a similar amount and costs to pay for being drunk in Page-lane. Jane Ainsworth had 10s. and costs to pay, or suffer 14 day's imprisonment, for having been drunk in Lugsdale-road. The cases were proved by the Inspector and P.C.'s Pitt and Strickland. THE LAMP BREAKING NUISANCE.—George' Ferbur, youth aged 13, was charged with breaking a street lamp. Mr. Themes Beasley. clerk to the Local Board, appeared to prosecute, and stated that the Board did not wish to press the case against the lad, but they had brought him up in order. that the action taken against him might prove a caution to others. A man named Adams was called, who said that on the 2nd inst. he lighted a lamp at the corner of Irwell and James-streets. In the morning he found it broken, and, hearing that the defendant had done the damage, he summoned him. Defendant pleaded guilty, and was fined 6d. arid 23.6 d. costs. Ttinrr OF A noun; AT Dtrrox.—Emma Craddick, a married woman living at Ditton, was charged, on remand, with stealing a florin from a woman named Mary Swift. The prosecutr;x said she had a florin and nd. in a tea canister on the mantelpiece of her house, and during a visit paid to her by the prisoner, she took something out of it. She and her daughter had occasion to go up stairs, and they left Craddick in the house. As she returned down stairs she WY tim prisoner putting the tin containing the florin back in its place, and examined it, and missed the florin. The prisoner pleaded not guilty. As this was her first offence, she was only fined 10s. and costs, or in default of payment, fourteen days' imprisonment. The money was paid. A WARNING TO Rouorts.—Two young men, named John Lappin and John Mulvey, were charged with having unlaw- fully obstructed the passage of Waterloo-road.—P. C. Ross said that on the 21st inst., about half-past six in the even- ing,he saw the defendants standing on the footpath, and passengers had to leave it in order to pass them. He had cautioned them several times before. Each defendant pleaded guilty, and was fined 2s. 6d. and costs, or seven days' imprisonment.—The magistrates said they hoped the case would be a warning to others. Crummy or; Fula.—John Samuel Lamb was fined ls. and 4s. costs for permitting the chimney of his dwelling. Louse to ke on fire on the 31st ult.—P.C. Moores gave evidence. KEEPING A DOG WITHOUT LICENSE —Samuel Hunt was fined ss. and costs, on the evidence of P.C. Ross, for keeping a dog without license on the 31st ult. THE WOMAN AND THE ROLLING Pipe.—Ellen Kernan was summoned by Emma Smith for assaulting her.—Complain- ant said that about half-past four on the previous Saturday night she went to the defendant's and asked her for some money she owed her. Kernan reached a rolling pin, and told her "to get out." She next took her by the hair and struck her in the mouth.—Two witnesses were called, who gave corroborative evidence, and the defendant was fined ss. and complainant ordered to pay the costs.

Several persons were injured—though only one of them very seriously—in a collision which occurred on Thursday morning at the Kirkgate Station, Wakefield, a passenger train from Goole being run into by a goods engine which was emerging from a siding. - -

• HONOUR GAINED BY A PRESCOT LADY.—We are glad to announce that Miss Quick, of flackley House, Prescot, has been awarded a first-class certificate from Trinity College, London, for pianoforte playing. The examination took place at Birkenhead, and was the first at which Miss Quick had put in an appearance. She pefortned before the examiners Beethoven's Sonata in R, and studies by Stephen Heller. Her numerous pupils and friends will be greatly pleased by the high recognition her ability has received. RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD.

A SCHOOL-AGE CENSUS DECIDED UPON. On Wednesday, the first monthly meeting of the newly- elected School Board was held. The Rev. Canon Barclay presided, and there were also present—The Rev. Father Fennelly, Messrs. John Simpson, Thomas Norman, James Pritchard, Richard Lea, Peter Briscoe, and Rigby (clerk). Mr. RIGBY took the chair pro tern, and after reading the certificate of the returning officer as to the late election, said the first business was to elect a chairman for the ensuing three years. Mr. BRISCOE remarked that three years since, he had the privilege of proposing that Canon Barclay be appointed chairman of the Board, and be had much pleasure in making a similar motion that day. He thought it was unnecessary for him to make any observations upon the able manner in which their late chairman had conducted the business.

Mr. JOHN SIMPSON had much pleasure in seconding the motion, and he remarked that he had no fear of any amend- ment being proposed. The reselution was earned unanimously, and Canon Barclay then took the chair. . .

The'enatirdaN returned thanks for the unanimity with which the motion had been carried, and said he had pleasore in welcoming the new member—Mr. Thomas Norman— amongst them. During the next three years they would have many important matters before them—much more so than had been the case during the past three. One of their duties would be to choose a site for the new school, and in doing so they would have to take care they did not pay any extravagant price for the land, such as would prove a burden upon the ratepayers. They would have to consider whether they should erect a school for the purpose of satis- fying their present wants, or one which would be of suffi- cient capacity to provide for the wants of the town ten or twelve years hence. Of course, if they adopted the latter alternative, it would involve a greater outlay. In conduc- ting the business of the Board, he had no doubt that, judg- ing from the capacities of the gentlemen he saw around him, they would steer clear of the various difficulties they would have to encounter; and of one thing be was very sure, viz., that they started their work with brave hearts and a deter- mination to do their best for the ratepayers. He had now to request them to elect a vice-chairman. Rev, Father FENNELY remarked that three years ago it was his pleasure to propose that Mr. John Simpson should be elected to the position. He was gratified to have the privilege of moving a similar motion that day. Mr. PRITCHARD seconded the motion with much pleasure. All the members knew that Mr. Simpson had been identified with the educational work of the town for a very long period—perhaps a longer time than any of them, with the exception of Canon Barclay. The motion was carried unanimously. Mr. Sliest:lß was very much obliged to them for the un- animity which lead characterised their election, and be could only trust to their kindness, and forbearance in the matter of his natural infirmity of deafness.

A SCHOOL AGE CENSUS RESOLVED UPON. The CLERK read a letter from the Education Department, dated the sth inst., and in reply to one of the 17th Novem- ber, enquiring what proceed iegs had been taken as to the site for the now school in Albert-street.

Mr. PRITCHARD : They are evidently determined not to let us alone. (Laughter.) The CHAntspar said he had received a letter from Mr. James Wilson, contractor, offering to sell the Board land for their new school, at prices ranging from 24. to 3d. per square yard, in Greenway road. # tMr. Pnrrmanu, after some preliminary observations, said he thought that was a proper time to review the position which the Board occupied as to the required accomodation. It was not six years since they took a census of the children of school age:in the town, and came to the decision that they ought to provide accommodation for 400 in some central school. The resolve of the Board was communicated to the Government Inspector, who recommended that a school for 1220 soould be erected in Newtown, and one at Mill brow, for 180. The recommendation was endorsed by the Educa- tion Department. Some five or six months ago, the Board received a Communication frem the department, stating that they had reviewed the correspondence with them as to the deficiency of school accommodation in Runcorn, and asking what steps were being taken for the purpose of providing ac- commodation for 200 children in Newtown. The Board re- plied to the letter, saying that they were negotiating for a site in Albert-street. At their December meeting, he raised the propriety of the course they were adopting, for the reason, that he considered they were falling into the same groove as in former years; and if they did so, he was of opinion that they might almost immediately be asked, by the Education Department to provide accommoda- tion at Mill Brow for 180 children. To be requested to do so, would place the Board in rather a difficult position. He did not see that they were at present in a position to speak definitely as to any land offered to them until they actually knew for what number they would have to erect the school, because if they got a site in Newtown district, they might be compelled to enlarge the school at Mill Brow, or obtain a site there for the 180 children. Since the correspondence of three years ago, the Board were in an altered position, be- cause since that time they had acquired the Mill Brow school, which was used for girls and infants; and he con- sidered it provided ample accommodation for that particular class at Mill Brow. What was, therefore, needed was a school in some central position, so as to meet the require- ments of Newtown, and also sufficiently large to meet the excess of accommodation that would be needed for the boys at Mill Brow. It was a question with him as to whether it would not be wise to re-open the whole Question of accom- modation, as they had at present no proper basis on which to proceed. Of course, since six years ago, when the census was taken, the population of the town had considerably in- creased. Would it not be well to have a new census?

The CHAIRMAN referred to the great increase of popula- tion which had taken place in Dukes-field, and other such places, during the past six years. Mr. NORMAN thought it would be a wise thing to have a new census; and the general feeling of the Board appeared to be in favour of the suggestion of Mr. Pritchard. Mr. PRITCHARD said he would propose that enquiries be made as to vacant sites in the neighbourhood of Newtown ; and steps proceeded with to take a census of the children of school age in the district, so that they might then be in a Position to see what their actual requirements were, and able to give the Education Department accurate information upon the subject. Mr. Bniscon seconded the proposition. Mr. SIMPSON thought it was the duty of the Board, ac- cording to the Act of Parliament, to see that all children on boats registered in Runcorn attended school. The CLERK: It will be time enough, I should think, to do that when the central authority take up the matter. The resolution was passed unanimously, and the Clerk was instructed to write to the Department stating the action which the goard proposed to take before deciding upon any site.

The Chairman, and Messrs. Briscoe, Pritchard, and Nor- man were appointed to visit any sites which were avAlable for a new school, or schools, and report at the next meeting. The proceedings then terminated.

div.head: RUNCORN PARLIAMENTARY DEBATING SKIETY.
div.p: RUNCORN PARLIAMENTARY DEBATING SKIETY.

The heavy snow storm on Tuesday evening did not pre- vent the members from assembling in Bethesda Schoolroom, to hear the Prime Minister wind up the long and interesting debate on Disestablishment. The Speaker arrived soon after eight o'clock looking like Father Christmas, minus his holly bough, an 4 there was a fair attendance of members on both sides of the House. In the stranger's gallery there were several ledies, to whom the description given of the !model house wife in the Scriptures would apply, at least in one particular,--" she was not afraid of the snow." The PROSE MINISTER (Mr. W. Handley),:rose amid the sheers of his gimp°, tars, and said he would,first draw the at- tention of the House to the terms of the resolution of the member for Sandwich :—"That in the opinion of this House the time has arrived for the disestablishment and die- endowment of the Episcopal Church." Honourable gentle- men opposite had looked upon the motion as an attempt to destroy the chui ch. He was sure the hon. member for Sandwich had no such intention. They distinguished be- tween the ecclesiastical or state institution, which was purely temporal, and the Church 15 hich was a Divine insti- tution. If hon. gentlemen opposite wished to assert that the Church was indissolubly bound up with its "beggarly elements,"—endowments and state patronage—then they (the Government) could claim credit for greater faith in the truth and vitality of that Christian truth, without which she could scarcely exist as a power for good. (Applause.) There had been some complaint from the other side at the manner that motion had been brought in. Charges of un- manliness and want of courage had been made, because a private member was allowed to bring it in, and that it was brought] in at the back door. The hon. member for Stoke had gone so far as to state that the member for Sandwich was the Government " warming pan." (Laughter.) He might say that they had no desire to re- dute their supporters to the level of "dumb driven cattle," and the motion being brought in, true to the instincts of the Liberal party, which, bad ever been on the side of civil and re- ligious liberty, they could not withhold their consent from its general principles. (Cheers.) The question of tithes had of necessity been often mentioned during the debate, and the right hon. member for Birkenhead had triumphantly asked where was the Act of Parliament conveying those tithes to the Church? and if it could be produced he was willing to admit that the Church was a State made institu- tion. One of his own supprwters—the member for Notting- ham—had supplied the answer when he said "Long before statutes were made, tithes were paid." It was often easier to raise a ghost than to lay one. He himself would ask, "Where was the Act of Parliament originating our code civil jurisdiction? The argument might be stated thus— If it could be proved that the State endowed the Church as a national institution, then it must be a creature of the State, and it could be dealt with by the State. That it was connected with the State in that sense was proved by the fact that as an ecclesiastical institution it had always been under the control of Parliament, both as regards doctrine and ritual. There was scarcely a reign when there had not been legislation for it, and always on the assumption that it was a national institution. The officers of the Church had been the servants of the State for its moral and religious work, as other persons had been for its legal and administrative acts. History informed them • that the clergy were originally charged with the duty and expense of relieving the.poot, educating the people and attending to their religious duties, the expense of which was borne by the endowments and other property given them for that purpose. Even at the present time bishops were simply the State's ecclesiastical servants, for the State appointed them and their dutlea, which waa acknowledged

RUNCORN AND 111—A NCII EST ER TIDAL NAVIO4 TION, The proposal to donstruat a tidal navigation from Run- corn to Manchester is just now attracting a considerable amount of attention. At the last meeting of the Salford Council, Mr. J. E. Middlehurst moved the following resolu- tion :—" That the Government be requested by this Council to appoint special commissioners for the purpose of taking evidence and considering the desirableness of widening and deepening the bed of the Irwell between this borough and Runcorn, in its connection with the river Mersey, so as to admit vessels of moderate tonnage direct from the shipper to the Port of Salford,' to discharge the cargoes, and thus save the consequent delay and xpense itridental to un- shipping at Liverpool or Runcorn. By reason of the Irwell being made a tidal stream, the frequent disastrous floods in the low-lying districts of that river, with proper embank- ments, would then be a thing of the past. The river would also be cleansed, docks, warehouses, and mills would spring up on its banks, the land abutting upon its course would be considerably enhanced in value, and the expense of carrying the scheme, if divided amongst the various boroughs, town- ships, and hamlets benefited, would amount to a less sum than is now expended in dispesing, of the sewage of the various districts." As, however, the subject did not come up for discussion until the latter end of the meeting, at the request of the Mayor the motion was postponed until the next meeting, and as it is one which is of immense im- portance to the whole of the population on the banks of the Mersey and the Irwell, the result of the discussion will be looked for with interest. Mr. Midlehurst says that he does not propose to ask the corporation to expend a farthing, I but simply—as the local authority having charge of a large area through which the treacherons Irwell flows, hav- ing property within the flood line in the borough of Salford of over £lOO,OOO annual value—to ask Parliament to ap- point peilroo,orei.inners who would collect important evidence and report upon the whole scheme. The cost could be secured upon the "the security of the various dis- tricts thus improved," the repayment to extend over 50 years. In the meantime the revenue from dues alone it is estimated would more than repay the outlay. The im- portance of such a great undertaking as this cannot be ever estimated, for, if in this age of gigantic enterprises, the Mersey and Irwell were made into a proper tidal and deep navigable river, the benefits that would be conferred would be very great. There cannot be a doubt that in that case a class of steamers would be built especially for the pur- pose of bringing freights right through from Chicago and other lake towns in America to Manchester, without trans- shipping goods either at New York or at Liverpool as at present. The cost of freight would thus be materially re- duced and live cattle would then be brought direct, whilst fresh meat, deer, game, and butter could be imported in refrigerators from America to Manchester in a fortnight. The proposal of Mr. Hamilton Fulton, Mem. Inst. C.E., for the construction of a tidal navigation from Runcorn to Manchester, is a plan which consists of a tidal navigation unencumbered with locks, similar to that of the river Clyde at Glasgow, and not of a canal as often referred to, with which is usually associated the presence of locks and other appendages. Mr. Fulton's proposed tidal navigation will be provided with a rise or range of spring tides at the Salford basin or terminus of 12 feet, and at neap tides of 10 feet and an average navigable depth at high water of 28 feet, so that the steamers of 3,000 or 4.000 tons, as at Glasgow, will be able to navigate the new channel. It may be mentioned that in the case of Glasgow the rise or range at high water spring tides is only 19 feet, and an average navigable depth at high water of 24 feet; so that the Salford basin, embracing art area of 80 acres, and the navigation generally would have the important advantage of four feet more depth than Glasgow. The improvement of the "'revel' and Mersey would be effected entirely by the strengthening, widening, and deepening of the present circuitous courses of those rivers. The upland flood waters at and above Manchester and Salford would thereby have a free and unimpeded exit to sea, and so prevent the seriously injurious accumu- lation as at present at Lower Broughton, the "lake district " of Salford, and elsewhere, and so put an end to all inundations. Glasgow in former times, before the execution of the river improvements, was subject to floods in its low- lying parts, as is at present the case in Manchester and Salford. These improvements of the Clyde, however, have entirely obviated this great nuisance. By these means, easy and simple in themselves, it is conceived that the Mersey and Irwell may be improved to the extent above referred to. The navigable facilities thus secured, combined with the mineral resources of the district, would greatly increase the demand for machinery and engineering work of all kinds, and doubtless make the banks of the navigation the seat of one of the largest shipbuilding trades in tke wrrld, and would result in the production of great com- mercial success, and perhaps contribute more to the indi- vidual prosperity of Manchester and Salford than has ever been attained by any similar river improvement. It is a question of great national importance, and its accomplish- ment would confer immense benefits, not only in the district through which the navigation would pass, but on the world at large. We have inspected a model of the proposed basin at Salford, which is intended to be a mile and a half long, giving three miles of quay accommodation. If this scheme is carried out, then we shall see steamers both for passengers and cargo plying on the new tidal stream, which would certainly be a new feature in the district. It is argued that what has been accomplished on the Clyde can be done on the Mersey, and we understand that several en- gineers say the scheme can be successfully carried out, that there are no engineering difficulties in the way, and that it would pay a private company to obtain parliamentary powers to proceed with the nndertaking. It is therefore evident that the proposal is worthy of serious consideration at the hands of those local authorities that would be likely to be affected thereby. Mr. Fulton's scheme provides that the depth of water at low.tide at the Manchester end, where it is proposed to con- struct a-basin, would be 22 feet, which would be sufficient to allow the largest vessels using the navigation to float at dead low water of ordinary spring tides. From the Man- chester end to the sea the minimum depth at high water spring tides would be 28 feet, or 4 feet more than in the Clyde navigation up to Glasgow. At low water spring tides the minimum depth of the channel would be 12 feet, or about two feet more water than exists at low water on the bar in the Queen's Channel at the mouth, of the Mersey, so that as scan as a vessel en the flood tide had sufficient depth to cross the bar, she could reach Man- chester probably somewhat later than she could obtain admission into the docks at Liverpool. It might not be out of place to draw attention to the fact that the width of the river Clyde Tl.hBr dids4o,tie N enotst, exceedwhere ftth efts ofp proposed se d Irwellto ibmelmowediGatl construct the intended basin. Means would be taken to pre- serve the existing wharf accommodation at Warrington with a greatly increased depth, so that vessels of a larger class could reach and lie afloat there. Facilities also would be afforded for the construction of docks if thought ex- pedient,

It consisted of 15 town- ships and of more than 20,000 acres, the tithe from which produced nearly £2,000 per annum. Was that sum being expended as it was originally intended? By whom were the duties appertaining to the revenues being performed? Net by the Rector, who was a layman. Sir R. Brooke, he, or those who preceded him were freed from so doing by legal enactment, though allowed to receive the revenues. Would their worthy Vicar (Canon Barclay) be better or worse off if the Church were disestablished ? He left it to their common sense to supply the answer. In conclusion, the Premier said: From what has been said, it must be ad- mitted that a continuous and present control has been exercised by the State over the Church, and that it would be no legal injustice to disestablish and disendow the Church, and to employ the revenues more in harmony with their original purpose. But the Government are not desirous of dealing with the question until the opinion of the nation warrants its being done with general consent. I therefore appeal to the hon. member for Sandwich to withdraw his motion. (Oh! oh! from the Opposition.) But whenever it happens—and happen it will—l am sanguine enough to be- lieve that the Church will not suffer as a power for good • but, from the firm hold it has on the affections of the people, it will be able to cope with the evils within itself which we all deplore, and be more able to do earnest Christian work in our land. (Cheers.) The hon. member for SANDWICH asked leave to withdraw the motion, which was accordingly given. The House went into Committee on the Ballot Act Amendment Bill, and the second clause was passed with a few amendments, all of a verbal character, which did not affect the principle of the Bill, The House then adjourned.
GAS AND WATER COMMITTEE.

The minutes of this committee approved of accounts amounting to £1,120 ss. 7d. for gas account, and £1,428 on water account, the latter including £750 to Messrs. Collin and Son on account of contract for Netherley buildings. Recommended that Mr. J. J. Marr's offer to provide, fix, and maintain five sets of telephone instruments, viz., at the Gas Works, Alforde-street offices, Pex Hill, Stocks-well, and Netherley, at an annual rate of £32, payable quarterly, and terminable at a qnarter's notice from either side be accepted. A further correspondence with the architect and contracters for the Netherley building was read, and the Engineer re- porting that very little progress has been made during the past month. Instructions were given to the Law Clerk to repeat the notice as to penalties, and to inform the architect that the committee, understanding that actual measurement of the work has been made, will only honour his further certificate under protest; also, to ascertain from him whether the accrued penalties have been taken into account, and to point out that only £550 (of the 80 per cent.) of the con- tract amount remains to be paid; instructions being also given to the Engineer to call on the architect and arrange for the Clerk of the Works to be supplied with a blank copy of the bill of quantities and the detail tracings required, and to the Law Clerk to enquire if the contractors have insured the kildings against fire. The re-arranged plan of the Sheffield and Midland Railway Company's branch railway had been approved of, on certain detailed conditions. The report of counsel's opinion (Mr. Wells) as to the charges which could be made to the consumers of water at Ditton was laid before the Committee. The chief clause in the "opinion" was as under:—" I am of opinion that the Board are entitled to make a higher charge in Ditton than in Widnes ref Water supplied by measure, or for other than domestic purposes (as well as for domestic purposes), pro- vided the excess charge is necessary in order to secure the profit of ten per cent, referred to in Section 59 of the Act of 1867, but not otherwise. Ditton is, by Section 5, within the limits of compulsory supply, and although the Act does not, in so many words, say that the Board may be com- pelled to afford a supply for other than domestic purposes, yet by the wording of Section 59 and 64, that result is, in my opinion, brought about. I am, therefore of opinion that, subject to the prior requirements of Widnes itself, under Section 61, and of domestic purposes generally, under Section 64, the people in Ditton are entitled to compel a supply for other than domestic purposes. That being so, the only differential rate which, in my opinion, Ditton can be lawfully subjected to, is that introduced in the securing of the 10 per cent, under section 59. Section 62 giving power to agree, and section 84, which provides that the rate for water, ether than for domestic purposes, shall be an agreed rate, are, in my opinion overridden by and are subject to the proviso in section 59." The committee had also resolved that the offer of Mr. Timmins to purchase the old purifiers and gearing at the gas yard, for £6O, be accepted, he find- ing all labour and tackle required to remove them. Mr. GOSSAGE moved the adoption of the minutes. He suggested that the dispute with the contractor for the Netherley buildings should be again referred back. Mr. CARLILE seconded:the motion ; and a brief discussion followed which was not of much public interest; and the minutes were approved.

div.head: HIGHWAY
div.p: HIGHWAY
-A BRIDGE DESTROYED.

The minutes of the Highway, Building and Street Com- mittee contained some correspondence with Mr. Gregson, the landowner, and his surveyors, as to the reconstruction of the bridge over the brook on the line of footpath from Albert- road to Warrington-road, which had fallen down (the land- lord disputing his liability to rebuild), the matter was re- forrod to kb° Iloara by tho oommittoo. _

Mr. BARROW moved the adoption of the minutes, and called attention to a bill for five guineas from Mr. Allcard. Mr. MATTHEWS seconded the proposition. Mr. CARLILE referred to the washing away of the bridge connected with some property of Mr. Gregson's. He said he should like to know how it was that three months had elapsed since the bridge was washed away and yet nothing had been done to replace it? A great many workmen were formerly in the habit of passing over the structure as they went to Messrs. Sullivans and Pilkington's works, and numerous children used to go that way with their fathers' dinners.

The LAW CLERK read several communications which had passed between the committee and Mr. Gregson in reference to the matter, in which that gentleman denied his liability to repair the. bridge. It appeared to be a question as to whether the landowner or the township authorities were liable.

Mr. BARROW: It has been repaired ft one time immemorial by the tenant or landlord, I know not which. ElMr. WELLS But we have no power to do it. Mr. BARROW (warmly): Then leave it as it is. We have thrown money enough away. The CHAIRMAN : But here are a large number of rate- payers suffering this inconvenience, and the gentleman who owns the property says, "Prove my liability, and I will pay for the work being done." Mr. BARROW: We are just in a similar position in regard to a footpath between Farnworth and Bold. He had heard Mr. Carlile was interested in the property. Mr. CARLILE protested against the insinuation thrown out by Mr. Barrow, and said he was not interested in the pro- perty in the least. Certainly he had got some land in the neighbourhood, but it was not within 300 yards of the bridge. Mr. BARROW: I heard so. Mr. CARLILE : Mr. Barrow should be careful before he makes insinuations of this kind. It was ultimately proposed by Mr. CARLILE. and seconded by the CHAIRMAN, that the committee be instructed to erect a bridge simply sufficient for foot passengers, pending the settlement of the question as to who was liable to do the work.

Mr. BARROW moved an amendment to the effect tdat the Law Clerk should write to Mr. Gregson, or the person responsible for the doing of the work, telling him that un- less it was carried out at once he would be proceeded against.

-- Mr. HEYES seconded the amendment, which only received three votes, and the original motion was carried. Mr. GAS/KELL : Do we incur liability by doing the work? Mr. BARROW: Of course we do. The CHAIRMAN. I now move that the Law Clerk be in- structed to write to Mr. Gregson, saying that the Board have decided to adopt his suggestion and to repair the bridge sufficiently to make a footpath; but that the work will only be done under protest, and pending the settlement of the question of liability tc carry it out. Mr. CARLILE seconded the proposition. Mr. BARROW: Aye, spend the money, and you will never get it back. The resolution was passed. Dr. O'KEEFFE wished to know if any member had in- structed Mr. Allcard to do certain work which gave him authority to send in a bill to the Board, such as that men- tioned by Mr. Barrow. He also enquired whether the amounts of £1.6 13s. 4d. to Mr. Wallace Copland for some work in connection with preparing the plans, and one of £lB 15s. to a Manchester firm for mounting and binding the plans, had been sanctioned by the committee. Mr. Bannovr 1 cannot answer your questions, Dr. Olcooffe, any further than by saying that I objected to each of those items when they were brought before the committee. Dr. OICEEFFE : Who have to pay for them? BARROW: All the answer you can get is the Highway Committee ; but what I wish to know is, is it right they should pay for them? The CHAIRMAN said two copies of the plans had been bound for the use of the office, and the others had been bound for private firms, who would pay for the work. Until the payment was made the account was very properly put down to the Highway Committee, or, in other words, it would, for the present, come out of the general district rate. . -

Mr. BARROW asked a further question on the matter, on which Mr. Carlile drew the attention of the Board to the fact that that gentleman had initialed the acCenntsp.ana they would have to be passed. (Laughter.) Dr. O'KEEFTE : Mr. Chairman, I am satisfied. No answer was returned as to Mr. Allcard's charges: The motion for the adoption of the committee's minutes was then passed.

• • - AO- R. • ESTABLISHMENT, DOG and WINE LICENCES.— The Commissioners of Inland Revenue remind those who keep Carriages, or Male Servants, or who use Armorial Bearings, that their Licences must be renewed in the month of January. Dog Licences must be renewed at the same time, and when- ever any additional Dog is kept ti Licence must be immediately obtained. Earmers and shepherds may obtain exemptions for Dogs kept and used solely for tending sheep or cattle on a farm, but a declaration that the dogs are so used must be made to the Supervisor of Excise for the district. Licences or exemptions are not transferable from one person ' to another. The penalty for keeping a dog without licence or exemption is £5. TAXING ORDERS TOR WINE, Ac.—The Commissioners also give notice that no person may solicit, take, or receive any order tor wine or spirits unless he holds a licence for that pur- pose or is the bona fide traveller for a firm duly licenced in the United Kingdom. The penalty for so acting without licence is £lOO. When the residence of the offender is not known, or is out of the United Kingdom, the summons will be left at the house or place where the offence was committed. London, let January, 1881.

HESHIRE CHAMBER OF AGRICULTURE.—LOCAL TAXATION.—A MEETING of MEMBERS will be held at the CREWE ARMS HOTEL, CREWE, on WEDNESDAY, the 19th instant, for the discussion of above subject when Iffiaos CRAIGIE, Secretary of the Central Camber of Agriculture, will attend and deliver an address. Chair will be taken at Two o'clock. THOMAS RIGBY, Secretary. January 11, 1881.

ji wounded. The Tnrcomans left hundreds of dead in front of the works. It was deemed advisable l,y; General Scobeleff to strengthen the force in the advanced works. AFGHANISTAN. Telegrams from Ganda har state that great excitement pre- vails in that city in consequence of the announcement in the Queen's Speech that the British troops are about to be withdrawn. PERSIA. Tlis Persian report that General Scobeleff had been de- feated at Geok Tepe must now be regarded as unfounded. An official report published in St. Petersburg from the General 'states that he has invested the Turcoman strong- hold on three sides with 8,000 men and 55 guns, and that he hopes to comp?l the enemy to surrender without being forced to szorm their works, an operation which must necessarily involve great loss of life. . FRANCE. The victory of the Republican party in the Paris munici- pal elections is not denied even bv MM. Rochefort and Clemenceau. A few days ago the Paris correspondent of the Times fell into a state of panic at seeing the immense attendance at the funeral of Blanqui, and he solemnly warned the Government that the Communists were a highly formidable power. To-day he remarks that "the mistake of the alarmists, who took the mere spectators for Communists, is now evident." THE THREE EMPERORS' ALLIANCE. The Vienna Presse, following the lead of the Agenee Rune, states that the recent friendly overtures to the Emperor of Austria from the Czar have resulted in the re- establishment of the Three Emperors' Alliance. This alliance was supposed to have been cast to the winds by the famous Austro-German compact. If the 'Presse is well informed, we shall shortly hear some grandiloquent lauda- tion of the Alliance ass "guarantee of the peace of Europe," —which would mean that the three Emperors were plann- ing some scheme of aggrandisement of Austria and Russia in the East, to the exclusion of British, French, and Italian interests.

MAKIN SON AND WILCOCK, in returning their sincere thanks to their numerous patrons and the public generally for the very kind and liberal support they have hitherto received, hope, by strist attention to the interests of their clients, and the prompt and faithful discharge of their duties, to continue to merit the same the more so, as they are able to offer ad- vantages not generally enjoyed by those engaged In the same business, Mr. Makinson having had from early youth practical experience of the English Timber, Stone and Building Trades, and of Farming in all its branches, being at the present time a farmer himself on a large scale; and, in addition, having served his apprenticeship to the ENGINEERING and MlLtwithawr busi- ness, besides having had, during the last TEN years, consider- able practice he Valuing and Selling Colliery, Quarry, and other Machinery and Working Plant, Growing and Fallen Timber, Farming Stocks, Growing and Gathered Produce, Stocks-in- Trade, Household Furniture Innkeepers' Effects, Houses, Buildings, Landed Estates and Property generally, and also in cases Involving Damage and Trespass. Mr. WILCOCK, also, has had the advantage of being brought up to Farming, together with that of having served an appren- ticeship to an eminent Veterinary Surgeon, combined with the expexience he has had since his connection with this firm, enables him to give judicious and valuable advice in all cases in which he may be consulted. In conclusion, M. and W. beg their friends and the public generally to note that they have a trustworthy and efficient staff of assistants in their employ, who have been carefully trained to watch over the interests of those who favour the firm with their patronage whilst last, but not least, their system of advertising, and the facilities they possess of ensuring an extensive circulation, enable them to offer the utmost pos- sible publicity to any sales entrusted to their management. ,

BRANCH & LEETE, On MONDAY, the 24th instant, and several following days (Saturdays and Sundays excepted), at eleven o'clock each day, on the premises, Canning-place, Liverpool (opposite the General P.:Malice), the most valuable, varied, and beautiful STOOK of PORCELAIN and OPAQUE CHINA. DIAMOND-CUT and ENGRAVBD GLASS, and exquisite decorative .objecse and articles of the rarest quality and the highest value both for purity of Work- manship and novelty of style, Mending many masterpieces of men eminently gifted as painters on china, who have won admiration in many exhibitions. The singular extent and vatiety of the goods comprised in this sale excludes the possibility of giving prominence in. the spsoo at command within the limits of an advertisement of the charmingly varied and the remarkable excellence of the stock, forming one of the largest atcumulations offered in the pro- vineei for some years. In this section there will be over one hundred table services, which cannot be described by any lengthened notice. -Their quality, elaborate finish, and the agencies employed in the pro- cesses of production show at once the high reputation of Messrs Davenport They comprehend clear china and stone, suitable for large and small numbers of persons. The patterns are thoroughly original in eonception, and of much elegsnce, covered with a profusion of gold, and in brilliant colours, known in the trade as the Japan, the Oriental, the Wellington, the Brilnewick, the Victoria, Ac. The Dessert Services are in the main uncommonly handsome, and in some instancss of almost matchlesscharacter, the skill of the exquisite hand-painting commanding the highest admira- tion for harmonious and artistic colouring. In addition to the British manufactures, there are some choice representative pieces of Dresden, Berlin, Sevres, Hungarian, Bohemian, and other European factories, that can- not be noticed in this bt lei outline, which only does the mag- nificent stock but scanty justice.
